school-c8-english.title: Class 8 English
school-c8-english.description: Class 8 English — every Honeydew chapter with its poem (original summaries, themes, vocabulary, writing), selected supplementary-reader stories, grammar, writing skills and Revision & Practice. Chapters follow the rationalised NCERT Class 8 textbooks (2023–24 editions onward). NCERT has been introducing new Class 8 books from 2025–26; if your school uses those, chapter names and order differ, but most topics here still apply. Independent material, not affiliated with NCERT or any board.

courses.title: Ch 1 · The Best Christmas Present in the World (with poem: The Ant and the Cricket)
courses.summary: A letter hidden in an old desk tells of the 1914 Christmas truce, when enemy soldiers met as friends for a day; and a fable-poem about planning ahead. Comprehension, themes, vocabulary and writing practice.
outcomes: Learners can retell the story in sequence and explain its historical background
Learners can discuss themes of peace, love and the futility of war
Learners can explain the moral of 'The Ant and the Cricket'
Learners can use new vocabulary and write a letter or diary entry

scenes.text: The narrator buys an old roll-top desk from a junk shop and repairs it.
In a hidden drawer he finds a small tin box with a letter dated December 1914.
It is from a soldier named Jim to his wife Connie.

steps.title: Plot in brief (original retelling)
steps.body:
- The narrator restores a damaged desk and discovers a secret drawer containing a letter.
- The letter, written by **Jim Macpherson** to his wife **Connie**, describes Christmas Day 1914 on the battlefield in France during the First World War.
- That morning, soldiers on both sides — British and German — came out of their trenches, shook hands, shared food and drink, talked about their families, and even played a game of football. A German officer, **Hans Wolf**, spoke with Jim about home and about how the war could end if people chose peace.
- Jim hopes to return home to Connie soon.
- Moved, the narrator travels to find Connie. He finds her, very old, in a nursing home. She thinks he is Jim come back from the war — and says it is the **best Christmas present in the world**. The narrator lets her believe it.

steps.title: Historical background
steps.body: The **Christmas truce of 1914** really happened: in places along the Western Front, soldiers stopped fighting informally for Christmas. It reminds readers that ordinary soldiers on both sides were human beings with the same hopes.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *Why did Connie think the narrator was Jim?* → She was very old and had waited all her life for Jim; seeing a man holding Jim's letter in his hand, she believed her husband had returned.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the narrator wrote the letter (Jim did).
- Saying the truce ended the war — it lasted only a short time.

activity.prompt: Put the events of the story in order
items: The narrator buys and repairs an old desk
He finds a secret drawer with a letter
The letter describes the Christmas truce of 1914
He travels to find Connie
Connie believes he is Jim — 'the best Christmas present in the world'

quiz.q: Where did the narrator find the letter?
options: In a secret drawer of an old desk
quiz.why: In the story, the narrator found the letter in a secret drawer of an old desk, bought from a junk shop.
The letter was written by Jim Macpherson to his wife Connie.

options: Shook hands, shared food and played football
quiz.why: During the Christmas truce, soldiers of both sides stopped fighting. They shook hands, shared food and played football.
The story is set in the First World War, with the Christmas truce of 1914.

quiz.q: Why is it 'the best Christmas present'?
options: Connie believes her husband has finally come home
She gets a letter from Hans
quiz.why: Old Connie believes her husband Jim has finally come home. This is the best Christmas present for her.

story.title: Enemies for a day? Friends for a day

scenes.text: Two soldiers who were shooting at each other on Christmas Eve play football together the next day.
'If we can be friends today, why fight tomorrow?'
The story asks us that question.

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- **Futility of war:** ordinary soldiers have no quarrel with each other; war is decided by others.
- **Peace and shared humanity:** given a chance, people find common ground (families, food, games).
- **Love and waiting:** Connie's lifelong love and hope.
- **Compassion:** the narrator chooses kindness instead of correcting a confused old woman.

steps.title: Characters
steps.body:
- **Narrator:** curious, sensitive, kind.
- **Jim:** honest, hopeful, longs for peace and home.
- **Hans Wolf:** friendly German officer who shares Jim's wish for peace.
- **Connie:** devoted wife who never stopped waiting.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *What message about war does the story give?* → War separates people who have no hatred for each other; the truce shows that peace is possible when people see their enemies as human beings.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Writing only the plot when a question asks about a theme — always link events to ideas.

activity.prompt: Match the character to the description
pairs: Soldier who writes about the truce
Elderly wife who waited for decades
German officer who talks of peace
Restores the desk and finds Connie

quiz.q: A main theme of the story:
options: The futility of war and shared humanity
quiz.why: The story shows how pointless war is, and that soldiers on both sides are fellow human beings.

quiz.q: The narrator's decision not to correct Connie shows:
quiz.why: The narrator did not correct Connie, because he did not want to hurt her. This shows compassion.
Hans Wolf was a German soldier, an officer, whom Jim met during the truce.

options: Had no personal hatred for each other
quiz.why: The truce suggests that ordinary soldiers had no personal hatred for one another. They fought because they were ordered to.

quiz.q: The story's tone at the end is:
quiz.why: The ending is touching and bittersweet. Connie is happy, but the reader knows the truth.

lessons.title: Poem: The Ant and the Cricket

scenes.text: A cricket sings all summer, never storing food.
Winter comes; hungry, he knocks at the ant's door.
The ant asks what he did all summer…

steps.title: Summary (original)
steps.body:
This poem is a retelling of a fable usually credited to **Aesop**. A carefree young cricket spends the warm months singing. When winter arrives he has nothing to eat, and he asks a thrifty ant for food and shelter, promising to repay. The ant asks what he did in summer; the cricket says he sang day and night. The ant replies, in effect, that since he sang all summer he can now dance the winter away — and refuses to lend.

**Moral:** plan and save for the future; enjoyment without preparation leads to hardship. Some readers also discuss whether the ant could have shown more kindness.

steps.title: Poetic devices
steps.body:
- **Fable/allegory:** animals stand for types of people (carefree vs hard-working).
- **Rhyme scheme:** regular rhyming couplets/quatrains (check your textbook).
- **Irony:** the ant's reply turns the cricket's 'singing' into 'dancing' through the cold.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *What lesson does the cricket learn?* → That one must work and save during good times to survive difficult times.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that the ant helps the cricket (it refuses).
- Missing the irony in 'dance'.

statements.s: The cricket saved food all summer.
The ant refuses to lend food.
statements.why: He says the cricket can dance the winter away.

statements.s: The poem is based on a fable.
The moral is to plan for the future.

quiz.why: In the poem the cricket spent the summer singing, not preparing for winter.
The ant stands for hard work and thrift, as it stores food for winter.

quiz.q: The fable is usually credited to:
quiz.why: This fable is usually credited to Aesop, an ancient storyteller.
The ant tells the cricket, who sang all summer, to dance now. This is irony, as it says the opposite of what it means to make a point.
The moral is to prepare for hard times, by working and saving when it is easy.

scenes.text: Jim's letter is full of feeling and detail.
Your task: write a letter or diary entry with the same honesty.
Good writing shows, not just tells.

steps.title: Useful words (from the chapter's world)
steps.body:
- **Truce:** an agreement to stop fighting for a time.
- **Trench:** long ditch dug by soldiers for protection.
- **Roll-top desk:** desk with a sliding cover.
- **Junk shop:** shop selling old, second-hand items.
- **Nursing home:** place where elderly or sick people are cared for.
- **Veneer:** thin decorative layer of wood.

steps.title: Grammar in context: tenses in a letter
steps.body: Letters about past events mostly use the **simple past** ('We played football'), with the **present** for feelings now ('I hope you are well') and **future** for plans ('I will be home soon').

steps.title: Model diary entry (short)
steps.body: *25 December 1914, the front.* Dear Diary, this morning, for the first time in weeks, no guns. We climbed out, unsure, and shook hands with the men we had been fighting. We shared what little food we had and spoke of home. Tonight I wonder: if we can be friends today, why not tomorrow? — Jim

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the date, salutation and closing in a letter/diary.
- Mixing tenses without reason.

activity.prompt: Fill in the right word: truce, trench, junk shop
activity.text: The soldiers climbed out of the ___ to meet. They agreed to a short ___. The narrator found the desk in a ___.

options: An agreement to stop fighting for a while
quiz.why: A truce is an agreement to stop fighting for a while.

options: A long ditch for soldiers' protection
quiz.why: A trench is a long ditch dug for soldiers to protect them from enemy fire.

quiz.q: In a letter about past events, the main tense is:
quiz.why: A letter about past events uses mainly the simple past tense, as the events are over.
A diary entry carries the date and the writer's personal feelings and thoughts.

quiz.q: Which sentence is in the simple past?
quiz.why: "We played football together" is in the simple past, as 'played' is the past form. The other options are present or future.

questions.q: The narrator found the letter in:
options: A secret drawer of a desk
questions.why: The narrator found the letter in a secret drawer of a desk he bought.

questions.q: Who wrote the letter?
questions.why: The letter was written by Jim, Jim Macpherson, to his wife Connie.

questions.q: The Christmas truce took place in:
questions.why: The Christmas truce took place in 1914, in the First World War.

questions.q: In the poem, who refuses to help?
questions.why: In the poem the ant refuses to help the hungry cricket, who did not store food.

questions.q: During the truce, soldiers played:
questions.why: During the truce, the soldiers played football together.

questions.q: Connie thought the narrator was:
questions.why: Old Connie, who is confused by age, believed the narrator was Jim, her husband, returned home.

questions.q: Assertion: The story shows the futility of war. Reason: Enemy soldiers became friends when given a chance.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: the story shows war is pointless. R is true: enemy soldiers became friends when given the chance, which is why war looks futile. R explains A.

questions.q: The moral of 'The Ant and the Cricket':
options: Plan and save for the future
questions.why: The moral is to plan and save for the future, so that hard times can be faced.

questions.q: 'Junk shop' means a shop selling:
questions.why: A junk shop sells old, second-hand items.

questions.q: Why did the narrator not tell Connie the truth?
options: Out of kindness — it made her happy
questions.why: The narrator saw how happy Connie was to think Jim had come home. He did not want to hurt her with the truth, so he stayed silent out of kindness.

questions.q: What does the ant's advice to 'dance' show?
questions.why: The ant tells the cricket, who sang all summer, to dance through the winter. It says the opposite of what it means, to mock him. That is irony.

questions.q: Case: A reader says, 'The war would have ended if soldiers decided.' Which part of the story supports this?
options: Jim and Hans's conversation about ending the war peacefully
questions.why: Jim and Hans talked about ending the war peacefully during the truce. That is the evidence that ordinary soldiers could have chosen peace.

questions.q: Which best describes Jim's letter?
questions.why: Jim's letter to Connie is hopeful, honest and loving. He writes about his feelings and about his hope to come home.

questions.q: Assertion: The cricket was punished for being lazy. Reason: He did not prepare for winter.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: the cricket suffers because he was lazy and sang all summer. R is true: he did not prepare for winter. That is why he suffers, so R explains A.

questions.q: Which title links best to the theme of peace?
options: Enemies for a Day, Friends Forever
questions.why: The story shows enemies who became friends for a day during the truce. So "Enemies for a Day, Friends Forever" matches the theme of peace.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses past tense for the story?
options: The narrator finds a letter Jim will write.
The narrator found a letter that Jim had written in 1914.
The narrator is finding a letter Jim writes.
questions.why: The narrator found the letter in the present, past tense 'found'. Jim wrote it earlier, so past perfect 'had written' is used for the earlier event.

courses.title: Ch 2 · The Tsunami (with poem: Geography Lesson)
courses.summary: Accounts of the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami — including a young girl whose geography lesson saved lives and animals that sensed danger — and a poem about seeing the world from a jet plane and wondering why people still divide it.
outcomes: Learners can explain what a tsunami is and narrate key accounts
Learners can discuss presence of mind and the value of knowledge
Learners can explain the central irony of 'Geography Lesson'
Learners can write a notice or report on disaster preparedness

scenes.text: On the morning of 26 December 2004, a huge earthquake strikes under the sea near Sumatra, Indonesia.
Within hours, giant waves hit coasts across the Indian Ocean.
The Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Tamil Nadu are badly hit.

steps.title: What is a tsunami?
steps.body: A **tsunami** is a series of huge sea waves usually caused by an **undersea earthquake** (or volcanic eruption/landslide). The 2004 earthquake (magnitude about 9.1) was one of the strongest ever recorded. The waves killed over 2 lakh people in many countries, including India, Sri Lanka, Indonesia and Thailand.

steps.title: Accounts in the chapter
steps.body: The chapter collects real stories of courage and loss from the islands and coastal areas: families separated and reunited, people climbing to safety, and survivors helping each other. (Read the textbook for each person's account.)

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *Why is a tsunami so dangerous?* → It can strike within hours of a distant earthquake with little warning; the waves are powerful enough to destroy homes and sweep people away.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a tsunami a 'storm' — it's caused by underwater disturbances, not wind.
- Thinking only India was affected.

statements.s: The 2004 tsunami was caused by an undersea earthquake.
Tsunamis are caused by strong winds.
The Andaman and Nicobar Islands were badly affected.
Only one country was affected.

quiz.why: The great Indian Ocean tsunami struck on 26 December 2004.

quiz.q: It was triggered by an earthquake near:
quiz.why: The tsunami was set off by a huge undersea earthquake near Sumatra, in Indonesia.

options: A series of huge sea waves
quiz.why: A tsunami is a series of huge sea waves, usually caused by an undersea earthquake or similar disturbance.

options: Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Tamil Nadu
quiz.why: Coastal areas such as the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Tamil Nadu were badly hit. Inland places like Punjab, Delhi and Rajasthan were not.
Tsunamis often come with little warning, which is what makes them so dangerous.

lessons.title: Knowledge saves lives: Tilly Smith and the animals

story.title: A geography lesson on a beach

scenes.text: Ten-year-old Tilly Smith, on holiday in Phuket, Thailand, sees the sea suddenly pull back and froth.
She remembers her geography lesson: these are signs of a tsunami!
She warns her parents; the beach is cleared before the waves arrive.

steps.title: Tilly Smith
steps.body: **Tilly Smith**, a young British girl, had learned about tsunamis in a geography class just before her holiday. On the beach in **Phuket, Thailand**, she noticed the sea receding and bubbling. She told her mother, who alerted others; the beach was evacuated, and lives were saved. Her story shows how **knowledge plus presence of mind** can save lives.

steps.title: Animals sensed danger
steps.body: In **Sri Lanka's Yala National Park**, it was reported that animals such as elephants moved to higher ground before the waves struck, and very few animal bodies were found. Many people believe animals can sense vibrations or changes in the environment that humans don't notice.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *What saved the tourists on Tilly's beach?* → Tilly recognised the warning signs she had studied, and adults acted quickly on her warning.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Tilly was in India (she was in Thailand).
- Saying animals predicted the earthquake scientifically — they seemed to sense danger.

a.text: You're on a beach. The sea suddenly pulls far back, exposing the sea floor, and froths. Others walk out to collect shells.

choices.label: Warn people and move immediately to high ground or upper floors
choices.feedback: Correct — a receding sea can be a tsunami warning sign.

choices.label: Walk out to see the fish
choices.feedback: Very dangerous — waves may arrive in minutes.

w.text: The water is coming back fast! Turn and run inland/uphill now and tell others.

e.text: Stay on high ground until officials say it's safe; more waves can follow. In India call 112 for emergencies.

quiz.why: Tilly Smith, a British schoolgirl, was on holiday at Phuket in Thailand when the tsunami struck.

quiz.q: Tilly recognised the danger because of:
quiz.why: Tilly had just studied tsunamis in her geography lesson. She remembered what she was taught and spotted the danger.

quiz.q: A warning sign of a tsunami:
quiz.why: One warning sign of a tsunami is the sea suddenly drawing back and frothing. This is what Tilly noticed.
Yala National Park is in Sri Lanka. Animals there moved to higher ground before the waves came.

options: Knowledge and quick action save lives
quiz.why: Tilly's story teaches that knowledge and quick action can save lives.

scenes.text: A plane climbs over a city.
From high above, the city's shape makes sense: it grew near water.
Higher still, the whole earth looks small. So why do people still fight over it?

steps.title: Summary (original)
steps.body: In **'Geography Lesson'** by **Zulfikar Ghose**, the speaker views the earth from a rising jet plane. At first he sees why a city has grown where it has (near a river/water). Higher up, he sees the valleys and mountains and understands the logic of geography. From the greatest height he sees the earth as a whole, and wonders **why people — who understand the earth's geography — still find reasons to hate each other and build walls across cities**.

steps.title: Central idea and devices
steps.body:
- **Irony:** humans understand geography (why cities grow near water) yet fail to understand one another.
- **Shift in perspective:** from city → landscape → whole earth.
- Theme: **unity of humankind** vs man-made divisions.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *What does the poet find difficult to understand?* → Why people who can see the earth is one and small still divide it with walls and hatred.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Treating the poem as only about geography facts — its real subject is human division.

activity.prompt: Order the speaker's views as the jet climbs
items: The city and why it grew near water
Valleys and mountains of the region
The earth as a whole, small and united
A question about why people still hate and build walls

quiz.why: 'Geography Lesson' is a poem by Zulfikar Ghose.

quiz.q: The speaker views the earth from a:
quiz.why: In the poem the speaker looks down at the earth from a jet plane, high in the sky.

options: Water is essential for life and trade
quiz.why: Cities grow near water because water is essential for life, farming and trade.

options: People understand geography but not each other
quiz.why: The irony is that people know so much geography, but do not understand one another. They have divided the world by walls and hatred.
The walls in the poem stand for divisions and hatred between people, not real geography.

lessons.title: Language and writing: notices and disaster preparedness

scenes.text: After learning about tsunamis, the school plans a disaster-preparedness drill.
Students must write a notice for the notice board.
Clear, short and complete — that's a good notice.

steps.title: Notice format
steps.body:
- Name of the institution
- **NOTICE** (heading)
- Date
- Title (what it's about)
- Body: what, when, where, who, any instructions (about 50 words)
- Name, designation (and signature)

steps.title: Model notice
steps.body:
**Green Valley School** · NOTICE · 2 December
**Disaster Preparedness Drill**
All students of Classes 6–8 are informed that a disaster-preparedness drill will be held on 5 December at 10 a.m. in the school ground. Students must follow their class teacher's instructions and learn the evacuation route. Attendance is compulsory.
Riya Sharma, Head Girl

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **Recede:** move back.
- **Evacuate:** move people away from danger.
- **Epicentre:** point on the surface directly above where an earthquake starts.
- **Debris:** broken pieces left after destruction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving out date, time or venue in a notice.
- Writing a notice like a story.

activity.prompt: Use the right word: evacuate, recede, debris
activity.text: The sea began to ___. Officials told people to ___ the beach. After the waves, ___ was everywhere.

quiz.why: To evacuate is to move people away from a place of danger.

options: Date, time, venue and issuing person
quiz.why: A notice should give the date, time, venue and the name of the person issuing it. It is short and to the point.

options: The point on the surface above an earthquake's origin
quiz.why: The epicentre is the point on the Earth's surface directly above where an earthquake begins.
A notice is short, about 50 words, as it must be brief and clear.
Debris means the broken pieces and rubbish left after something is destroyed.

questions.q: The 2004 tsunami struck on:
questions.why: The tsunami struck on 26 December 2004, the day after Christmas.

questions.q: Tilly Smith was:
questions.why: Tilly Smith was a British schoolgirl who was on holiday in Thailand.

questions.q: 'Geography Lesson' is written by:
questions.why: Zulfikar Ghose wrote the poem 'Geography Lesson'.

questions.q: A tsunami is usually caused by:
questions.why: A tsunami is usually caused by an undersea earthquake, which suddenly moves a lot of water.

questions.q: Animals in Yala National Park:
questions.why: Animals in Yala National Park moved to higher ground before the tsunami, as reports said.

questions.q: Assertion: Tilly's knowledge saved lives. Reason: She recognised the receding sea as a tsunami sign.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: Tilly's knowledge saved lives. R is true: she saw the receding sea and knew it was a tsunami sign. She warned people, so R explains A.

questions.q: In the poem, from the highest point the poet sees:
questions.why: From the highest point the poet sees the earth as a whole, without borders. That makes divisions seem foolish.

questions.q: 'Recede' means:
questions.why: To recede means to move back or go away, as the sea did before the tsunami.

questions.q: The poet's main question is about:
options: Why people still hate and divide the world
questions.why: The poet asks why people still hate and divide the world, though from above it looks like one.

questions.q: Which is a correct notice title?
questions.why: A notice has a clear title that tells the subject. 'Disaster Preparedness Drill' fits. The others belong to diaries, letters and stories.

questions.q: Case: A teacher wants students to remember what to do if the sea suddenly recedes. Which lesson from the chapter fits best?
questions.why: Tilly Smith's story shows what to do when the sea suddenly recedes, because she knew it meant a tsunami and warned people.

questions.q: Why are cities often built near rivers (as the poem notes)?
options: Water for drinking, farming and trade
questions.why: Cities grow near rivers because they give water for drinking and farming, and routes for trade.

questions.q: Assertion: The poem praises walls between people. Reason: The poet wonders why people build walls despite seeing the earth is one.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is false: the poem does not praise walls, it criticises them. R is true: the poet wonders why people build walls though the earth is one.

questions.q: Which literary device best describes the poem's contrast between knowing geography and not knowing each other?
questions.why: The contrast between knowing geography and not knowing each other is irony. The words and the situation point in opposite directions.

questions.q: Which action is correct after a tsunami warning?
options: Go to the beach to watch
Swim out to meet the wave
Move to high ground and stay till officials declare safety
questions.why: After a tsunami warning, go to high ground and stay there until officials say it is safe. More waves may follow the first.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Glimpses of the Past (with poem: Macavity: The Mystery Cat)
courses.summary: A comic-strip history of India from about 1757 to 1857 — the Company's rise, social reformers and the revolt — and T.S. Eliot's playful poem about a cat who is never caught.
outcomes: Learners can sequence the main events shown in the comic-strip history
Learners can explain how the Company gained power and why people rebelled
Learners can describe Macavity and the poem's humour
Learners can use reported speech and write a short historical narrative

scenes.text: The chapter tells a hundred years of history in pictures and speech bubbles.
Indian rulers quarrel; the East India Company steps in.
By 1857, anger boils over into revolt.

steps.title: Key scenes (original summary)
steps.body:
- Indian rulers were divided and fought among themselves; the **East India Company** made alliances, trained armies and gradually took control of territory.
- Ordinary people suffered: heavy taxes, cheap foreign goods hurting Indian craftsmen, and loss of land.
- Reformers such as **Raja Rammohun Roy** questioned harmful customs and called for education and reform.
- Laws and policies (e.g. annexations) angered rulers and sepoys; rumours about greased cartridges sparked the **Revolt of 1857**.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *How did the Company take advantage of Indian rulers?* → Rulers were disunited; the Company sided with one against another, offered 'protection' for money and territory, and expanded its power.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the Company came as a government — it came as traders and gradually became rulers.
- Forgetting the role of reformers in the comic.

activity.prompt: Order the scenes
items: Indian rulers are divided and quarrel
The Company makes alliances and gains territory
People suffer from taxes and loss of trade
Reformers question harmful customs
Anger leads to the Revolt of 1857

quiz.q: The chapter is presented as a:
quiz.why: 'Glimpses of the Past' is presented as a comic strip, with pictures and short text.

quiz.q: The Company first came to India as:
quiz.why: The East India Company first came to India as traders, in search of goods like cloth and spices.

quiz.q: A reformer shown in the chapter:
quiz.why: Raja Rammohun Roy is shown as a reformer in the chapter. Tipu Sultan, Dalhousie and Mir Jafar were rulers or officials.

quiz.q: Indian rulers were weak against the Company mainly because they were:
quiz.why: Indian rulers were divided and often fought each other. That made it easier for the Company to take power.
The comic strip goes up to the Revolt of 1857.

scenes.text: Farmers lost land to high taxes.
Weavers lost work to cheap machine-made cloth from Britain.
Sepoys feared their faith was being attacked.

steps.title: Causes of discontent shown
steps.body:
- **Economic:** heavy land revenue; Indian handicrafts ruined by imported goods.
- **Political:** annexation of kingdoms; insult to rulers.
- **Social/religious:** fear of interference in customs; the greased-cartridge rumour.

(Your History course has the full details of these events.)

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *Why did Indian weavers suffer?* → Cheap machine-made cloth from Britain flooded Indian markets, so demand for handwoven cloth fell.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Giving only one cause for 1857; it had many.

activity.prompt: Type of cause

quiz.why: Cheap British cloth made by machines hurt Indian weavers, whose handloom cloth lost buyers.

quiz.q: Annexation of kingdoms is a ___ cause.
quiz.why: Taking over kingdoms (annexation) is a political cause, since it is about power and territory.
The rumour that cartridges were greased with animal fat hurt the religious feelings of the sepoys.
Heavy taxes mainly hurt peasants, who had to pay land revenue even in bad years.

quiz.q: The comic suggests the revolt was caused by:
quiz.why: The comic shows that the revolt had many causes, such as economic, political and religious grievances, not just one.

scenes.text: A crime is discovered — jewels gone, a window broken, milk missing.
Scotland Yard rushes in.
But Macavity? He's never there.

steps.title: Summary (original)
steps.body: In this humorous poem by **T.S. Eliot** (from *Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats*), **Macavity** is a ginger cat who is a master criminal — called the 'Hidden Paw' and compared to Napoleon as a mastermind of crime. He breaks every law, yet whenever a crime is discovered, he is **not there**. He is described as tall and thin, with sunken eyes, a lined forehead, a domed head, an uncombed, dusty appearance and a swaying walk. He looks respectable but is deceitful. Even Scotland Yard cannot catch him; he always has an alibi.

steps.title: Devices and humour
steps.body:
- **Repetition/refrain** of 'Macavity's not there' builds humour.
- **Hyperbole:** comparing a cat to master criminals.
- **Personification:** a cat with human cunning, alibis and gang leadership.
- Rhythm and rhyme make it fun to read aloud.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *Why is Macavity called the 'Hidden Paw'?* → He commits crimes so cleverly that no one can ever find proof or catch him at the scene.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Macavity is a real criminal person — he's a cat, humorously personified.
- Missing the repeated refrain as a device.

statements.s: Macavity is a mystery cat in a poem by T.S. Eliot.
Macavity is always caught at the scene.
The poem uses repetition for humour.
Macavity is compared to a famous mastermind.

quiz.why: In the poem Macavity is called the Hidden Paw, because he is never caught at a crime.
'Macavity: The Mystery Cat' is a poem by T.S. Eliot.
Scotland Yard, the police, fails to catch Macavity.

quiz.q: The repeated line 'Macavity's not there' is an example of:
quiz.why: The repeated line 'Macavity's not there' is a refrain, a line repeated through the poem.
Macavity is a ginger cat, as the poem describes him.

lessons.title: Language: reported speech and narrative writing

scenes.text: In the comic, a character says: 'We must unite against the Company.'
A news report would write: He said that they must unite against the Company.
That's reported speech.

steps.title: Reported speech basics
steps.body:
- Remove quotation marks; use **that** (optional).
- Change pronouns as needed.
- Usually move tense one step back after a past reporting verb: *is → was*, *will → would*, *can → could*.
- *'I am hungry,' said Ravi.* → Ravi said that he was hungry.
- Questions: *'Where is the cat?' she asked.* → She asked where the cat was.

steps.title: Practice
steps.body: *'Macavity is not here,' said the inspector.* → The inspector said that Macavity was not there.

steps.title: Writing a historical narrative
steps.body: Use the past tense, a clear sequence (first, then, after that, finally), and a point of view (e.g. a weaver telling how his life changed).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to change 'here' → 'there', 'now' → 'then'.
- Keeping question marks in reported questions.

activity.prompt: Convert to reported speech.
activity.text: 'I will come tomorrow,' she said. → She said that she ___ come the next day. 'Is the cat here?' he asked. → He asked if the cat ___ there.

quiz.q: 'I am tired,' said Ali. → Ali said that he ___ tired.
quiz.why: In reported speech the present tense 'am' becomes the past tense 'was'. So Ali said that he was tired.

quiz.q: 'Can you help?' she asked. → She asked if I ___ help.
quiz.why: In reported speech the modal 'can' changes to 'could'. So she asked if I could help.
In reported speech 'here' usually changes to 'there'.
A reported question becomes a statement form, so it ends with a full stop, not a question mark.

quiz.q: A historical narrative is mainly in the:
quiz.why: A historical account of past events is mainly written in the past tense.

questions.q: 'Glimpses of the Past' is told as a:
questions.why: 'Glimpses of the Past' is told as a comic strip.

questions.q: Macavity is a:
questions.why: Macavity is a mystery cat in T.S. Eliot's poem.

questions.q: Who wrote 'Macavity: The Mystery Cat'?
questions.why: T.S. Eliot wrote 'Macavity: The Mystery Cat'.

questions.q: The Company came to India first as:
questions.why: The Company first came to India as traders, not as rulers or soldiers.

questions.q: Macavity is called the:
questions.why: Macavity is called the Hidden Paw, because he leaves no trace of his crimes.

questions.q: Assertion: Indian rulers lost power to the Company. Reason: They were divided and fought each other.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: Indian rulers lost power to the Company. R is true: they were divided and fought each other, which weakened them. R explains A.

questions.q: A reformer in the chapter:
questions.why: Raja Rammohun Roy is shown as a reformer in the chapter. Clive and Mir Jafar were part of the Company's story.

questions.q: 'Macavity's not there' is repeated to create:
questions.why: The repeated line 'Macavity's not there' adds humour and emphasis, showing again and again that he escapes.

questions.q: Reported speech: 'We are ready,' they said. →
options: They said we will be ready.
They said that we are ready.
They said that they were ready.
questions.why: In reported speech, 'We are ready' changes to 'they were ready'. 'We' becomes 'they' and the present 'are' becomes past 'were'.

questions.q: Why did weavers suffer under Company rule?
options: Cheap machine-made imports reduced demand for handloom cloth
questions.why: Cheap machine-made cloth from Britain was imported in large amounts, so there was less demand for handloom cloth. The weavers suffered.

questions.q: Case: A crime is discovered, police arrive, but the cat has an alibi and is far away. This describes:
questions.why: A cat that always escapes with an alibi, as the police arrive too late, is Macavity, the mystery cat.

questions.q: Which device: comparing Macavity to Napoleon?
questions.why: Comparing Macavity to Napoleon is exaggeration, and it alludes to a famous figure. This is hyperbole or allusion.

questions.q: Assertion: The Revolt of 1857 had a single cause. Reason: The comic shows economic, political and religious grievances.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is false: the revolt had many causes. R is true: the comic shows economic, political and religious grievances.

questions.q: Reported question: 'Where are you going?' she asked me. →
options: She asked where are you going.
She asked me where I was going.
She asked me where was I going?
questions.why: In a reported question the word order of a statement is used, and the tense shifts back. So: She asked me where I was going.

questions.q: Which best summarises the chapter?
options: How the Company rose to power and why Indians resisted, told in pictures
questions.why: The chapter shows, in pictures, how the Company rose to power and why Indians resisted it.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Bepin Choudhury's Lapse of Memory (with poem: The Last Bargain)
courses.summary: Satyajit Ray's story of a businessman who is made to believe he has forgotten a holiday — and the surprising reason why — and Rabindranath Tagore's poem about a seeker who is finally 'hired' by a child's freedom.
outcomes: Learners can narrate the story and explain the twist
Learners can discuss pride, kindness and the consequences of ignoring others
Learners can explain the symbolism of 'The Last Bargain'
Learners can practise character sketches and formal emails/letters

lessons.title: The story: a trip he can't remember

scenes.text: Bepin Choudhury, a busy, reserved man, buys his usual pile of books.
A stranger greets him: 'You were in Ranchi eight years ago — we met there!'
Bepin remembers nothing. Is his memory failing?

steps.title: Plot in brief (original retelling)
steps.body:
- **Bepin Choudhury** is a successful but solitary man who loves reading crime and ghost stories.
- A stranger (**Parimal Ghosh**) insists they spent time together in **Ranchi** years ago, describing details of the trip — even an accident Bepin supposedly had.
- Bepin is certain he never went, but when others seem to confirm the story, he panics that he has lost his memory. He even goes to Ranchi to check, feels confused, and becomes ill with worry. A doctor says such memory loss has no easy cure.
- Finally, an old friend, **Chunilal**, reveals the truth: it was all a **trick**. Chunilal had asked Bepin for help (a job) when he was in difficulty, and Bepin had turned him away rudely. Chunilal planned the trick to teach him a lesson.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *Why did Chunilal play the trick?* → To get back at Bepin, who had refused to help him when he was in need — and to show him what it feels like to be helpless.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Bepin really lost his memory.
- Missing why the trick was played — it's the heart of the story.

activity.prompt: Order the story
items: A stranger says he met Bepin in Ranchi
Bepin insists he never went
He fears he is losing his memory
He goes to Ranchi and becomes ill with worry
Chunilal reveals it was a trick to teach him a lesson

quiz.why: Bepin Choudhury loved reading, particularly crime and ghost stories, and he was proud of his memory.

quiz.q: The stranger claimed they met in:
quiz.why: The stranger claimed that he had met Bepin in Ranchi, years ago.
Bepin began to fear that he had lost his memory, since he could not recall meeting the stranger.
The truth was that Chunilal had arranged the whole trick, using the stranger and others.

options: Bepin had refused to help him when he needed it
quiz.why: Chunilal wanted to teach Bepin a lesson, because Bepin had refused to help him when he needed it.

scenes.text: Bepin dismissed his friend's request without a thought.
Then he felt helpless and confused himself.
Sometimes we understand others only after walking in their shoes.

steps.title: Character sketches
steps.body:
- **Bepin Choudhury:** hard-working, proud of his sharp memory, solitary, somewhat self-centred; shaken when his certainty is attacked.
- **Chunilal:** an old friend who had fallen on hard times; hurt by Bepin's rudeness; clever and mischievous in his revenge.
- **Parimal Ghosh:** the convincing stranger who plays his part well.

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- **Empathy and kindness:** ignoring others' difficulties can hurt them deeply.
- **Pride:** over-confidence in oneself.
- **Power of suggestion:** how others' certainty can make us doubt ourselves.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *Was Chunilal right to trick Bepin?* → (Opinion) His trick was cruel because Bepin fell ill, but it did make Bepin realise how unkind he had been; a direct conversation would have been better.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - In opinion questions, giving no reason — always support your view with an example from the story.

activity.prompt: Match the character to the trait
pairs: Hurt friend who plans the trick
Says such memory loss has no easy cure

quiz.why: A major theme is empathy and kindness. Bepin's unkindness comes back to him.
Bepin was proud of his memory, and thought it never failed.

options: The power of suggestion — others seemed certain
quiz.why: The trick worked by the power of suggestion. Many people seemed certain, so Bepin doubted himself.

quiz.q: Bepin's treatment of Chunilal earlier was:
quiz.why: Bepin had earlier been unkind and dismissive to Chunilal, which led to the trick.

quiz.q: In an opinion answer you must:
options: Support your view with evidence from the text
quiz.why: In an opinion answer, you state your view and support it with evidence from the text.

scenes.text: A king offers power; an old man offers gold; a young woman offers her smile.
Then a child playing with shells on the beach says: 'I will hire you with nothing.'
And the seeker becomes truly free.

steps.title: Summary (original)
steps.body: In **'The Last Bargain'** by **Rabindranath Tagore**, a speaker goes looking for someone to 'hire' him (to give his life to). A **king** offers **power**; an **old man** offers **gold**; a **fair maid** offers her **smile** — but each offer turns empty. Finally, a **child playing with shells** on the seashore offers to hire him for **nothing**. The bargain made in play sets him free: he becomes a free man.

steps.title: Symbolism
steps.body:
- King = power; old man = wealth; maid = beauty/attachment.
- The child = innocence, joy and freedom; working 'for nothing' in a spirit of play brings true happiness.
- Theme: **true happiness lies not in power, money or beauty but in simple, selfless joy**.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *Why does the speaker accept the child's offer?* → The child offers nothing material, but in that simple, joyful bargain he finds freedom — something power and wealth could not give.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Taking 'hire' literally — it means choosing what to devote one's life to.

activity.prompt: Match the offer to what it symbolises

quiz.why: 'The Last Bargain' is a poem by Rabindranath Tagore.
The speaker is finally hired by a child who is playing with shells.
The child offers nothing, no pay at all. That is why the speaker chooses to work for him.

quiz.q: After the last bargain, the speaker feels:
quiz.why: After the last bargain the speaker feels free, as he has found simple joy and not wealth or power.

options: True happiness comes from simple, selfless joy
quiz.why: The poem says true happiness comes from simple, selfless joy, not gold, power or beauty.

lessons.title: Writing: character sketch and formal email

scenes.text: The teacher asks for a character sketch of Bepin Choudhury.
Then, a formal email apologising to a friend you let down.
Clear structure + evidence = strong writing.

steps.title: Character sketch structure
steps.body:
- Introduction: who the character is.
- 2–3 traits, each with an example from the story.
- Conclusion: how the character changes or what we learn.

steps.title: Model sketch (short)
steps.body: Bepin Choudhury is a busy, well-off man who trusts his memory completely. He is solitary — he spends evenings reading alone. He can be unkind: he refused to help his old friend Chunilal. When strangers insist he visited Ranchi, his confidence collapses, showing how fragile pride can be. By the end, he learns that his actions have consequences.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **Lapse:** a temporary failure (of memory).
- **Incident:** an event.
- **Nervous breakdown:** severe stress causing a person to be unable to cope.
- **Hazy:** unclear.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Listing traits without examples.
- Writing a summary instead of a sketch.

activity.prompt: Use the right word: lapse, hazy, incident
activity.text: His memory of the trip was ___. He worried about a ___ of memory. The ___ in Ranchi never happened.

quiz.why: A lapse is a temporary failure, as when memory fails for a short while.
A character sketch lists a person's traits and backs each with examples from the text.
'Hazy' means unclear or blurred, as with a hazy memory.

options: Subject line, greeting, clear body, polite closing
quiz.why: A formal email has a subject line, a greeting, a clear body and a polite closing.

quiz.q: Best opening for a formal apology email:
options: Dear Chunilal, I am writing to apologise for…
quiz.why: A formal apology begins politely, as in 'Dear Chunilal, I am writing to apologise for…'. Slang and no greeting are not suitable.

questions.q: 'Bepin Choudhury's Lapse of Memory' is by:
questions.why: Satyajit Ray wrote 'Bepin Choudhury's Lapse of Memory'.

questions.q: 'The Last Bargain' is by:
questions.why: Rabindranath Tagore wrote 'The Last Bargain'.

questions.q: The stranger said they met in:
questions.why: The stranger said that he and Bepin had met in Ranchi.

questions.q: Who played the trick?
questions.why: Chunilal arranged the trick to teach Bepin a lesson.

questions.q: In the poem, the old man offers:
questions.why: In the poem the old man offers gold, which the speaker refuses. The child offers nothing.

questions.q: Assertion: Bepin was tricked by Chunilal. Reason: Bepin had refused to help Chunilal earlier.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: Chunilal tricked Bepin. R is true: Bepin had refused to help him earlier. That is the motive, so R explains A.

questions.q: The child in the poem symbolises:
questions.why: The child in the poem stands for innocence and freedom.

questions.q: 'Lapse' means:
questions.why: A lapse is a temporary failure, such as of memory.

questions.q: Bepin's main weakness:
questions.why: Bepin's main weakness was his pride, and he lacked empathy for others, like Chunilal.

questions.q: Why did Bepin become ill?
options: Constant worry that he had lost his memory
questions.why: Bepin fell ill from constant worry that he had lost his memory. The stress made him sick.

questions.q: Case: A friend asks you for help and you brush them off; later you're in trouble and no one helps. Which text explores this?
options: The Ant and the Cricket only
questions.why: The story shows how a person who brushes off a friend's request can face trouble himself. Bepin's unkindness to Chunilal returned to him.

questions.q: The king, old man and maid fail because:
options: Power, wealth and beauty cannot give true freedom
questions.why: The king, old man and maid offer power, wealth and beauty. These cannot give true freedom, so the speaker does not accept them.

questions.q: Assertion: The speaker is 'hired' for gold at the end. Reason: The child offers him nothing.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is false: at the end the speaker is hired by the child, who offers nothing, not gold. R is true.

questions.q: Which is a well-supported character trait?
options: Bepin is proud — he is sure his memory never fails.
questions.why: A well-supported trait is backed by evidence. 'Bepin is proud, as he is sure his memory never fails' gives the trait and the proof.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the story's message?
options: Our unkindness to others can return to us; empathy matters
questions.why: The message is that unkindness can come back to us, and so empathy matters.

courses.title: Ch 5 · The Summit Within (with poem: The School Boy)
courses.summary: An Everest climber reflects on what it means to reach the top of the world — and the harder 'summit within' — and William Blake's poem about a boy who longs for summer mornings instead of a dreary classroom.
outcomes: Learners can describe the climber's feelings on and after the summit
Learners can explain what the 'summit within' means
Learners can explain the imagery and message of 'The School Boy'
Learners can write a reflective paragraph and use adjectives of emotion

story.title: At the top of the world

scenes.text: In 1965, members of an Indian team stand on the summit of Mount Everest.
The writer, Major H.P.S. Ahluwalia, feels joy, humility — and a strange sadness.
'Why do we climb?' he asks.

steps.title: Summary (original)
steps.body: The writer, **Major H.P.S. Ahluwalia**, a member of the 1965 Indian expedition to **Mount Everest**, describes his mixed feelings at the summit: **joy** at achieving a dream, **humility** at the vastness of nature, gratitude, and a touch of **sadness** — the climb was over, and there was nowhere higher to go. Climbers left religious offerings at the summit as signs of reverence. He reflects on **why people climb mountains**: the challenge, the beauty, the sense of adventure and the urge to test oneself.

steps.title: The 'summit within'
steps.body: Climbing a mountain teaches endurance, courage and determination. But the writer says every person also has a **summit within** — the climb to conquer one's own fears, weaknesses and ego. That climb is even harder and lasts a lifetime; the physical climb helps prepare for it.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *What is the 'summit within'?* → The inner struggle to overcome one's fears, doubts and selfishness and become a better person.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the climber felt only happiness — his feelings were mixed.
- Taking 'summit within' literally.

activity.prompt: Which emotion is the writer describing?

items.text: We had reached the top of our dream
We felt small before such grandeur
The climb was over; nothing higher remained
We offered prayers at the summit

quiz.why: The writer climbed Everest in 1965, as part of an Indian expedition. The first ascent by Hillary and Tenzing was in 1953.

quiz.q: At the summit the writer felt:
options: Mixed feelings — joy, humility and some sadness
quiz.why: At the summit the writer felt mixed feelings: joy at success, humility before the mountain, and a little sadness.
The 'summit within' is a metaphor for conquering one's own inner weaknesses, like fear and doubt.

quiz.q: Why did the writer feel sad?
options: The climb was over and there was nowhere higher to go
quiz.why: The writer felt a little sad because the climb was over and there was nowhere higher to go.
Mountain climbing teaches endurance, courage and determination.

scenes.text: Birds sing; the huntsman's horn sounds far away; the skylark joins in.
But the boy must go to school, under a cruel, watchful eye.
'How can a bird born for joy sit in a cage and sing?'

steps.title: Summary (original)
steps.body: In **'The School Boy'** by **William Blake**, a boy loves rising on a summer morning when birds sing and nature is alive. Going to school on such a day drives all joy away; he spends the day in dismay, drooping over books, unable to enjoy learning. He compares himself to a **bird in a cage** that cannot sing. He asks his parents: if young buds are nipped and blossoms stripped away, how can there be fruit in summer? — i.e. if children's joy is crushed, how can they grow well?

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Metaphor:** child = bird in a cage; childhood = spring buds and blossoms.
- **Imagery** of nature: skylark, huntsman's horn, summer morning.
- **Rhetorical questions** to parents.
- Theme: **rigid schooling crushes children's natural joy and curiosity**.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *Why does the boy compare himself to a caged bird?* → Like a caged bird that cannot sing, he loses his joy when confined in a strict classroom on a beautiful day.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking the poem is against learning — it criticises joyless, rigid schooling.

activity.prompt: Match the image to its meaning
pairs: Child confined in a strict school

quiz.why: 'The School Boy' is a poem by William Blake.
The boy loves summer mornings in nature, with birds singing.
The boy compares himself to a bird in a cage, since school feels like a prison to him.
The poem criticises rigid, joyless schooling that crushes a child's joy.

options: Joy crushed before it can grow
quiz.why: 'Buds nipped' means joy crushed before it can grow, as a bud nipped off cannot become a flower.

lessons.title: Language: emotion words and reflective writing

scenes.text: Think of your own 'summit' — a race, an exam, a performance.
Describe how you felt before, at the top, and after.
Reflective writing explores feelings and lessons.

steps.title: Emotion vocabulary
steps.body: **Elated, humble, awestruck, grateful, nostalgic, melancholy, determined, anxious, relieved, triumphant.**

steps.title: Reflective paragraph structure
steps.body:
- What happened (briefly).
- How you felt (use precise emotion words).
- What you learned about yourself ('my summit within').

steps.title: Model paragraph
steps.body: When I finally crossed the finish line of the school marathon, I felt elated and relieved, yet strangely melancholy that months of training were over. Standing there, I realised the real victory was over my own doubts — I had kept going when I wanted to quit. That was my summit within.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using only 'happy' and 'sad'.
- Telling events without reflecting on meaning.

activity.prompt: Choose: elated, awestruck, melancholy
activity.text: On reaching the top, he felt ___. Seeing the endless peaks, he was ___. Knowing the climb was over, he felt slightly ___.

quiz.why: 'Elated' means extremely happy.
'Awestruck' means filled with wonder at something great.
Reflective writing includes the writer's feelings and the lessons learned.
'Melancholy' means gentle, quiet sadness.
'Grateful' means thankful. The others show worry, anger and jealousy.

scenes.text: Mountaineers prepare for months: training, teamwork, planning.
They rely on each other and on Sherpa guides.
Every big goal needs the same.

steps.title: Values from the chapter
steps.body:
- **Perseverance:** keep going despite difficulty.
- **Teamwork:** no one climbs Everest alone.
- **Humility:** nature is greater than us.
- **Self-mastery:** the inner summit.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *Why does the writer call the climb to the 'summit within' harder?* → Physical mountains can be climbed with training and equipment, but overcoming one's own fears, anger and selfishness is a lifelong struggle.

steps.title: Model answer (poem)
steps.body: *What does the boy request from his parents?* → To understand that crushing a child's joy harms their growth, just as nipping buds prevents fruit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Writing very long answers without the key point in the first line.

activity.prompt: What is one 'summit within' you want to climb this year?
activity.hint: Example: managing anger, overcoming stage fear, being more patient.

quiz.why: Mountaineers show perseverance, which means not giving up despite difficulty.
Everest expeditions depend on teamwork. Climbers, guides and support staff help each other.

quiz.q: Humility in the chapter comes from:
quiz.why: Humility comes from realising how great nature is, compared with a human being.

quiz.q: The boy in Blake's poem asks his parents to:
options: Understand how crushing joy harms growth
quiz.why: The boy asks the adults to understand that crushing a child's joy harms growth, as with a bud.

quiz.q: Good exam answers put the key point:
quiz.why: A good exam answer puts the key point in the first line, so the reader sees it straight away.

questions.q: 'The Summit Within' is about climbing:
questions.why: 'The Summit Within' is about the writer's climb of Mount Everest.

questions.q: 'The School Boy' poet:
questions.why: William Blake wrote 'The School Boy'.

questions.q: The writer climbed in:
questions.why: The writer made the climb in 1965.

questions.q: The schoolboy loves:
questions.why: The schoolboy loves summer mornings, with birds and sunshine.

questions.q: The writer's feelings at the summit were:
questions.why: At the summit the writer felt mixed emotions: joy, humility and a little sadness.

questions.q: Assertion: The 'summit within' is harder to climb. Reason: Conquering one's inner weaknesses is a lifelong struggle.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: the summit within is harder to climb. R is true: beating one's inner weaknesses is a lifelong struggle. That explains why it is harder, so R explains A.

questions.q: A caged bird in the poem symbolises:
questions.why: The caged bird in the poem stands for a child confined in a strict school, who longs for freedom.

questions.q: 'Awestruck' means:
questions.why: 'Awestruck' means filled with wonder.

questions.q: Why did the writer feel sad at the summit?
options: There was nowhere higher to go; the climb was over
questions.why: The writer felt sad because there was nowhere higher to go, and the climb was over.

questions.q: The poem's message is mainly about:
questions.why: The poem is mainly about joyless, rigid schooling, which harms children's growth.

questions.q: Case: A student overcomes stage fright to speak at assembly. This is like:
questions.why: Overcoming stage fright is a win over one's inner fear. It is like climbing the summit within.

questions.q: 'If buds are nipped, how can there be fruit?' This is a:
questions.why: 'If buds are nipped, how can there be fruit?' is a question asked for effect, not for an answer, so it is rhetorical. The buds are a metaphor for children.

questions.q: Assertion: The writer climbed only for fame. Reason: He reflects on challenge, beauty and self-testing as reasons to climb.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is false: the writer climbed not only for fame. R is true: he reflects on challenge, beauty and testing himself as reasons.

questions.q: Which best expresses both texts' shared idea?
options: Growth needs freedom, effort and inner strength
questions.why: Both texts show that growth needs freedom, effort and inner strength, whether climbing a mountain or growing up.

questions.q: Which is the best reflective sentence?
options: I felt triumphant, but I learned that beating my own doubts mattered most.
questions.why: A reflective sentence shows both feeling and learning. 'I felt triumphant, but I learned that beating my own doubts mattered most' does both.

courses.title: Ch 6 · This is Jody's Fawn (with poem: The Duck and the Kangaroo)
courses.summary: From 'The Yearling': a boy insists on rescuing an orphaned fawn whose mother was killed to save his father's life — a story of responsibility and compassion — and Edward Lear's nonsense poem about an unlikely friendship.
outcomes: Learners can retell the story and explain Jody's motives
Learners can discuss responsibility, compassion and parenting in the story
Learners can enjoy and explain nonsense verse
Learners can write dialogue and use adverbs correctly

lessons.title: The story: a life for a life

scenes.text: Jody's father, Penny, is bitten by a rattlesnake.
To draw out the poison, he kills a doe and uses her heart and liver.
Her little fawn is left alone. Jody can't stop thinking about it.

steps.title: Plot in brief (original retelling)
steps.body: This chapter is from **Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings'** novel *The Yearling*. **Penny Baxter**, Jody's father, was bitten by a rattlesnake and saved himself by killing a **doe** and using her heart and liver to draw out the poison. **Doc Wilson** treated him. **Jody** realises the doe's **fawn** is now alone and will starve. He asks his parents to let him bring it home. **Ma Baxter** worries about feeding it, but **Penny** agrees: they owe the fawn a debt, since its mother saved his life. Jody goes with **Mill-wheel**, a neighbour, to the place; they find the frightened fawn. Jody gently holds it, carries it home, and teaches it to drink milk from a gourd by dipping his fingers in milk. The fawn becomes his responsibility.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *Why did Penny agree to bring the fawn home?* → He felt it was only fair, as the doe had given her life to save him; leaving the fawn to starve would be ungrateful.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the fawn's mother was killed for food (it was to save Penny's life).
- Forgetting that Jody takes responsibility for feeding the fawn.

lessons.title: Poem: The Duck and the Kangaroo

scenes.text: A duck tired of her pond wants to hop like the kangaroo.
The kangaroo worries her wet feet will give him rheumatism.
She promises to wear woollen socks and a cloak — and off they go!

steps.title: Summary (original)
steps.body: In **Edward Lear's** humorous poem, a **duck** who finds life in her pond dull asks a **kangaroo** to take her on his back so she can see the world. The kangaroo hesitates — her wet, cold feet might give him a chill or rheumatism. The duck solves the problem by buying **woollen socks** and wearing a cloak. Delighted, they set off and **hop around the world** (three times, in the poem) — happy together.

steps.title: Nonsense verse
steps.body: Lear is famous for **nonsense poetry**: playful, absurd situations, talking animals, strong rhythm and rhyme, and made-up humour. Underneath the fun is a gentle idea: **friendship and compromise** — each solves the other's concern.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *How does the duck overcome the kangaroo's objection?* → By wearing woollen socks to keep her feet dry and warm, and a cloak.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Looking for a serious moral everywhere — nonsense verse is mainly for fun, though friendship and compromise are visible.

The kangaroo fears the duck's wet feet.

quiz.why: The poem shows friendship and compromise, as the duck solves the kangaroo's worry.

scenes.text: 'Please, Pa,' Jody said softly. 'Let me bring it home.'

steps.title: Writing dialogue
steps.body:
- Put spoken words inside quotation marks.
- Start a new line for each new speaker.
- Use reporting verbs (asked, pleaded, whispered) and adverbs (gently, anxiously, firmly).

steps.title: Adverbs
steps.body: Adverbs describe verbs, adjectives or other adverbs: *how* (gently), *when* (soon), *where* (outside), *how often* (always), *how much* (very). Many end in -ly.

steps.title: Model dialogue
steps.body:
'Can I go now?' Jody asked eagerly.
'Take Mill-wheel with you,' Penny said quietly.
'And be back before dark,' Ma added firmly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing two speakers in one paragraph.
- Using adjectives where adverbs are needed: 'He spoke soft' → 'He spoke softly'.

courses.title: Ch 7 · A Visit to Cambridge (with poem: When I set out for Lyonnesse)
courses.summary: An Indian writer who uses a wheelchair meets the physicist Stephen Hawking in Cambridge and reflects on courage and disability; and Thomas Hardy's poem about a journey that magically changes the traveller.

Learners can discuss attitudes to disability with sensitivity

story.title: A phone call to a genius

scenes.text: Visiting Cambridge, writer Firdaus Kanga calls Stephen Hawking's house — and is invited to meet him.
Hawking speaks through a computer with a synthetic voice; each answer takes time.
The writer is moved by the man's courage and humour.

steps.title: Summary (original)
steps.body: **Firdaus Kanga**, an Indian writer who was born with a condition that made his bones brittle and who uses a wheelchair, travelled to Cambridge, England. He wanted to meet **Stephen Hawking**, the famous physicist who had motor neurone disease and could not move or speak naturally, communicating through a **computer and voice synthesiser**. During the short meeting, Kanga felt the frustration and patience of their conversation, the strength of Hawking's mind, and a sense of kinship: both lived full lives in bodies that did not obey them. He came away inspired — feeling that what matters is what one can do, not what one cannot.

steps.title: Ideas about disability
steps.body: The writer notes how people often call disabled persons 'brave' simply for living their lives, and how this can feel patronising. Real respect means seeing the person and their achievements, not only the disability, and making the world accessible (ramps, lifts, assistive technology).

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *Why was the writer inspired by the meeting?* → Hawking, despite severe physical limitations, had achieved greatness through his mind; it showed the writer that disability need not limit one's dreams.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing about Hawking's science instead of the meeting and its emotions.
- Using hurtful words for disability — use respectful, person-first language.

Firdaus Kanga uses a wheelchair.

lessons.title: Poem: When I set out for Lyonnesse

scenes.text: On a frosty night, a young man sets out on a lonely journey to a faraway place.
When he returns, there is magic in his eyes.
No one could have guessed what he would find there.

steps.title: Summary (original)
steps.body: In this poem by **Thomas Hardy**, the speaker recalls setting out on a long journey (about a hundred miles) to **Lyonnesse**, a legendary/remote place, in winter, alone, on a cold, frosty night. No wise person or prophet could have predicted what would happen to him there. When he returned, he was so changed — with **'magic in his eyes'** and radiance — that everyone noticed, though no one could guess its cause. (Many readers connect it to Hardy's own journey to Cornwall, where he met the woman he later married.)

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Repetition** of the opening line in each stanza.
- **Contrast:** lonely, cold beginning vs magical, glowing return.
- **Mystery:** the poet doesn't say exactly what happened.
- Theme: **life-changing experiences** that come unexpectedly.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *How did the speaker change after visiting Lyonnesse?* → He went lonely and cold but returned radiant and joyful, with 'magic in his eyes' — transformed by an experience he doesn't fully reveal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Saying the poet explains exactly what happened — he keeps it a mystery.

steps.title: Interview format
steps.body:

- End with thanks.

steps.title: Model interview (extract)
steps.body:
**Interviewer:** What keeps you motivated on hard days?
**Para-athlete:** Small goals. I tell myself — one more lap.
**Interviewer:** What would you tell young people facing obstacles?
**Para-athlete:** Focus on what you can do, and ask for the support you need.

steps.title: Vocabulary

- **Accessible:** easy to reach or use for everyone, including people with disabilities.

courses.title: Ch 8 · A Short Monsoon Diary (with poem: On the Grasshopper and Cricket)
courses.summary: Ruskin Bond's diary of the monsoon in the hills — mist, rain, birds, insects and changing moods — and John Keats's sonnet celebrating nature's never-ending music, from the summer grasshopper to the winter cricket.
outcomes: Learners can describe how Bond captures the monsoon in his diary entries

lessons.title: The diary: monsoon in the hills

scenes.text: In the hills of Mussoorie, mist rolls in and hides the valley.
Day after day the rain drums on the roof; ferns and wildflowers spring up.
The writer notes every bird, insect and change in light.

steps.title: About the text (original summary)
steps.body: **Ruskin Bond**, who lives in **Landour, Mussoorie**, kept a diary during the monsoon. His short entries capture the coming of the rains, the **mist** that blots out the mountains, the sound and smell of rain, swollen streams, **birds** that appear in the wet season, **insects** and creatures such as leeches and crawling things, ferns and wildflowers on the hillsides, and the moods of people and animals waiting for the sun. The diary shows his love for nature and his close **observation** of small details.

steps.title: Features of Bond's writing
steps.body:
- Simple, clear language.
- **Sensory details:** sights, sounds, smells, textures.
- Dates heading each entry.
- A calm, gentle, humorous tone.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *What does the diary tell us about the writer?* → He is a keen observer who loves nature, notices tiny details like insects and birds, and enjoys solitude and the changing seasons.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing a story summary — the text is a series of diary observations.
- Ignoring the sensory language.

quiz.why: Ruskin Bond wrote 'A Short Monsoon Diary'.
The diary is set in the hills of Mussoorie, in Landour, where Bond lives.

options: Simple language and close observation of nature

Each diary entry is headed by a date.
Sensory details appeal to the five senses: sight, sound, smell, touch and taste. They make the writing vivid.

lessons.title: Poem: On the Grasshopper and Cricket

scenes.text: In high summer, when birds fall silent in the heat, a grasshopper chirps in the hedges.
On a frosty winter evening, a cricket sings by the warm stove.
The poetry of earth never ends.

steps.title: Summary (original)
steps.body: In this **sonnet** by **John Keats**, the poet says that the **poetry of earth is never dead**. In **summer**, when birds hide from the hot sun, the **grasshopper's** voice is heard among the hedges and meadows; it leads the summer's song and rests when tired under a weed. In **winter**, on a lonely, frosty evening when all is silent, the **cricket's** song rises from the stove, and a drowsy listener may think it is the grasshopper singing in summer grass.

steps.title: Form and devices
steps.body:
- **Sonnet** (14 lines): first part (octave) about summer and the grasshopper, second part (sestet) about winter and the cricket.
- **Imagery** of seasons; **personification** of nature's 'poetry'; contrast of hot and cold.
- Theme: **nature's beauty and music are continuous through all seasons**.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: *How is the poetry of earth 'never dead'?* → In every season some creature sings — the grasshopper in summer, the cricket in winter — so nature's music goes on.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up which insect belongs to which season.
- Calling the poem a ballad — it's a sonnet.

quiz.why: In winter the song comes from the cricket, by the warm stove.

lessons.title: Writing a diary entry with sensory details

scenes.text: This week, keep a three-day diary about the weather where you live.
Note one sight, one sound and one smell each day.
Small details make writing come alive.

steps.title: Diary entry format
steps.body:
- Date (and day/time).
- Personal, informal tone; first person ('I').
- Describe what happened and how you felt.
- Use sensory details and precise words.

steps.title: Model entry
steps.body: *Monday, 14 July, 6 p.m.* The rain came at last — first a few fat drops, then a rush that hissed on the courtyard. The air smelled of wet earth and jasmine. A frog began croaking from the drain, as if it had waited all summer. I sat by the window with hot tea, happy to do nothing at all.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **Torrential:** very heavy (rain).
- **Drizzle:** light, fine rain.
- **Petrichor:** the pleasant smell of earth after rain.
- **Murky:** dark and unclear.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Making entries too formal or factual — diaries are personal.
- Forgetting the date.

quiz.why: A diary entry begins with the date. Bibliographies and receivers' addresses do not belong to it.

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body:
- Both texts celebrate **nature's continuity and small wonders**.

questions.why: In the poem, the cricket's winter song reminds a drowsy listener of the summer grasshopper's song, because both are the earth's music.

questions.q: Case: A student writes, 'Tuesday. It rained.' How can this diary entry improve?
options: Add sensory details, feelings and precise words
questions.why: 'Tuesday. It rained.' lacks detail. Adding sensory details, feelings and precise words makes a diary entry better.

questions.q: Assertion: Bond's diary is a fictional adventure story. Reason: It records observations of the monsoon in dated entries.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is false: Bond's diary is not a fictional adventure. R is true: it records observations of the monsoon in dated entries.

questions.q: The sonnet's two parts deal with:
questions.why: The sonnet's two parts deal with summer (the grasshopper) and winter (the cricket).

questions.q: Which best links both texts?
options: Close, loving observation of nature across seasons
questions.why: Both Bond's diary and Keats's sonnet show close, loving observation of nature across seasons: the monsoon in one, summer and winter insects in the other.

questions.q: Best diary sentence:
options: The first drops hissed on the hot stones, and the air filled with the smell of wet earth.
questions.why: The best diary sentence uses sensory detail: 'hissed on the hot stones' appeals to hearing and touch, and 'smell of wet earth' to smell. Plain statements like 'It rained' tell little.

lessons.title: How the Camel Got His Hump

scenes.text: Long ago, a lazy camel lives in the desert and refuses to work.
The horse, dog and ox ask him to help; he only says 'Humph!'
The Djinn of All Deserts gives him a hump — his very own 'humph'.

steps.title: Story (original retelling)
steps.body: In **Rudyard Kipling**'s *Just So* tale, the world is new and all animals work for Man — except the **Camel**, who lives idly in the desert and answers every request with 'Humph!'. The **Horse**, **Dog** and **Ox** complain to **Man**, who makes them work extra. The **Djinn in charge of All Deserts** asks the Camel to work; he keeps saying 'Humph!'. The Djinn magically puffs up a **hump** on his back, explaining that he can now work for **three days without eating**, living on his hump — making up for the days he missed. Ever since, the camel has had a hump and has never quite behaved well.

steps.title: Moral
steps.body: Laziness has consequences; everyone must share the work. (Kipling also uses humour and wordplay — 'humph' becomes 'hump'.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking the hump was a gift of comfort — it was a consequence of laziness.

activity.prompt: Order the story
items: The Camel refuses to work, saying 'Humph!'
Horse, Dog and Ox complain to Man
Man asks them to work harder
The Djinn asks the Camel to work
The Djinn gives the Camel a hump

quiz.why: 'How the Camel Got His Hump' is a story by Rudyard Kipling, from his Just So Stories.
The Camel answered every request with only 'Humph!', refusing to work.

quiz.q: Who gave the Camel his hump?
quiz.why: The Djinn of All Deserts, a magical being, gave the Camel his hump as punishment for his laziness.

quiz.q: The hump allows the Camel to:
quiz.why: The hump stores food, so the Camel can work for three days without eating. It makes up for the work he had refused to do.
The moral is that laziness has consequences. The Camel's refusal to work led to his getting the hump.

lessons.title: Children at Work

story.title: A boy alone at a big station

scenes.text: Eleven-year-old Velu runs away from his village and arrives at a huge city railway station.
A girl named Jaya, in rags, shows him how to survive — by picking and sorting rubbish.
He earns a little money, but it is hard, dirty work for a child.

steps.title: Story (original retelling)
steps.body: **Velu** leaves his village to escape a harsh home life and reaches **Chennai Central** station. Hungry and lost, he meets **Jaya**, a ragpicker girl, who takes him to a place where children collect and sort waste (plastic, paper, glass) for very low pay. Velu realises city life is not what he imagined; the work is tiring and unhealthy, but it's a way to survive.

steps.title: Issues raised
steps.body:
- **Child labour** and lost childhood.
- Children's right to education (6–14) and protection.
- Why children run away; the need for safe homes and support. Childline **1098** helps children in difficulty.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Romanticising Velu's adventure — the story highlights hardship.

activity.prompt: Questions readers ask

items.q: Is child labour legal in India?
items.a: Employing children under 14 is prohibited in almost all work (with limited family exceptions), and adolescents 14–18 cannot work in hazardous jobs.

items.q: What can a child in trouble do?
items.a: Find a trusted adult, a railway police officer or call 1098 (Childline).
Waste can contain sharp objects, chemicals and germs; children may get injured or ill.

quiz.why: In 'Children at Work', Velu arrives at Chennai Central, the railway station.
Jaya worked as a ragpicker, collecting waste to sell.
The story highlights child labour and the loss of childhood among poor children.
Childline is 1098, a free helpline for children in need.
Velu's new work was sorting waste for very little money, a hard and low-paid job.
