lessons.title: The Selfish Giant

scenes.text: A giant builds a wall around his garden and puts up a notice: no trespassers.
Spring never comes there; only Snow, Frost and the North Wind.
When children creep back in, spring returns — and his heart melts.

steps.title: Story (original retelling)
steps.body: In **Oscar Wilde**'s fairy tale, children play every afternoon in a **giant's** beautiful garden. Returning after years away, the giant drives them out and builds a high **wall** with a notice forbidding trespassers. Spring and summer avoid his garden; it is always winter. One day children creep in through a hole in the wall, and where they sit, trees blossom. In one corner a **little boy** cannot climb a tree; the giant gently lifts him up, the tree blossoms, and the giant knocks down the wall. Years later, the giant, now old, sees the little boy again — with marks of wounds on his hands and feet — who tells him that because the giant once let him play in his garden, he will take the giant to his own garden, Paradise. The children find the giant lying dead under the tree, covered with white blossoms.

steps.title: Message
steps.body: Selfishness makes life cold and barren; love and sharing bring joy and 'spring' into our lives.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Saying the giant stayed selfish — he changes completely.

statements.s: The giant built a wall to keep children out.
Spring came to the garden when the wall was built.
The giant helped a little boy climb a tree.
The story is by Oscar Wilde.

quiz.q: Why was it always winter in the garden?
options: Because the giant was selfish and shut out the children
quiz.why: The giant was selfish and shut the children out of his garden with a wall. So it stayed winter there, as spring did not come.
The children, creeping back in through a hole in the wall, brought spring back to the garden.

quiz.q: The giant knocked down the wall after:
quiz.why: The giant knocked down the wall after helping a little boy up into a tree. He understood the joy of sharing.
The main message is that love and sharing bring joy. Selfishness brings a cold, empty life.
'The Selfish Giant' is by Oscar Wilde.

lessons.title: The Treasure Within

story.title: Bad at maths, great at buildings

scenes.text: As a boy, Hafeez Contractor struggled with maths at school.
But he loved drawing and imagining spaces.
He became one of India's best-known architects.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: An **interview** with the architect **Hafeez Contractor** about his school days and career. He was not a top student and found some subjects hard, but he was creative and confident, enjoyed sports and drawing, and found his calling in **architecture**. He talks about thinking for yourself, enjoying childhood, and how marks alone don't define a person's future.

steps.title: Message
steps.body: Everyone has a 'treasure within' — talents and interests that may not show in marks. Discover and develop them.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Concluding that studies don't matter — the message is that different talents matter and should be nurtured.

activity.prompt: What is your 'treasure within' — a talent or interest that marks don't always show?
activity.hint: Think of what you lose track of time doing: drawing, building, coding, helping, music, sport…

quiz.why: Hafeez Contractor is a well-known architect, who designs buildings.

quiz.q: The text is in the form of an:
quiz.why: 'The Treasure Within' is in the form of an interview, with questions and answers.
As a boy he found some subjects, like maths, difficult at school, but he was gifted at drawing.
The 'treasure within' means one's hidden talents, which are worth finding and developing.
The message is to discover and nurture your talents, not to judge yourself by marks alone.

lessons.title: Princess September

story.title: The bird in the golden cage

scenes.text: The King of Siam has nine daughters, named after the months.
Each gets a parrot; September's dies, and a little wild bird comes to sing for her.
Her sisters tell her to cage it. What will she choose?

steps.title: Story (original retelling)
steps.body: In **W. Somerset Maugham**'s story, the King and Queen of Siam name their nine daughters after the months; the youngest is **September**. On the King's birthday, the princesses receive green parrots in golden cages. September's parrot dies, and she is heartbroken — until a little **bird** flies in and sings beautifully for her. Her jealous sisters persuade her to put it in a cage so it can't fly away. In the cage, the bird stops singing and grows ill. September realises it must be **free** to be happy, and opens the cage. The bird flies away — and then returns to sing for her every day of its own free will.

steps.title: Message
steps.body: True love respects freedom; we cannot possess those we love.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Saying the bird never came back — it returned freely.

activity.prompt: Order the story
items: Princesses receive parrots in golden cages
September's parrot dies
A little bird comes and sings for her
Sisters persuade her to cage it
The caged bird grows sad and ill
September frees it; it returns by choice

quiz.why: Princess September was the youngest of the king's daughters, with two older sisters.
The bird stopped singing because it was caged. Without freedom it had no joy to sing about.

quiz.q: Who persuaded September to cage the bird?
quiz.why: Her jealous sisters persuaded September to cage the bird.
The message is that love respects freedom. Keeping a bird in a cage is not love.
'The Princess September' is by Somerset Maugham.

lessons.title: The Fight

scenes.text: Ranji, new in town, finds a clear forest pool and swims in it.
A local boy, Suraj, claims the pool is his. They fight — and neither wins.
Days later they meet again… and become friends.

steps.title: Story (original retelling)
steps.body: In **Ruskin Bond**'s story, **Ranji**, a boy new to a hill town, discovers a beautiful pool in the forest. **Suraj**, a local boy, says the pool belongs to him and his friends and challenges Ranji. They wrestle and fight to exhaustion; neither clearly wins. Their next meeting brings another standoff, but gradually respect grows: Suraj admires Ranji's diving, Ranji admires Suraj's swimming skill, and they agree to teach each other. The 'fight' turns into **friendship**.

steps.title: Message
steps.body: Conflicts born of ego can turn into friendship when we respect each other's strengths.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking one boy won decisively.

statements.s: Ranji and Suraj fought over a forest pool.
Ranji clearly won the fight.
They became friends in the end.
The story is by Ruskin Bond.

quiz.why: Ranji and Suraj fought over a pool in the forest, each wanting to use it.
Neither won. The fight ended in a draw, and both were left exhausted.

options: They came to respect each other's skills
quiz.why: They became friends because they came to respect each other's skills, such as swimming and wrestling.
'The Fight' is by Ruskin Bond.
The message is that a quarrel driven by ego can turn into friendship, once the two respect one another.

courses.title: English Grammar for Class 8
courses.summary: The grammar most tested in Class 8: tenses, active and passive voice, direct and reported speech, modals, subject–verb agreement, determiners and prepositions, and clauses — with rules, examples, common errors and practice.
outcomes: Learners can choose and form the correct tense
Learners can change sentences between active and passive voice and direct and reported speech
Learners can use modals, determiners and prepositions accurately
Learners can apply subject–verb agreement and identify clauses

scenes.text: 'I have finished', 'I finished', 'I had finished' — Riya gets confused.
Her teacher draws a timeline.
Each tense places an action on the line.

steps.title: The 12 tense forms
steps.body:
- **Present:** simple (I write), continuous (I am writing), perfect (I have written), perfect continuous (I have been writing).
- **Past:** wrote / was writing / had written / had been writing.
- **Future:** will write / will be writing / will have written / will have been writing.

steps.title: Key uses
steps.body:
- Simple present: habits, facts (Water boils at 100 °C).
- Present perfect: past action with present result, no exact time (I have lost my key).
- Simple past: finished action at a known time (I lost it yesterday).
- Past perfect: the earlier of two past actions (The train had left when we arrived).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
- She ___ (live) here since 2020. → *has lived* (since + present perfect).
- When I reached, the film ___ (start). → *had started*.
- Look! It ___ (rain). → *is raining*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'I have seen him yesterday' ✘ → 'I saw him yesterday'.
- 'He is knowing the answer' ✘ → 'He knows' (stative verbs rarely take -ing).

activity.prompt: Fill in the correct tense.
activity.text: We ___ (know) each other since Class 1. Yesterday I ___ (meet) her at the market. By the time the bell rang, we ___ (finish) the test.

quiz.why: 'Already' goes with the present perfect, so 'have done' is right. 'Did' or 'do' would not show completion up to now.
A habit (every day) uses the simple present. For 'she', the verb takes -s: walks.
The bus left before we arrived, so the earlier action takes the past perfect: had left.
'Listen!' shows the action is happening now, so the present continuous is used: is crying.
'Yesterday' shows a finished time in the past, so the simple past 'saw' is right. The present perfect is not used with 'yesterday'.

scenes.text: 'Virat hit the ball.' — the doer is the hero.
'The ball was hit by Virat.' — now the ball is the focus.
Same event, different focus.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
Passive = **object + be (in the right tense) + past participle (+ by + doer)**.

- Simple present: is/am/are + V3 → *Letters are written.*
- Simple past: was/were + V3 → *The ball was hit.*
- Present perfect: has/have been + V3 → *The work has been done.*
- Future: will be + V3 → *It will be finished.*
- Modals: can/must be + V3 → *It must be done.*

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
- They built this bridge in 1990. → This bridge **was built** in 1990.
- The teacher has checked the copies. → The copies **have been checked** by the teacher.
- Someone stole my bag. → My bag **was stolen** (doer unknown — 'by someone' can be dropped).

steps.title: When to use passive
steps.body: When the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious — common in notices, science and news: *Visitors are requested…*; *The solution was heated.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrong tense of 'be': 'The cake is baked yesterday' ✘ → 'was baked'.
- Using V2 instead of V3: 'was wrote' ✘ → 'was written'.

activity.prompt: Match active to passive
pairs: A song is sung by her.
A letter was written by him.
A school has been built by them.
Trees will be planted by us.

options: The wall is painted by Ravi.
The wall was painted by Ravi.
Ravi is painted by the wall.
quiz.why: In the passive, the object comes first. For the simple present: is/are + past participle. So: The wall is painted by Ravi.

quiz.q: Passive of 'They will announce the results':
quiz.why: The future passive is 'will be' + past participle, so: The results will be announced.

quiz.q: Passive of 'Someone has broken the window':
quiz.why: The present perfect passive is 'has been' + past participle: The window has been broken.

options: The book is written in 1950 yesterday.
quiz.why: The simple past passive is 'was/were' + past participle. 'Written' is the past participle of write: The book was written in 1950.

quiz.q: Passive voice is often used when:
options: The doer is unknown or unimportant
quiz.why: The passive is used when the doer is unknown or unimportant, so the focus is on the action or the receiver.

scenes.text: Mum: 'I will be late today.'
Later, you tell your brother: 'Mum said that she would be late that day.'
Words change when we report them.

steps.title: Rules (reporting verb in past)
steps.body:
- Tense backshift: present → past; present perfect → past perfect; past → past perfect; will → would; can → could; may → might.
- Pronouns change to fit the speaker.
- Time/place: now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the previous day, here → there, this → that.
- **Questions:** asked + if/whether (yes/no) or wh-word; statement word order; no question mark.
- **Commands/requests:** told/asked/ordered + (not) to + verb.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
- He said, 'I am busy now.' → He said that he was busy then.
- She asked, 'Have you eaten?' → She asked if I had eaten.
- The teacher said, 'Open your books.' → The teacher told us to open our books.
- He said, 'Don't shout.' → He told me not to shout.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'She asked where was I going' ✘ → 'where I was going'.
- Keeping 'tomorrow' unchanged when reporting later.

activity.prompt: Change into reported speech.
activity.text: He said, 'I can swim.' → He said that he ___ swim. She said, 'I will come tomorrow.' → She said she would come ___ ___ ___.

options: She said that I am happy.
She said that she was happy.
She said she is being happy.
quiz.why: In reported speech, 'I am' becomes 'she was', so the pronoun and tense both change: She said that she was happy.

quiz.q: 'Where do you live?' he asked me. →
options: He asked where do you live.
He asked me where did I live?
He asked me where I lived.
quiz.why: A reported question uses statement order, with the tense shifted back: He asked me where I lived.

quiz.q: 'Please help me,' she said to him. →
options: She requested him to help her.
quiz.why: 'Please help me' is a request, so the reporting verb is 'requested': She requested him to help her.

options: The teacher told us to not running.
The teacher told us not to run.
The teacher asked we not run.
quiz.why: A negative command is reported with 'told ... not to' and the base verb: The teacher told us not to run.
In reported speech 'yesterday' becomes 'the previous day' (or 'the day before').

scenes.text: 'You must stop' vs 'You may stop' — very different!
'A few apples' vs 'few apples' — different too.
'In', 'on', 'at' — the tiny words that trip everyone.

steps.title: Modals
steps.body:
- **can/could:** ability, permission (could = past/polite).
- **may/might:** possibility, permission.
- **must:** necessity/obligation; **mustn't:** prohibition.
- **should/ought to:** advice, duty.
- **will/would:** future, willingness, polite requests.
- **need not:** no necessity.
Modals are followed by the base verb: *She can swim* (not *can swims*).

steps.title: Determiners
steps.body:
- **a/an/the:** a + consonant sound (a university), an + vowel sound (an hour).
- **some/any:** some in positive, any in negatives/questions.
- **few/a few, little/a little:** few/little = hardly any (negative); a few/a little = some (positive). Few/a few with countable; little/a little with uncountable.
- **much** (uncountable) / **many** (countable).

steps.title: Prepositions of time and place
steps.body:
- **at** a point (at 5 p.m., at the door); **on** days/dates/surfaces (on Monday, on the table); **in** months/years/enclosed spaces (in July, in the box).
- **since** a point in time; **for** a duration (since 2019; for three years).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
- You ___ wear a helmet; it's the law. → *must*
- We have ___ milk left — enough for tea. → *a little*
- I have lived here ___ 2015. → *since*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'He can sings' ✘.
- 'a hour' ✘ → 'an hour'.
- 'I am here since two hours' ✘ → 'I have been here for two hours'.

activity.prompt: Which word fits? (choose the bucket)

quiz.why: 'Must not' shows a prohibition, which means something that is forbidden, such as shouting in the library.
'Honest' begins with a vowel sound (the h is silent), so we use 'an'.
'For' is used with a length of time, such as ten years. 'Since' is used with a starting point.
We use 'on' with days of the week, as in 'on Monday'.
'Hardly any time' has a negative sense, so 'little' is used. 'A little' would mean some time is left.

scenes.text: 'The bunch of keys is/are on the table?'
The subject is 'bunch' — singular.
'The bunch of keys is on the table.'

steps.title: Subject–verb agreement rules
steps.body:
- Singular subject → singular verb; plural → plural.
- Phrases between subject and verb don't change agreement: *The box of pencils is…*
- **Each, every, either, neither, everyone, nobody** take singular verbs.
- **Either…or / neither…nor:** verb agrees with the nearer subject: *Neither the teacher nor the students were late.*
- Collective nouns (team, family) usually singular in Indian/British usage when acting as one unit.
- **The number of** (singular) vs **a number of** (plural).

steps.title: Clauses
steps.body:
- **Main (independent) clause:** complete sense alone.
- **Subordinate clause:** depends on the main clause.
  - Noun clause: *I know **that she is right**.*
  - Adjective (relative) clause: *The boy **who won** is my friend.*
  - Adverb clause: *We stayed inside **because it rained**.*

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
- Each of the girls ___ (has/have) a book. → *has*.
- A number of students ___ (is/are) absent. → *are*.
- Identify: *The book that I borrowed is torn.* → 'that I borrowed' = adjective clause.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'One of my friends are…' ✘ → 'is'.
- Treating the nearest noun in a phrase as the subject.

statements.s: 'Every student has a locker' is correct.
'Neither Ram nor his friends was there' is correct.
'The number of cars is increasing' is correct.
'The boy who won the race' contains an adjective clause.
'One of the books are missing' is correct.

quiz.why: The subject is 'list', which is singular. 'Items' is just part of the phrase, so the verb is 'is'.
With 'either...or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'I', so 'am' is used.
'A number of' means several, so it takes a plural verb: are waiting.

quiz.q: In 'I think that he is honest', 'that he is honest' is a:
quiz.why: 'That he is honest' is the object of 'think', so it works as a noun. It is a noun clause.

quiz.q: 'We left early because it was raining' — the adverb clause:
quiz.why: 'Because it was raining' tells the reason for leaving early, so it is an adverb clause of reason.

questions.q: 'She ___ here since morning.'
questions.why: 'Since morning' needs the present perfect, so 'has been' is right.

questions.q: Passive of 'He reads a book':
options: He is read by a book.
A book is read by him.
A book was read by him.
questions.why: The passive of the simple present puts the object first, with is + past participle: A book is read by him.

questions.q: '___ apple a day'
questions.why: 'Apple' starts with a vowel sound, so we use 'an'.

questions.q: 'Each of them ___ a prize.'
questions.why: 'Each' is singular, so the verb is 'gets'.

questions.q: 'I ___ him yesterday.'
questions.why: 'Yesterday' points to a finished time in the past, so we use the simple past: met.

questions.q: Reported: 'I am tired,' he said. →
options: He said that he was tired.
He told that he is tired.
He said that I am tired.
questions.why: In reported speech 'I am tired' becomes 'he was tired'. The pronoun changes from I to he, and am becomes was.

questions.q: 'You ___ not worry; I will help.'
questions.why: 'Need not' means there is no necessity. 'You need not worry' fits, as the speaker will help.

questions.q: Passive: 'They have finished the project.' →
options: The project was finished by them.
The project has been finished by them.
questions.why: The present perfect passive is 'has been' + past participle: The project has been finished by them.

questions.q: 'Neither the players nor the coach ___ happy.'
questions.why: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'coach', which is singular. So 'was' is used.

questions.q: Reported: 'Did you call me?' she asked. →
options: She asked if I had called her.
She asked did I call her?
She said if I call her.
She asked that I called her.
questions.why: A yes/no question is reported with 'if' and statement order, and the past simple moves back to the past perfect: She asked if I had called her.

questions.q: 'By the time we reached, the show ___.'
questions.why: The show began before we reached, so the earlier action takes the past perfect: had begun.

questions.q: Identify the clause type: 'The house where I was born is old.'
questions.why: 'Where I was born' describes the noun 'house', so it is an adjective clause.

questions.q: Passive: 'Who wrote this letter?' →
options: By whom was this letter written?
questions.why: A passive question of 'Who wrote this letter?' is 'By whom was this letter written?'

questions.q: Correct sentence:
options: I have waited since two hours.
I am waiting since two hours.
I have been waiting for two hours.
questions.why: A time period of two hours takes 'for', and an action that continues up to now takes the present perfect continuous: have been waiting.

questions.q: Reported: The teacher said, 'The earth revolves around the sun.' →
options: The teacher said that the earth revolved around the sun yesterday.
The teacher told the earth revolve.
The teacher asked the earth revolves.
The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.
questions.why: A universal truth stays in the present tense in reported speech, so: The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.

courses.title: Writing Skills for Class 8
courses.summary: Formats, model answers and checklists for notices, formal and informal letters, emails, diary entries, articles and story writing — the writing tasks most common in Class 8 exams.
outcomes: Learners can write notices and messages in the correct format
Learners can write formal and informal letters and emails
Learners can write diary entries and articles with clear structure
Learners can write a short story from a prompt

scenes.text: Someone loses a blue water bottle at school.
The notice board needs a clear, short notice.
Who, what, when, where, whom to contact.

steps.title: Notice format
steps.body: Institution name · NOTICE · Date · Title · Body (≈50 words: what, when, where, who, how) · Name & designation. Use a box; no greetings.

steps.title: Model notice
steps.body:
**ABC Public School** · NOTICE · 10 July
**Lost: Blue Water Bottle**
A blue steel water bottle with a sticker of a rocket was lost in the school playground on 9 July. The finder is requested to hand it over to the undersigned or the school office.
Aarav Mehta, Class 8 B

steps.title: Message writing
steps.body: Short note for someone who was absent: Date, time, 'Dear …', the message (who called, what, any action), your name. ~50 words.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing date/venue.
- Writing like a letter with 'Dear Sir'.

activity.prompt: Notice checklist
items: School name and NOTICE heading
Date
Clear title
What, when, where, who
Name and designation of the writer
About 50 words

quiz.why: A notice should have a title, the date, and the name and designation of the person who issues it.
A notice is short, about 50 words, so it can be read and understood quickly.
A notice usually begins with the name of the institution and the word NOTICE.

options: Someone who was absent when a call or visit came
quiz.why: A message is written for someone who was absent when a call or a visit came, to pass on information.

quiz.q: Which is NOT needed in a notice?
quiz.why: A notice does not need a closing like 'Yours lovingly'. It has a title, date and writer's name.

scenes.text: To grandma: 'Dear Nani, I miss you…'
To the Principal: 'Respected Ma'am, I request…'
Format and tone change with the reader.

steps.title: Formal letter format
steps.body: Sender's address · Date · Receiver's designation and address · Subject · Salutation (Sir/Madam) · Body (introduction, details, request/conclusion) · Complimentary close (Yours faithfully/sincerely) · Name.

steps.title: Informal letter format
steps.body: Sender's address · Date · Salutation (Dear Nani) · Body (friendly, personal) · Closing (With love / Your loving grandson) · Name.

steps.title: Email format
steps.body: To · Subject (short, clear) · Greeting · Body in short paragraphs · Polite close · Name. Keep it concise; no slang in formal emails.

steps.title: Model formal letter (body)
steps.body:
**Subject: Request for a water cooler on the second floor**
Respected Madam,
I am writing on behalf of the students of Class 8 to request a water cooler on the second floor. At present, students must go to the ground floor during breaks, which wastes time and crowds the stairs. A cooler would help everyone stay hydrated in summer.
Kindly consider our request.
Yours sincerely,
Neha Rao, Class Representative, 8 C

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing subject line in formal letters/emails.
- Mixing informal language ('Hey!') into formal letters.

activity.prompt: Formal or informal?

items.text: Letter to the Principal for leave
Letter to a friend about your holiday
Email to a company about a faulty product
Letter to your cousin congratulating her
Letter to the editor about traffic

quiz.q: A formal letter must have a:
quiz.why: A formal letter must have a subject line, which gives the purpose briefly.
A formal letter closes with 'Yours sincerely' or 'Yours faithfully'. Casual closings do not suit it.
For a friend we use an informal salutation like 'Dear Priya'. 'Respected Sir' and 'To whom it may concern' are formal.
A good email subject is short and clear, so the reader knows the topic at once.
A letter to the editor is a formal letter written to a newspaper about a public issue.

scenes.text: The editor wants an article: 'Why we should save water'.
Title, byline, introduction, points, conclusion.
Tonight, a diary entry about writing it.

steps.title: Article format
steps.body: **Title** (catchy) · **By: Name** · Introduction (hook + topic) · 2–3 body paragraphs (causes/effects/solutions with examples) · Conclusion (call to action). About 120–150 words.

steps.title: Model article opening
steps.body:
**Every Drop Counts** — by Kabir Singh
Imagine turning on the tap and finding it dry. For millions in India, this is real. Saving water is not a choice; it is our responsibility…

steps.title: Diary entry
steps.body: Date/day/time · personal tone · events + feelings + reflection · first person. Avoid formal greetings (optional 'Dear Diary').

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Article without title or byline.
- Diary entry that reads like a news report.

activity.prompt: Order an article's parts
items: Catchy title
Byline (By: name)
Introduction with a hook
Body paragraphs with points and examples
Conclusion with a call to action

quiz.why: An article has a title and a byline (the writer's name). It does not have a salutation or a subject line.

quiz.q: A diary entry is written in:
quiz.why: A diary entry is written in the first person, with a personal tone.

options: Ends with a call to action or strong idea
quiz.why: A good article ends with a strong idea or a call to action, which leaves the reader thinking.
A Class 8 article is usually about 120–150 words.
A hook is an interesting opening line that catches the reader's attention.

scenes.text: Prompt: 'The lights went out, and then I heard a knock at the door…'
Beginning, problem, climax, resolution.
Make the reader see and feel it.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body:
- **Beginning:** setting and characters (who, where, when).
- **Problem/conflict:** what goes wrong.
- **Rising action → climax:** tension builds to the turning point.
- **Resolution:** how it ends; a lesson if suitable.
- Give it a **title**. Use past tense, dialogue and sensory details. 150–200 words.

steps.title: Model (short)
steps.body: **The Knock** — The lights went out, and then I heard a knock at the door. My heart thudded. I tiptoed to the window: a small figure stood in the rain. 'Who's there?' I called. 'It's me, Arnav — our lights went out too, and Grandpa needs his medicine from the fridge!' We lit candles, found the box, and walked him home with an umbrella. Fear had turned into help — the best way an evening could end.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- No clear conflict.
- Sudden ending ('and then I woke up') without resolution.
- Switching tenses randomly.

activity.prompt: Story checklist
items: Title
Clear setting and characters
A problem or conflict
A climax
A satisfying resolution
Past tense, dialogue and sensory details

quiz.q: The turning point of a story is the:
quiz.why: The climax is the turning point of a story, where tension is highest.
Stories are usually written in the past tense.

options: 'And then I woke up' with no resolution
quiz.why: 'And then I woke up' with no resolution is a weak ending, since it avoids solving the story's problem.

options: See, hear and feel the scene
quiz.why: Sensory details help readers see, hear and feel the scene, which makes it vivid.

quiz.q: The first part of a story sets up:
quiz.why: The beginning of a story sets up the setting and the characters.

questions.q: A notice is about:
questions.why: A notice is about 50 words long, short and to the point.

questions.q: Closing of a formal letter:
questions.why: A formal letter closes with 'Yours sincerely' or 'Yours faithfully'.

questions.q: An article needs a:
questions.why: An article needs a title and a byline.

questions.q: A diary entry begins with:
questions.why: A diary entry begins with the date or day.

questions.q: Which is a formal letter?
options: To the Municipal Commissioner about garbage
questions.why: A letter to the Municipal Commissioner about garbage is formal, as it is addressed to an official on a public matter.

questions.q: Assertion: A formal letter has a subject line. Reason: It tells the reader the purpose at a glance.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: a formal letter has a subject line. R is true: it tells the reader the purpose at a glance. R explains A.

questions.q: The climax of a story is:
options: The turning point of highest tension
questions.why: The climax is the turning point of a story, where the tension is at its highest.

questions.q: Which is a good email subject?
questions.why: 'Request for leave on 12 July' is clear and says what the email is about. 'Hi', capitals and a blank subject are poor.

questions.q: A message is usually written for:
questions.why: A message is written for someone who was absent when the information came, so they get it later.

questions.q: Case: You must inform all students about a science quiz. Best format:
questions.why: To inform all students about an event, a notice is the right format, as it is short and put up for everyone.

questions.q: Which sentence suits a formal letter?
options: I request you to kindly take action.
questions.why: 'I request you to kindly take action' is polite and formal, which suits a formal letter. Slang and casual words do not.

questions.q: Assertion: Diary entries should be written in a formal tone. Reason: Diaries are personal records of feelings and events.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is false: a diary is personal, so its tone is informal, not formal. R is true: diaries record personal feelings and events.

questions.q: Best article conclusion:
options: Let us start today — every drop we save is a gift to tomorrow.
questions.why: A good conclusion ends with a call to action or a strong idea. 'Let us start today — every drop we save is a gift to tomorrow' does so.

questions.q: Which is the best story opening?
options: Rain hammered the windows as the lights flickered and died.
questions.why: A good story opening is a hook that creates a scene. 'Rain hammered the windows as the lights flickered and died' builds mood at once.

questions.q: Which order is correct for a formal letter?
options: Sender's address → date → receiver's address → subject → salutation → body → close
questions.why: A formal letter runs in this order: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation, body and closing.

courses.title: Class 8 English · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: Quick-revision cards for every Honeydew chapter and poem, a grammar rule sheet, two mixed mock papers (reading, literature, grammar, writing) and exam tips.
outcomes: Learners can recall authors, characters and themes of all chapters
Learners can apply grammar rules quickly
Learners can attempt mixed literature, grammar and writing questions under time pressure

scenes.text: Authors, poets and themes on cards.
Shuffle, recall, check.
Five minutes a day keeps forgetting away.

steps.title: Prose
steps.body:
- The Best Christmas Present in the World — Michael Morpurgo — Christmas truce 1914; peace; Jim, Connie, Hans Wolf.
- The Tsunami — accounts of 26 Dec 2004; Tilly Smith (Phuket); animals sensing danger.
- Glimpses of the Past — comic-strip history 1757–1857.
- Bepin Choudhury's Lapse of Memory — Satyajit Ray — Chunilal's trick; empathy.
- The Summit Within — Major H.P.S. Ahluwalia — Everest 1965; inner summit.
- This is Jody's Fawn — Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings — responsibility, compassion.
- A Visit to Cambridge — Firdaus Kanga — meeting Stephen Hawking; disability and courage.
- A Short Monsoon Diary — Ruskin Bond — nature observation.

steps.title: Poems
steps.body:
- The Ant and the Cricket (fable) — plan ahead.
- Geography Lesson — Zulfikar Ghose — why divide a small world?
- Macavity: The Mystery Cat — T.S. Eliot — the Hidden Paw.
- The Last Bargain — Tagore — freedom in joy.
- The School Boy — William Blake — caged bird, joyless school.
- The Duck and the Kangaroo — Edward Lear — nonsense verse, friendship.
- When I set out for Lyonnesse — Thomas Hardy — magical transformation.
- On the Grasshopper and Cricket — John Keats — 'poetry of earth is never dead'.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: In literature answers, name the character and give one specific detail from the text as evidence.

activity.prompt: Match author/poet to text
pairs: When I set out for Lyonnesse

quiz.why: Zulfikar Ghose wrote 'Geography Lesson'.

quiz.q: Who climbed Everest in 1965 and wrote about it?
quiz.why: H.P.S. Ahluwalia climbed Everest in 1965 as part of an Indian team and wrote 'The Summit Within'.
In T.S. Eliot's poem, Macavity is the Hidden Paw, a cat who is never caught.

quiz.q: Tilly Smith was on a beach in:
quiz.why: Tilly Smith was on the beach at Phuket, Thailand, when the tsunami came.
'The Best Christmas Present in the World', about the 1914 truce, is by Michael Morpurgo.

scenes.text: Tenses, voice, speech, modals, agreement.
Learn the rule, then the exception.
Test yourself immediately.

steps.title: Core rules
steps.body:
- Present perfect with since/for/already/just/yet; simple past with yesterday/ago/last.
- Passive: object + be + V3 (+ by doer); keep tense of 'be'.
- Reported speech: backshift; pronoun and time/place changes; questions in statement order; commands with 'to'.
- Modals + base verb; must (obligation), should (advice), may/might (possibility).
- a/an by sound; few/little negative, a few/a little positive.
- Each/every/either/neither → singular verb; either…or/neither…nor → nearer subject; the number (sing.) vs a number (pl.).

steps.title: Quick checks
steps.body:
- 'He have gone' ✘ → 'has gone'.
- 'The work was did' ✘ → 'was done'.
- 'She asked what was my name' ✘ → 'what my name was'.

steps.title: Speed tip
steps.body: Underline the subject and time words first — they tell you the verb form.

statements.s: 'An university' is correct.
'Neither of the boys is ready' is correct.
'The letter was written by her' is passive.
'He can plays' is correct.
'She has left yesterday' is correct.

quiz.why: 'Last week' shows a finished past time, so the simple past 'won' is right.
The simple present passive is is/are + past participle: Cakes are baked by Mira.

quiz.q: 'He said, "I like tea."' → He said that he ___ tea.
quiz.why: In reported speech 'I like tea' becomes 'he liked tea', as the present tense shifts back to the past.
'Should' is used to give advice, as in 'You should see a doctor'.
The subject is 'one', which is singular, so the verb is 'is', not 'are'.

scenes.text: 15 minutes.
Literature + grammar + writing sense.
7+ correct = on track.

steps.title: Instructions
steps.body: Attempt all eight. Then read explanations and correct mistakes in your notebook.

steps.title: Model literature answer
steps.body: *How does Penny Baxter show fairness?* → He agrees Jody may bring the fawn home, because the doe had given her life to save his; leaving the fawn to starve would be ungrateful.

steps.title: Model writing answer
steps.body: A notice for a lost ID card: school name, NOTICE, date, title 'Lost ID Card', details (where/when lost, description), contact, name and class.

activity.prompt: Which question type took you longest in Mock A — literature, grammar or writing? Why?
activity.hint: Plan to practise that type for ten minutes a day.

quiz.q: A1. The narrator in 'The Best Christmas Present' found the letter in:
options: A tin can on a beach
quiz.why: The narrator found the letter in a secret drawer of an old desk, which he had bought.

quiz.q: A2. The ant tells the cricket to:
quiz.why: The ant tells the cricket to dance the winter away. This is ironic, as the cricket sang all summer.

quiz.q: A3. Passive of 'The police caught the thief':
options: The thief was caught by the police.
The thief is caught by the police.
quiz.why: The simple past passive is 'was/were' + past participle: The thief was caught by the police.
'Listen!' shows something is happening now, so the present continuous 'is knocking' is used.

quiz.q: A5. Who hires the speaker in 'The Last Bargain'?
quiz.why: In Tagore's 'The Last Bargain' the speaker is finally hired by a child, who offers nothing.

quiz.q: A6. A formal letter closes with:
quiz.why: A formal letter closes with 'Yours sincerely' or 'Yours faithfully'.

quiz.q: A7. 'The poetry of earth is never dead' is from:
quiz.why: 'The poetry of earth is never dead' comes from Keats's poem 'On the Grasshopper and Cricket'.

quiz.q: A8. Assertion: Bepin really went to Ranchi. Reason: Chunilal arranged for people to say so.
options: A and R true; R explains A
quiz.why: A is false: Bepin never went to Ranchi, as it was a trick. R is true: Chunilal arranged for people to say so.

scenes.text: New day, new paper.
More application questions.
Read every option before choosing.

steps.title: Instructions
steps.body: 15 minutes. Eliminate clearly wrong options first.

steps.title: Model answer (poem)
steps.body: *What is the irony in 'Geography Lesson'?* → People understand why cities grow near water and can see the earth is small, yet they still hate each other and build walls.

steps.title: Reported-speech tip
steps.body: Questions become statements: *asked + if/wh-word + subject + verb*.

activity.prompt: Final-week English plan
items: Day 1: Literature cards + Mock A
Day 2: Grammar sheet + 20 practice sentences
Day 3: Write one notice, one letter, one article
Day 4: Mock B + correct mistakes
Day 5: Read one chapter aloud and rest well

quiz.q: B1. The schoolboy compares himself to:
quiz.why: In Blake's poem the schoolboy compares himself to a caged bird.

quiz.q: B2. Macavity is never caught because:
options: He's never at the scene; he has alibis
quiz.why: Macavity is never caught because he is never at the scene of the crime. He has alibis.

quiz.q: B3. Reported: 'Are you ready?' she asked. →
options: She asked that I am ready.
She asked if I was ready.
quiz.why: A reported yes/no question uses 'if', statement order and a past tense: She asked if I was ready.
'Since' goes with a point of time, such as Monday. 'For' goes with a period of time.

quiz.q: B5. Case: A writer meets a scientist who speaks through a computer and feels inspired. Which chapter?
quiz.why: A writer meeting Stephen Hawking, who speaks through a computer, is in 'A Visit to Cambridge'.

quiz.q: B6. The duck solved the kangaroo's worry by:
quiz.why: The duck bought woollen socks, which solved the kangaroo's worry about his wet feet.

quiz.q: B7. 'Neither the teacher nor the students ___ late.'
quiz.why: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'students', which is plural. So 'were' is used.

quiz.q: B8. Best title for a notice:
quiz.why: A notice has a clear title like 'Inter-House Debate Competition', which tells the reader the subject.

questions.q: 'This is Jody's Fawn' is from the novel:
questions.why: 'This is Jody's Fawn' is from the novel The Yearling by Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings.

questions.q: 'The Last Bargain' poet:
questions.why: Rabindranath Tagore wrote 'The Last Bargain'.

questions.q: Passive of 'She writes poems':
questions.why: The simple present passive is is/are + past participle: Poems are written by her.

questions.q: '___ hour ago'
questions.why: 'Hour' begins with a vowel sound (the h is silent), so we use 'an'.

questions.q: Who is the writer of 'A Short Monsoon Diary'?
questions.why: Ruskin Bond wrote 'A Short Monsoon Diary'.

questions.q: Assertion: Tilly Smith saved lives. Reason: She recognised tsunami warning signs from a geography lesson.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: Tilly saved lives. R is true: she recognised the warning signs from a geography lesson and warned others. R explains A.

questions.q: 'If buds are nipped…' appears in:
questions.why: 'If buds are nipped' comes from William Blake's poem 'The School Boy'.

questions.q: Reported: 'I will help you,' he said to me. →
options: He told me that he would help me.
He told that he will help me.
He told me that I will help you.
questions.why: In reported speech 'I will help you' becomes 'he would help me'. 'Will' shifts to 'would', and the pronouns change.

questions.q: Which is an informal letter?
options: To your friend about a trip
questions.why: A letter to a friend about a trip is informal. The others are formal letters.

questions.q: The central idea of 'Geography Lesson':
options: Humans divide a world that is small and one
questions.why: The poem's central idea is that humans divide a world that is small and one, though they know its geography well.

questions.q: 'Each of the students ___ a laptop.'
questions.why: 'Each' is singular, so it takes 'has'.

questions.q: Case: A friend is cruelly ignored by someone who later suffers the same feeling. Which story mirrors this?
questions.why: Someone who ignores a friend and later faces the same neglect is the lesson in Bepin Choudhury's story. His unkindness comes back to him.

questions.q: Assertion: 'The Duck and the Kangaroo' is nonsense verse. Reason: It presents playful, absurd situations with strong rhythm and rhyme.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: the poem is nonsense verse. R is true: it presents playful, absurd situations with rhythm and rhyme. That defines nonsense verse, so R explains A.

questions.q: Passive: 'Who has taken my pen?' →
options: By whom has my pen been taken?
Who has been taken my pen?
My pen has taken by whom?
questions.why: The passive of a question 'Who has taken my pen?' is 'By whom has my pen been taken?'

questions.q: Which two texts share the idea of a journey that transforms a person?
options: A Visit to Cambridge and When I set out for Lyonnesse
The Tsunami and The Ant and the Cricket
Jody's Fawn and Glimpses of the Past
questions.why: 'A Visit to Cambridge' and 'When I Set Out for Lyonnesse' both show a journey that changes the traveller.

questions.q: Which is the best evidence-based literature answer?
options: Jody is responsible: he patiently teaches the fawn to drink milk.
questions.why: A strong literature answer makes a point and backs it with evidence. 'Jody is responsible: he patiently teaches the fawn to drink milk' does this.

school-c8-maths-a.title: Class 8 Mathematics (part 1 of 2)
school-c8-maths-a.description: Every chapter of Class 8 Maths as its own course — concepts, solved examples in steps, common mistakes, quizzes and 15–20 question chapter tests — plus Revision & Practice. Chapters follow the rationalised NCERT Class 8 textbooks (2023–24 editions onward). NCERT has been introducing new Class 8 books from 2025–26; if your school uses those, chapter names and order differ, but most topics here still apply. Independent material, not affiliated with NCERT or any board.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Rational Numbers
courses.summary: Rational numbers p/q, their properties (closure, commutativity, associativity, distributivity), identities and inverses, the number line, and finding rational numbers between two given ones.
outcomes: Learners can decide whether a number is rational and write it as p/q
Learners can test closure, commutative and associative properties for each operation
Learners can find additive and multiplicative inverses and use distributivity to simplify
Learners can place rationals on a number line and insert any number of rationals between two given ones

lessons.title: What is a rational number? Closure

scenes.text: Riya halves a recipe, then needs 3/4 of the half.
Is 3/8 cup still a 'proper' number? Can every such answer be written as a fraction?
Yes — that idea is called *closure*.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
A **rational number** is any number that can be written as **p/q**, where p and q are integers and **q ≠ 0**.

- Every integer is rational: 5 = 5/1, −7 = −7/1, 0 = 0/1.
- Every fraction is rational: 3/4, −2/9.
- Terminating and repeating decimals are rational: 0.25 = 1/4, 0.333… = 1/3.

Numbers such as √2 and π cannot be written as p/q; they are *irrational* (you study them in Class 9).

steps.title: Closure property
steps.body:
A set is **closed** under an operation if doing that operation on any two members always gives a member of the same set.

- **Addition:** a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/bd → rational. **Closed.**
- **Subtraction:** always rational. **Closed.**
- **Multiplication:** (a/b)(c/d) = ac/bd → rational. **Closed.**
- **Division:** NOT closed, because division by 0 is not defined (5 ÷ 0 has no value). For non-zero rationals, the quotient is rational.

Compare: whole numbers are not closed under subtraction (3 − 5 = −2); integers are not closed under division (3 ÷ 5 = 3/5).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Show that −3/5 + 7/10 is rational.

- Step 1: LCM of 5 and 10 is 10, so −3/5 = −6/10.
- Step 2: −6/10 + 7/10 = 1/10.
- Step 3: 1/10 has integer numerator and non-zero integer denominator → rational. ✔

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Is (−4/9) × (3/8) rational?

- Multiply numerators: −4 × 3 = −12. Multiply denominators: 9 × 8 = 72.
- −12/72 = −1/6 (divide by HCF 12).
- −1/6 is of the form p/q → rational. ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'rationals are closed under division' — forgetting the zero divisor.
- Thinking negative numbers or integers are not rational.
- Writing 0/5 as undefined. 0/5 = 0 is perfectly fine; it is 5/0 that is undefined.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: When asked 'Is the set closed under ÷?', always give the counter-example **a ÷ 0**.

activity.prompt: Sort each set–operation pair: is it closed?

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a rational number?
quiz.why: 5/0 has a zero denominator, so it is undefined and not a rational number. Rationals have the form p/q with q not zero.
Rationals are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication. They are not closed under division, because we cannot divide by zero.

quiz.q: Which set is NOT closed under subtraction?
quiz.why: Whole numbers are not closed under subtraction. For example, 2 − 5 = −3, which is not a whole number.

quiz.q: 0.6 written as p/q in lowest terms is:
quiz.why: 0.6 = 6/10. Dividing numerator and denominator by 2 gives 3/5, which is in lowest terms.

scenes.text: Arjun adds 1/2 + 1/3 and his sister adds 1/3 + 1/2.
They get the same 5/6.
But 1/2 − 1/3 and 1/3 − 1/2 are different… why?

steps.title: Commutative property
steps.body:
An operation is **commutative** if changing the order of the two numbers does not change the result.

- a + b = b + a ✔ for rationals
- a × b = b × a ✔
- a − b ≠ b − a in general ✘ (e.g. 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6 but 1/3 − 1/2 = −1/6)
- a ÷ b ≠ b ÷ a in general ✘

steps.title: Associative property
steps.body:
An operation is **associative** if grouping does not change the result: (a ∗ b) ∗ c = a ∗ (b ∗ c).

- Addition ✔ and multiplication ✔ are associative for rationals.
- Subtraction ✘ and division ✘ are not.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Show that subtraction is not associative using 1/2, 1/3, 1/4.

- (1/2 − 1/3) − 1/4 = 1/6 − 1/4 = 2/12 − 3/12 = −1/12.
- 1/2 − (1/3 − 1/4) = 1/2 − 1/12 = 6/12 − 1/12 = 5/12.
- −1/12 ≠ 5/12, so subtraction is not associative.

steps.title: Why this helps
steps.body: Commutativity + associativity let you **regroup** to make sums easy: 2/5 + 7/3 + 3/5 = (2/5 + 3/5) + 7/3 = 1 + 7/3 = 10/3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using one example where a − b = b − a (like a = b) to 'prove' subtraction is commutative. One counter-example disproves; one agreeing example proves nothing.
- Mixing up 'commutative' (order) with 'associative' (grouping).

statements.s: For rationals, a × b = b × a.
(a ÷ b) ÷ c = a ÷ (b ÷ c) for all non-zero rationals.
Addition of rationals is associative.
statements.why: Grouping does not change a sum.

statements.s: Subtraction of rationals is commutative.
Whole numbers are commutative under addition.

quiz.why: Swapping the two numbers in an addition gives the same sum. That is the commutative property.

quiz.q: Which operation on rationals is associative?
quiz.why: Multiplication of rationals is associative: (ab)c = a(bc). Subtraction and division are not.

quiz.q: A single counter-example is enough to show a property:
quiz.why: A property must hold for all numbers, so one counter-example shows it fails.
Regroup 5/8 + 3/8 first, which gives 1. Then 1 + 4/9 = 13/9. This is easier than adding unlike fractions.

scenes.text: A shopkeeper adds and removes the same weight from a pan.
+3/4 kg then −3/4 kg leaves nothing changed — that pair are *additive inverses*.
Multiplying by 1 changes nothing too.

steps.title: Identities
steps.body:
- **Additive identity: 0.** a + 0 = 0 + a = a.
- **Multiplicative identity: 1.** a × 1 = 1 × a = a.
- a × 0 = 0 for every rational a.

steps.title: Inverses
steps.body:
- **Additive inverse (negative)** of a/b is −a/b, because a/b + (−a/b) = 0.
- **Multiplicative inverse (reciprocal)** of a/b (a ≠ 0) is b/a, because (a/b)(b/a) = 1.
- 0 has no reciprocal. 1 and −1 are their own reciprocals.
- The reciprocal of a negative number is negative: reciprocal of −3/7 is −7/3.

steps.title: Distributive property
steps.body:
Multiplication distributes over addition and subtraction:

- a(b + c) = ab + ac
- a(b − c) = ab − ac

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Find the reciprocal of (−3/4) × (5/9).

- Product = −15/36 = −5/12.
- Reciprocal = −12/5.
- Check: (−5/12)(−12/5) = 1 ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the reciprocal of −3/7 is 7/3 (the sign stays: −7/3).
- Confusing additive inverse (change sign) with multiplicative inverse (flip).
- Saying 0 is its own reciprocal — 0 has no reciprocal.

activity.prompt: Match each number with what is asked

quiz.why: The reciprocal of −1 is −1, because (−1) × (−1) = 1.
The additive inverse of −7/19 is 7/19, because −7/19 + 7/19 = 0.
0 has no reciprocal, since no number multiplied by 0 gives 1.

quiz.q: a(b − c) = ab − ac is the:
quiz.why: a(b − c) = ab − ac is the distributive property of multiplication over subtraction.
x is the reciprocal of −4/3, which is −3/4. Check: (−3/4)(−4/3) = 1.

lessons.title: Rational numbers on the number line

scenes.text: Kabir must mark −5/4 on a number line for homework.
He divides each unit into 4 equal parts and counts 5 parts to the left of 0.
The mark lands between −1 and −2.

steps.title: How to represent p/q
steps.body:
- Divide each unit length into **q** equal parts (the denominator tells how many parts).
- Count **p** parts: to the right of 0 if positive, to the left if negative.
- Improper fractions first: 7/3 = 2 1/3, so go to 2 and then 1 more third.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Represent 5/3.

- 5/3 = 1 2/3.
- Divide the segment from 1 to 2 into 3 equal parts.
- Mark the 2nd point after 1. That point is 5/3.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Represent −3/4.

- Divide 0 to −1 into 4 equal parts.
- Count 3 parts to the left from 0.
- The point lies three-quarters of the way to −1.

steps.title: Order
steps.body: On a number line, a number to the right is always greater. So −1/2 > −3/4 because −1/2 lies to the right of −3/4.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing into p parts instead of q parts.
- Counting a negative number to the right.
- Forgetting that −1/2 is greater than −3/4 (the minus signs reverse the usual size feeling).

activity.prompt: On a number line from 0 to 1 divided into 8 equal parts, how many parts from 0 is 3/4?

quiz.q: To mark 7/5, each unit is divided into:
quiz.why: To mark 7/5, divide each unit into 5 equal parts, since the denominator is 5, and count 7 parts from 0.
−7/4 = −1 3/4, which lies between −1 and −2.
−2/3 = −8/12 and −3/4 = −9/12. On the number line −8/12 is to the right of −9/12, so −2/3 is greater.

quiz.q: The point halfway between 0 and 1/2 is:
quiz.why: The point halfway between 0 and 1/2 is their average: (0 + 1/2) ÷ 2 = 1/4.
11/3 = 3 2/3, which lies between 3 and 4.

scenes.text: Meera notices a train line could add a stop between any two stops.
Between those, another… and another.
Rational numbers are like that: between any two there are infinitely many.

steps.title: Density of rationals
steps.body: Between any two different rational numbers there are **infinitely many** rational numbers. (Between two consecutive integers like 2 and 3 there is no *integer*, but there are endless rationals.)

steps.title: Method 1 — equivalent fractions
steps.body: Write both numbers with a common, large denominator. Example: between 1/3 and 1/2 → 4/12 and 6/12 → 5/12 lies between. Need more? Use 40/120 and 60/120 → 41/120 … 59/120 (19 numbers).

steps.title: Method 2 — mean (average)
steps.body: For rationals a < b, the number (a + b)/2 always lies between them. Repeat with the new number to get more.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Find 3 rational numbers between −2 and 0.

- Write −2 = −20/10 and 0 = 0/10.
- Choose −15/10, −10/10, −5/10, i.e. −3/2, −1, −1/2. ✔

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Find a rational number between 1/4 and 1/2 by the mean method.

- (1/4 + 1/2)/2 = (3/4)/2 = 3/8.
- Check: 1/4 = 2/8 < 3/8 < 4/8 = 1/2 ✔.
- Again: (1/4 + 3/8)/2 = 5/16 gives another.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying there are no rationals between 1/3 and 1/2 because their numerators are 'consecutive'.
- Adding numerators and denominators: (1+1)/(3+2) = 2/5 happens to lie between here, but that is not the mean method, and you must still check order.

activity.prompt: Fill in the rational number exactly halfway between the two given numbers.
activity.text: Halfway between 1/5 and 2/5 is ___. Halfway between −1 and 0 is ___.

quiz.q: How many rational numbers lie between 1 and 2?
quiz.why: Between any two rational numbers there are infinitely many more. This is the density of rationals.

quiz.q: A rational number between 2/7 and 3/7 is:
quiz.why: 2/7 = 4/14 and 3/7 = 6/14. The number 5/14 lies between them.
−1/2 = −4/8 and −1/4 = −2/8. So −3/8 lies between them.

quiz.q: To find 10 rationals between 3/5 and 4/5 quickly, multiply numerator and denominator by:
quiz.why: Multiplying by 11 gives 33/55 and 44/55, which have ten numbers between them: 34/55 to 43/55.

questions.q: Which of these is a rational number?
questions.why: −11/13 is of the form p/q with q not zero, so it is rational. √2, √3 and π are not.

questions.q: Rational numbers are NOT closed under:
questions.why: Rationals are not closed under division, because dividing by 0 is undefined.

questions.q: The additive inverse of 0 is:
questions.why: The additive inverse of 0 is 0, since 0 + 0 = 0.

questions.q: The reciprocal of −2/9 is:
questions.why: The reciprocal of −2/9 is −9/2, because (−2/9)(−9/2) = 1.
Multiplying a number over a sum and splitting it is the distributive property.

questions.q: Assertion (A): 0 has no reciprocal. Reason (R): 0 × any number = 0, never 1.
options: A and R true; R explains A
A and R true; R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: 0 has no reciprocal. R is true: 0 times any number is 0, never 1. So R explains A.
The LCM of 16 and 12 is 48. −5/16 = −15/48 and 7/12 = 28/48. The sum is 13/48.
(1/2 ÷ 1/4) = 2, and 2 ÷ 1/8 = 16. Also 1/4 ÷ 1/8 = 2, and 1/2 ÷ 2 = 1/4. The values differ, so division is not associative.

questions.q: Which number lies between −3/4 and −1/2?
questions.why: −3/4 = −6/8 and −1/2 = −4/8. So −5/8 lies between them.

questions.q: Using distributivity, 99/100 × 7 + 1/100 × 7 =
questions.why: Use distributivity: (99/100 + 1/100) × 7 = 1 × 7 = 7.

questions.q: The product of a non-zero rational and its reciprocal is:
questions.why: A non-zero rational times its reciprocal is 1, by the definition of reciprocal.

questions.q: Case: A rope is 15/4 m long. Asha cuts off 5/6 m, then 2/3 m. Length left?
questions.why: Length left = 15/4 − 5/6 − 2/3. With 12 as the denominator: 45/12 − 10/12 − 8/12 = 27/12 = 9/4 m.

questions.q: If the sum of two rationals is −4/5 and one is −13/20, the other is:
By what should −8/39 be multiplied to get 1/26?
Number of rationals strictly between 3/10 and 4/10 with denominator 100:
questions.why: 3/10 = 30/100 and 4/10 = 40/100. The numbers with denominator 100 strictly between are 31/100 to 39/100, which are 9 numbers.

questions.q: Where is −13/5 on the number line?
questions.why: −13/5 = −2 3/5, which lies between −2 and −3.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Linear Equations in One Variable
courses.summary: Solving linear equations with the variable on one or both sides, transposing, reducing equations with fractions to simpler form, and turning word problems (numbers, ages, money, geometry, digits) into equations.
outcomes: Learners can solve linear equations by balancing or transposing
Learners can solve equations with the variable on both sides and with fractions
Learners can translate word problems into equations and check answers
Learners can recognise when an equation is linear

lessons.title: Linear equations and solving by transposing

scenes.text: A magician says: 'Think of a number, double it, add 7. Tell me the answer.'
Sanya says 31.
'Your number was 12!' — he solved 2x + 7 = 31 in his head.

steps.title: What is a linear equation?
steps.body:
An **equation** is a statement that two expressions are equal. It is **linear in one variable** if the highest power of the variable is **1**: e.g. 2x + 7 = 31, 3(y − 2) = y/2.

Not linear: x² + 1 = 5 (power 2), 1/x = 4 (variable in denominator, reduces to a non-linear form in general).

steps.title: Balancing and transposing
steps.body:
Whatever you do to one side, do to the other. A shortcut is **transposing**: move a term to the other side and change its sign.

- +a becomes −a, −a becomes +a
- ×a becomes ÷a, ÷a becomes ×a (a ≠ 0)

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Solve 2x + 7 = 31.

- Transpose 7: 2x = 31 − 7 = 24.
- Divide by 2: x = 12.
- Check: 2(12) + 7 = 31 ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to change the sign when transposing.
- Dividing only one term: from 2x + 6 = 10 writing x + 6 = 5. Correct: 2x = 4, x = 2.
- Not checking the answer by substitution.

steps.title: Habit
steps.body: Always end with a **check line**. Examiners give marks for it and it catches sign errors.

activity.prompt: Put the steps for solving 3x − 5 = 16 in order
items: Write the equation 3x − 5 = 16
Transpose −5: 3x = 16 + 5
Simplify: 3x = 21
Divide by 3: x = 7

quiz.q: Which is a linear equation in one variable?
quiz.why: 3x + 2 = 11 has one variable with power 1, so it is linear in one variable. x² − 4 = 0 has power 2, and x + y = 5 has two variables.

quiz.q: When transposing '+8' to the other side it becomes:
quiz.why: When we move a term across the equals sign, its sign changes. So +8 becomes −8.

scenes.text: Plan A: ₹200 + ₹2 per minute. Plan B: ₹100 + ₹4 per minute.
After how many minutes do they cost the same?
200 + 2m = 100 + 4m — variables on both sides!

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
- Collect variable terms on one side (usually the side with the larger coefficient, to keep it positive).
- Collect constants on the other side.
- Simplify and divide.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sign slip when expanding −2(2x − 7): it is −4x **+14**, not −14.
- Moving x but forgetting to change its sign.
- Stopping at 5x = 25/2 without dividing.

steps.title: Real world
steps.body: Comparing plans (mobile, gym, taxi) is exactly this: fixed charge + rate × usage on both sides.

activity.prompt: Solve 8x − 3 = 3x + 22. x = ?

quiz.why: 3x = 2x + 18, so 3x − 2x = 18, which gives x = 18.
2y + 9/2 = 4y − 1/2. Moving terms: 9/2 + 1/2 = 2y, so 5 = 2y and y = 5/2.
4(z + 3) = 4z + 12 and 2(2z + 6) = 4z + 12. Both sides are equal for every z, so it is an identity.

scenes.text: Grandma: 'I am 5 times as old as Tara. In 8 years I'll be 3 times as old.'
Tara: 'Let my age be x.'
5x + 8 = 3(x + 8) → x = 8. Tara is 8, Grandma 40.

steps.title: The 5-step plan
steps.body:
- **Read** and identify the unknown.
- **Let** x = the unknown (write it!).
- **Translate** each sentence into algebra.
- **Solve** the equation.
- **Check** in the words of the problem and answer with units.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — consecutive numbers
steps.body:
Sum of three consecutive multiples of 8 is 888. Find them.

- Let them be 8x, 8x + 8, 8x + 16.
- 24x + 24 = 888 → 24x = 864 → x = 36.
- Numbers: 288, 296, 304. Check: sum 888 ✔.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — money
steps.body:
Bansi has ₹2, ₹5 coins in ratio 3 : 5, total ₹93. How many of each?

- Let ₹2 coins = 3x, ₹5 coins = 5x.
- 2(3x) + 5(5x) = 93 → 6x + 25x = 93 → 31x = 93 → x = 3.
- ₹2 coins = 9, ₹5 coins = 15. Check: 18 + 75 = 93 ✔.
- If x ever comes out as a fraction of a coin, re-read the question — you have mistranslated something.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — ages
steps.body:
Ratio of ages of Hari and Harry is 5 : 7. Four years later it will be 3 : 4.

- Ages 5x and 7x. (5x + 4)/(7x + 4) = 3/4.
- 4(5x + 4) = 3(7x + 4) → 20x + 16 = 21x + 12 → x = 4.
- Ages 20 and 28 years ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not stating what x stands for.
- Adding the years to only one person in age problems.
- Giving x as the final answer when the question asks for 5x.

a.text: A number is 12 more than another. Their sum is 74. How will you start?

g.text: Guessing wastes time in exams. Let's define x instead: smaller = x, larger = x + 12.

c.text: x = 31, so the numbers are 31 and 43. Check: 31 + 43 = 74 ✔

quiz.q: The sum of two consecutive odd numbers is 56. The smaller is:
quiz.why: Let the smaller odd number be x. Then x + (x + 2) = 56, so 2x = 54 and x = 27.

quiz.q: A number's 2/5 is 14. The number is:
quiz.why: 2/5 of the number is 14, so the number is 14 × 5/2 = 35.

quiz.q: Father is 3 times as old as son; sum of ages is 48. Son's age:
quiz.why: If the son is x, the father is 3x. Then 4x = 48, so x = 12.

quiz.q: Perimeter of a rectangle is 13 cm and width is 11/4 cm. Length?
In an age problem 'after 5 years' means you should:
quiz.why: After 5 years, every person is 5 years older, so 5 is added to each person's age.

scenes.text: Dev sees (6x + 1)/3 + 1 = (x − 3)/6 and panics.
Teacher: 'Multiply every term by the LCM, 6.'
The fractions vanish.

steps.title: Clearing fractions
steps.body: Multiply **every term on both sides** by the LCM of all denominators. Then solve normally.

steps.title: Cross-multiplication
steps.body: If (ax + b)/(cx + d) = m/n, then n(ax + b) = m(cx + d). This turns an equation with the variable in the denominator into a linear one (valid when cx + d ≠ 0).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying only the fraction terms and forgetting plain terms like '+1'.
- Forgetting brackets: 2(6x + 1), not 12x + 1.
- Cross-multiplying when there are extra terms outside the fractions — first combine into one fraction on each side.

activity.prompt: Solve x/2 − 1/5 = x/3 + 1/4. x = ? (as a decimal)

quiz.why: The LCM of 3 and 4 is 12, so multiply the equation by 12 to clear the fractions.
Multiply by 12: 4x + 3x = 84, so 7x = 84 and x = 12.
Cross-multiply: 8(x + 1) = 3(2x + 3), so 8x + 8 = 6x + 9. Then 2x = 1 and x = 1/2.
Multiplying both sides by 3: 2x − 1 = 15. The whole numerator 2x − 1 stays together.

scenes.text: Ali: 'Reverse the digits of my number and add it to the original: you get 143.'
Digits add to 13 since 11 × 13 = 143.
With one more clue, the number is pinned down.

steps.title: Digit numbers
steps.body: A two-digit number with tens digit a and units digit b is **10a + b**. Reversed: **10b + a**. Sum = 11(a + b), difference = 9(a − b).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Digits of a two-digit number differ by 3. Reversing and adding gives 143. Find the number.

- Let units = x, tens = x + 3. Number = 10(x + 3) + x = 11x + 30.
- Reversed = 10x + (x + 3) = 11x + 3.
- 22x + 33 = 143 → x = 5. Number = 85 (or 58 if tens is smaller). Check 85 + 58 = 143 ✔.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — angles
steps.body:
Angles of a triangle are in ratio 2 : 3 : 4. Find them.

- 2x + 3x + 4x = 180° → 9x = 180° → x = 20°.
- Angles: 40°, 60°, 80° ✔.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — rectangle
steps.body:
Length is 2 cm more than twice the breadth; perimeter 46 cm.

- 2(2b + 2 + b) = 46 → 3b + 2 = 23 → b = 7 cm, l = 16 cm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the number 'ab' as a × b or a + b instead of 10a + b.
- Forgetting the triangle angle sum (180°) or quadrilateral sum (360°).

activity.prompt: Complete the digit algebra.
activity.text: A two-digit number with tens digit 7 and units digit x is ___ + x. Reversing gives 10x + ___.

quiz.q: Number with tens digit p and units digit q:
quiz.why: A two-digit number with tens digit p and units digit q is 10p + q, by place value.

quiz.q: The difference between a two-digit number and its reverse is always a multiple of:
quiz.why: (10a + b) − (10b + a) = 9a − 9b = 9(a − b). So the difference is always a multiple of 9.

quiz.q: Two supplementary angles differ by 20°. The larger is:
quiz.why: Let the larger angle be x. Then x + (x − 20) = 180, so 2x = 200 and x = 100°.

quiz.q: Sides of a triangle are x, x + 2, x + 4 cm; perimeter 30 cm. Longest side:
quiz.why: Perimeter: x + (x + 2) + (x + 4) = 30, so 3x + 6 = 30 and x = 8. The longest side is x + 4 = 12 cm.

quiz.q: Base angles of an isosceles triangle are each 40°. Vertex angle:
quiz.why: The angles of a triangle add to 180°. The vertex angle = 180° − (40° + 40°) = 100°.

questions.q: Which is linear in one variable?
questions.why: 2x + 5 = 9 has one variable with power 1, so it is a linear equation in one variable.

questions.q: Solve x + 7 = 3
Solve 3x/5 = 9
Solve 2x − 3 = x + 2

questions.why: Multiply by the LCM 12: 6n − 9n + 10n = 252. So 7n = 252 and n = 36.

questions.q: Sum of three consecutive integers is 51. The middle one is:
questions.why: If the middle number is x, the three numbers are x − 1, x, x + 1. Their sum is 3x = 51, so x = 17.

questions.q: A number is multiplied by 5 and 21 is subtracted, giving 4 more than twice the number. The number is:
Assertion: x = 2 is the solution of 3x + 1 = 7. Reason: substituting x = 2 makes both sides 7.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: x = 2 solves 3x + 1 = 7. R is true: substituting gives 3(2) + 1 = 7, which checks the solution. So R explains A.

questions.q: Amina is 3 times as old as her son. 5 years ago she was 4 times as old. Son's present age:
questions.why: Let the son's age be x, so Amina is 3x. Five years ago: 3x − 5 = 4(x − 5), so 3x − 5 = 4x − 20, and x = 15.

questions.q: Case: A shop sells pens at ₹8 and pencils at ₹3. Neha buys 4 more pencils than pens and pays ₹78. How many pens?
questions.why: Let pens be p, so pencils are p + 4. Then 8p + 3(p + 4) = 78, so 11p = 66 and p = 6.

questions.q: Digits of a two-digit number add to 9. Adding 27 reverses the digits. The number is:
questions.why: Let the digits be a and b. a + b = 9 and (10a + b) + 27 = 10b + a, giving b − a = 3. So a = 3 and b = 6, and the number is 36.

questions.q: Perimeter of a rectangle is 64 m and length is 4 m more than breadth. Area?
questions.why: With breadth b, length = b + 4. The perimeter 2(2b + 4) = 64 gives b = 14 and l = 18. Area = 14 × 18 = 252 m².

questions.q: Half of a number added to 7 gives one-third of the number added to 9. Number:
questions.why: x/2 + 7 = x/3 + 9, so x/2 − x/3 = 2. This gives x/6 = 2, and x = 12.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Understanding Quadrilaterals
courses.summary: Polygons and their classification, convex and concave shapes, regular polygons, the angle-sum and exterior-angle-sum properties, and the properties of trapeziums, kites, parallelograms, rhombuses, rectangles and squares.
outcomes: Learners can classify polygons by sides and as convex/concave, regular/irregular
Learners can use (n − 2) × 180° and the 360° exterior-angle sum
Learners can state and apply properties of parallelograms and special quadrilaterals
Learners can solve angle and side problems in quadrilaterals step by step

lessons.title: Polygons: names, diagonals, convex and regular

scenes.text: Zoya spots a STOP sign (8 sides), floor tiles (6 sides) and a kite in the sky.
'Which of these are polygons? Which are regular?'
Let's sort shapes like a mathematician.

steps.title: Polygon
steps.body:
A **polygon** is a simple closed curve made only of line segments. Curves with arcs (like a circle) are not polygons; open figures are not polygons.

Names by number of sides: 3 triangle · 4 quadrilateral · 5 pentagon · 6 hexagon · 7 heptagon · 8 octagon · 9 nonagon · 10 decagon · n sides: n-gon.

steps.title: Diagonals
steps.body: A **diagonal** joins two non-consecutive vertices. A polygon with n sides has **n(n − 3)/2** diagonals. Triangle: 0, quadrilateral: 2, pentagon: 5, hexagon: 9.

steps.title: Convex vs concave; regular
steps.body:
- **Convex:** no portion of any diagonal lies outside the polygon (all interior angles < 180°).
- **Concave:** at least one diagonal goes partly outside (one interior angle > 180°, a 'dent').
- **Regular polygon:** all sides equal AND all angles equal (equilateral triangle, square). A rhombus has equal sides but not equal angles → not regular. A rectangle has equal angles but not equal sides → not regular.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
How many diagonals does an octagon have?

- n = 8: 8 × (8 − 3)/2 = 8 × 5/2 = 20 diagonals.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A polygon has 14 diagonals. How many sides?

- n(n − 3)/2 = 14 → n(n − 3) = 28.
- Try n = 7: 7 × 4 = 28 ✔. It is a heptagon.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling every equal-sided shape regular (rhombus!).
- Counting sides as diagonals.
- Thinking a circle is a polygon.

activity.prompt: Sort the shapes

quiz.q: A polygon with 9 sides is a:
quiz.why: A polygon with 9 sides is a nonagon.

quiz.q: Number of diagonals of a hexagon:
quiz.why: A polygon with n sides has n(n − 3)/2 diagonals. For a hexagon: 6 × 3 / 2 = 9.

quiz.q: A polygon with one interior angle greater than 180° is:
quiz.why: A concave polygon has at least one interior angle greater than 180°, which makes a 'dent'. In a convex polygon all interior angles are less than 180°.
A regular polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal. Only the square has both. A rectangle has equal angles but unequal sides, and a rhombus the reverse.
A polygon is a closed figure made of line segments. A circle is curved and has no line segments, so it is not a polygon.

scenes.text: Ravi draws all diagonals from one corner of a pentagon.
He gets 3 triangles.
3 × 180° = 540° — the angle sum of any pentagon.

steps.title: Angle-sum property
steps.body:
From one vertex of an n-gon you can draw (n − 3) diagonals, splitting it into **(n − 2) triangles**. So the sum of interior angles is

**(n − 2) × 180°**

- Triangle 180° · Quadrilateral 360° · Pentagon 540° · Hexagon 720° · Octagon 1080°.

steps.title: Regular polygons
steps.body: Each interior angle of a **regular** n-gon = (n − 2) × 180° ÷ n. Regular hexagon: 720° ÷ 6 = 120°.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Three angles of a quadrilateral are 50°, 110° and 80°. Find the fourth.

- Sum = 360°.
- Fourth = 360° − (50° + 110° + 80°) = 360° − 240° = 120°.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using n × 180° instead of (n − 2) × 180°.
- Dividing by n for an irregular polygon (only valid for regular ones).

steps.title: Memory hook
steps.body: Each extra side adds one more triangle = 180° more.

activity.prompt: Find the sum of interior angles of a decagon (10 sides).

quiz.why: The sum of the interior angles of an n-gon is (n − 2) × 180°. For a hexagon: 4 × 180° = 720°.

quiz.q: Each interior angle of a regular octagon:
quiz.why: The angle sum of an octagon is 6 × 180° = 1080°. A regular octagon has 8 equal angles, so each is 1080° ÷ 8 = 135°.

quiz.q: A quadrilateral has angles 90°, 90°, 60°. The fourth is:
quiz.why: The angles of a quadrilateral add to 360°. The fourth angle = 360° − (90° + 90° + 60°) = 120°.

quiz.q: How many triangles are formed by diagonals from one vertex of a heptagon?
quiz.why: Diagonals from one vertex split an n-gon into n − 2 triangles. For a heptagon, 7 − 2 = 5.

quiz.q: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 108°. Number of sides:
quiz.why: Each exterior angle = 180° − 108° = 72°. The number of sides = 360° ÷ 72° = 5.

scenes.text: Anu walks around a pentagon-shaped park, turning at every corner.
When she's back at the start she has turned one full round.
The total turn is 360° — for ANY polygon.

steps.title: Exterior-angle sum
steps.body: At each vertex, interior angle + exterior angle = 180° (linear pair). The **sum of the exterior angles** (one at each vertex) of any convex polygon is **360°**.

steps.title: Regular polygons
steps.body: Each exterior angle = **360° ÷ n**, so n = 360° ÷ (exterior angle). An exterior angle must divide 360 exactly for a regular polygon to exist.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Find the number of sides of a regular polygon whose each exterior angle is 45°.

- n = 360° ÷ 45° = 8. It is a regular octagon.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Is it possible to have a regular polygon with each exterior angle 22°?

- 360 ÷ 22 = 16.36… not a whole number → **No**.

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
The exterior angles of a pentagon are 70°, 80°, 60°, 90° and x. Find x.

- 70 + 80 + 60 + 90 + x = 360 → x = 60°.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking exterior angles add to (n − 2) × 180°.
- Forgetting interior = 180° − exterior.
- The largest possible exterior angle of a regular polygon is 120° (triangle); the smallest interior angle is 60°.

activity.prompt: Match the regular polygon to its exterior angle

quiz.q: Sum of exterior angles of a 15-gon:
quiz.why: The exterior angles of any convex polygon add to 360°, whatever the number of sides.

quiz.q: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 24°. Sides:
quiz.why: The number of sides = 360° ÷ exterior angle = 360 ÷ 24 = 15.

quiz.q: Interior angle 150° in a regular polygon means sides =
Can a regular polygon have interior angle 22°?
quiz.why: A 22° interior angle would give an exterior angle of 158°, and 360 ÷ 158 is not a whole number. Also, the smallest interior angle of a regular polygon is 60°, so it is not possible.

quiz.q: Minimum interior angle possible for a regular polygon:
quiz.why: The regular polygon with the fewest sides is the equilateral triangle, whose angles are 60°. Others have larger angles, so 60° is the minimum.

scenes.text: A shop's folding gate is a chain of parallelograms.
As it opens, angles change but opposite sides stay equal and parallel.
Those unchanging facts are its properties.

steps.title: Definition and properties
steps.body:
A **parallelogram** is a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel. In parallelogram ABCD:

- Opposite sides are **equal**: AB = CD, BC = DA.
- Opposite angles are **equal**: ∠A = ∠C, ∠B = ∠D.
- Adjacent angles are **supplementary**: ∠A + ∠B = 180°.
- Diagonals **bisect each other** (cut each other into halves).

steps.title: Why adjacent angles add to 180°
steps.body: AD ∥ BC with AB as a transversal, so ∠A and ∠B are co-interior angles on the same side → they sum to 180°.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
In parallelogram RING, ∠R = 70°. Find the other angles.

- ∠I = 180° − 70° = 110° (adjacent).
- ∠N = ∠R = 70°, ∠G = ∠I = 110° (opposite).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Perimeter of a parallelogram is 30 cm and one side is 4 cm longer than the other. Find sides.

- 2(x + x + 4) = 30 → 4x + 8 = 30 → x = 5.5 cm. Sides 5.5 cm and 9.5 cm.

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Diagonals of parallelogram HELP meet at O; OE = 4 cm and HL is 5 cm more than PE. Find OH.

- PE = 2 × OE = 8 cm, so HL = 13 cm.
- OH = HL ÷ 2 = 6.5 cm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming a parallelogram's diagonals are equal (only in rectangles and squares).
- Assuming diagonals are perpendicular (only in rhombuses and squares).

statements.s: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.
Diagonals of every parallelogram are equal.
Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add to 180°.
Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
statements.why: Each cuts the other in half.

statements.s: A trapezium is always a parallelogram.
statements.why: A trapezium needs only one pair of parallel sides.

quiz.why: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add to 180°. So 3x + 2x = 180°, giving 5x = 180° and x = 36°.

quiz.q: In a parallelogram, if one angle is 90°, it is a:
quiz.why: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal and adjacent angles add to 180°. If one angle is 90°, all four are 90°, so it is a rectangle.

quiz.q: Diagonals of a parallelogram are 10 cm and 16 cm. They cut each other into parts of:
quiz.why: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. So the 10 cm diagonal is cut into 5 and 5, and the 16 cm diagonal into 8 and 8.

quiz.q: Two adjacent sides of a parallelogram are 5 cm and 3.5 cm. Perimeter:
quiz.why: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal, so the perimeter is 2(5 + 3.5) = 17 cm.

quiz.q: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram are in ratio 3 : 2. The smaller angle:
quiz.why: Adjacent angles add to 180° and are in ratio 3 : 2. The smaller angle = 2/5 × 180° = 72°.

scenes.text: Ms Thomas draws a family tree: quadrilateral → trapezium → parallelogram → rhombus/rectangle → square.
'A square is a rhombus AND a rectangle?'
Yes — it has every property of both.

steps.title: Special parallelograms
steps.body:
- **Rhombus:** all four sides equal; diagonals are **perpendicular bisectors** of each other; diagonals bisect the angles.
- **Rectangle:** all angles 90°; diagonals **equal** and bisect each other.
- **Square:** all sides equal + all angles 90°; diagonals equal, perpendicular, bisect each other and the angles.

steps.title: Kite and trapezium
steps.body:
- **Kite:** two pairs of equal *adjacent* sides; diagonals are perpendicular; one diagonal bisects the other. A kite is NOT a parallelogram in general.
