- **Trapezium:** exactly one pair of parallel sides (by the Class 8 definition, at least one pair). **Isosceles trapezium:** non-parallel sides equal.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Diagonals of a rhombus are 16 cm and 12 cm. Find its side.

- Half-diagonals: 8 cm and 6 cm, meeting at 90°.
- Side = √(8² + 6²) = √100 = 10 cm.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
In rectangle PQRS, diagonals meet at O. If OP = 3x + 1 and OS = 2x + 4, find x.

- Rectangle diagonals are equal and bisect each other → OP = OS.
- 3x + 1 = 2x + 4 → x = 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'a rhombus is a square' (only if its angles are 90°).
- Saying a kite's diagonals bisect each other (only one bisects the other).

steps.title: Quick test
steps.body: If you can prove 'parallelogram + equal diagonals' → rectangle; 'parallelogram + perpendicular diagonals' → rhombus; both → square.

activity.prompt: Match the quadrilateral with its key property
pairs: All sides equal and all angles 90°
Two pairs of equal adjacent sides

quiz.why: A square has four equal sides, like a rhombus, and four right angles, like a rectangle. So it is both.

quiz.q: Diagonals of a rhombus 24 cm and 10 cm. Side:
quiz.why: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles. Half-diagonals are 12 and 5, so the side = √(12² + 5²) = √169 = 13 cm.

quiz.q: Which has equal diagonals but they need not be perpendicular?
quiz.why: A rectangle's diagonals are equal but meet at right angles only when it is a square. A rhombus has perpendicular, unequal diagonals.

quiz.q: A quadrilateral with all sides equal but angles not 90° is a:
quiz.why: A quadrilateral with all sides equal is a rhombus. It is a square only if its angles are also 90°.
In a kite the diagonals meet at right angles. They are not equal, and not both bisect each other.

questions.q: Sum of interior angles of a quadrilateral:
questions.why: The sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral is (4 − 2) × 180° = 360°.

questions.q: A regular polygon has each exterior angle 40°. Number of sides:
questions.why: The number of sides = 360° ÷ 40° = 9.

questions.q: Number of diagonals of a decagon:
questions.why: Diagonals of a decagon = 10 × (10 − 3)/2 = 10 × 7/2 = 35.

questions.q: Which is always true for a rhombus?
questions.why: The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular bisectors of each other. They are not always equal, and its angles are not always 90°.

questions.q: Angles of a quadrilateral are in ratio 1 : 2 : 3 : 4. The largest angle:
questions.why: The angles are x, 2x, 3x and 4x, which add to 360°. So 10x = 360°, x = 36°, and the largest is 4x = 144°.

questions.q: Interior angle of a regular 20-gon:
questions.why: The exterior angle of a regular 20-gon is 360° ÷ 20 = 18°. The interior angle is 180° − 18° = 162°.

questions.q: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A − ∠B = 40°. ∠A =
questions.why: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add to 180°. With ∠A + ∠B = 180° and ∠A − ∠B = 40°, ∠A = (180° + 40°)/2 = 110°.

questions.q: Assertion: Every rectangle is a parallelogram. Reason: A rectangle has both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: every rectangle is a parallelogram. R is true: its opposite sides are parallel in both pairs, which is exactly the definition. So R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion: Diagonals of every parallelogram are equal. Reason: Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is false: a parallelogram's diagonals are equal only in a rectangle (and square). R is true: they always bisect each other.

questions.q: Is a regular polygon with each interior angle 165° possible? If so, sides =
questions.why: Exterior angle = 180° − 165° = 15°. Sides = 360° ÷ 15° = 24, so it is possible.

questions.q: A pentagon has angles 100°, 110°, 120°, x, x. x =
questions.why: The angles of a pentagon add to 540°. 100 + 110 + 120 = 330, so 2x = 210 and x = 105°.

questions.q: Case: A tiler uses only regular hexagons. At each meeting point, how many hexagons fit without gaps?
questions.why: A regular hexagon has an interior angle of 120°. Three hexagons make 3 × 120° = 360° around a point, so they fit without gaps.

questions.q: Diagonals of a square ABCD meet at O. ∠OAB =
questions.why: The diagonals of a square bisect the 90° angles at the corners. So ∠OAB = 45°.

questions.q: In rhombus PQRS, ∠P = 70°. The angle between diagonal PR and side PQ is:
questions.why: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect the vertex angles. So the angle between PR and PQ is 70° ÷ 2 = 35°.

questions.q: The ratio of interior to exterior angle of a regular polygon is 5 : 1. Number of sides:
questions.why: Interior : exterior = 5 : 1, and they add to 180°. So the exterior angle is 180° ÷ 6 = 30°, and sides = 360° ÷ 30° = 12.

questions.q: In a kite ABCD with AB = AD and CB = CD, ∠B = 110°. ∠D =
questions.why: A kite is symmetric about the diagonal AC, so the opposite angles at B and D are equal. So ∠D = 110°.

questions.q: Isosceles trapezium ABCD with AB ∥ DC and ∠A = 70°. ∠B and ∠D are:
questions.why: In an isosceles trapezium the base angles are equal, so ∠B = ∠A = 70°. Angles along a leg add to 180°, so ∠D = 180° − 70° = 110°.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Data Handling
courses.summary: Organising raw data into grouped frequency tables, drawing and reading histograms and pie charts (central angles), and the basics of chance and probability with equally likely outcomes.
outcomes: Learners can build grouped frequency tables with class intervals and tally marks
Learners can draw and interpret histograms
Learners can calculate central angles and read pie charts
Learners can find the probability of simple events

scenes.text: Mr Pillai has 40 maths marks out of 50 in a jumbled list.
Reading them one by one tells him nothing.
Grouping them into 0–10, 10–20… shows the pattern instantly.

steps.title: Key words
steps.body:
- **Raw data:** unorganised observations.
- **Frequency:** how many times a value or class occurs.
- **Class interval:** a group like 10–20. **Lower limit** 10, **upper limit** 20.
- **Width (size)** = upper − lower = 10.
- Convention: an observation equal to an upper limit (e.g. 20) is counted in the **next** class (20–30).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: From a table, the class 20–30 has the highest frequency 7. Which class has the most students? 20–30. What is its class size? 10.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting 20 in 10–20 instead of 20–30.
- Totals that don't match the number of observations — re-count tallies.
- Unequal class widths when the question wants equal ones.

steps.title: Tally tip
steps.body: Use bundles of five: four strokes and a cross stroke |||| — easier to count.

activity.prompt: Fill the facts about the class interval 30–40.
activity.text: Lower limit = ___, upper limit = ___, class size = ___. The observation 40 goes in the class 40–___.

quiz.q: In class 25–30, the class size is:
quiz.why: The class size is the difference between the limits: 30 − 25 = 5.
An observation equal to the upper limit goes into the next class. So 50 goes to 50–60.

quiz.q: Number of times an observation occurs is its:
quiz.why: The number of times an observation occurs is its frequency.

quiz.q: Data collected but not arranged is called:
quiz.why: Data collected but not yet arranged is raw data.

quiz.q: If frequencies are 4, 9, 7, x and total is 25, x =
quiz.why: The frequencies must add to 25. 4 + 9 + 7 = 20, so x = 25 − 20 = 5.

scenes.text: A PE teacher groups students' heights: 130–140 cm, 140–150 cm…
She draws bars touching each other.
That's a histogram — bars touch because the classes are continuous.

steps.title: What is a histogram?
steps.body:
A **histogram** shows grouped (continuous) data. Class intervals are on the horizontal axis; frequency on the vertical axis. Bars have **equal width** for equal classes and **no gaps**. Bar height = frequency.

If the axis does not start at zero, a **kink (zig-zag)** is drawn on it.

steps.title: Bar graph vs histogram
steps.body:
- Bar graph: separate categories (favourite fruit), gaps between bars.
- Histogram: continuous classes (ages 10–15, 15–20), no gaps.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Weekly pocket money (₹): 0–50: 4, 50–100: 10, 100–150: 6, 150–200: 2.

- Most common group: ₹50–100 (tallest bar).
- Students with at least ₹100: 6 + 2 = 8.
- Total students: 22.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A histogram has bars 1–2 h: 8, 2–3 h: 15, 3–4 h: 5 for TV watched. How many watch less than 2 hours? 8. How many watch 2 hours or more? 15 + 5 = 20.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving gaps between bars.
- Reading the bar's width instead of height.
- Forgetting the kink when the axis starts at, say, 130.

statements.s: Histogram bars have no gaps between them.
A histogram is best for showing favourite colours.
The height of a bar shows frequency.
All bars must have the same height.
A kink shows the axis does not start at 0.

quiz.why: A histogram shows grouped, continuous data in class intervals, with bars of equal width side by side.

quiz.q: In a histogram, the class with the tallest bar has the:
quiz.why: In a histogram, the height of a bar equals the frequency. So the tallest bar belongs to the class with the highest frequency.
Total observations = 3 + 7 + 12 + 5 = 27.

quiz.q: A histogram for ages 10–15, 15–20, 20–25 has bars of width:
quiz.why: Each class is 5 units wide (15 − 10 = 5), so each bar has width 5 units.

quiz.q: Gap between bars appears in a:
quiz.why: A bar graph has gaps between bars to separate categories. A histogram has no gaps because classes are continuous.

scenes.text: A family spends ₹20,000 a month: food ₹8,000, rent ₹6,000, education ₹4,000, savings ₹2,000.
Mum shows it as a pie.
Food takes the biggest slice — 144°.

steps.title: Central angle
steps.body:
A **pie chart** shows parts of a whole as sectors of a circle. Whole = 360°.

**Central angle = (value ÷ total) × 360°** = (percentage ÷ 100) × 360°.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
In a pie chart for 720 students, the 'cricket' sector is 90°. How many prefer cricket?

- 90/360 = 1/4 → 720 × 1/4 = 180 students.

steps.title: Drawing steps
steps.body:
- Compute each central angle; check sum = 360°.
- Draw a circle and a radius.
- Use a protractor to mark each angle from the previous radius.
- Label sectors and give a title.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 100 instead of 360.
- Angles not adding to 360° because of rounding — adjust the last one carefully.
- Using a pie chart for data that is not parts of one whole.

activity.prompt: 25% of a pie chart is 'reading'. What is its central angle?

quiz.q: Central angle for 1/3 of the total:
quiz.why: The central angle for a fraction is that fraction of 360°. For 1/3: 360° ÷ 3 = 120°.

quiz.q: A sector of 72° shows what fraction?
quiz.why: Fraction = 72/360 = 1/5.

quiz.q: If 30% of 600 pupils walk to school, the sector angle is:
quiz.why: The angle = 30% of 360° = 0.3 × 360° = 108°. The number of pupils does not change the angle.

quiz.q: Sum of all central angles in a pie chart:
quiz.why: The central angles of all the sectors add up to the full circle, 360°.
The fraction is 45/360 = 1/8, so people = 1200 × 1/8 = 150.

scenes.text: Ishaan needs a 6 to start his game.
'Why does it never come?'
Each face is equally likely: chance of 6 is 1 in 6. Over many throws, about 1/6 of results are 6.

steps.title: Words
steps.body:
- **Random experiment:** outcome cannot be predicted exactly (tossing a coin).
- **Outcomes:** possible results (H, T).
- **Equally likely:** each outcome has the same chance.
- **Event:** a collection of outcomes (getting an even number = {2, 4, 6}).

steps.title: Probability
steps.body:
For equally likely outcomes:

**P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of outcomes**

0 ≤ P ≤ 1. P = 0 impossible, P = 1 certain. P(not E) = 1 − P(E).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
A die is thrown. Find P(prime number).

- Primes on a die: 2, 3, 5 → 3 outcomes.
- P = 3/6 = 1/2.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A bag has 4 red, 3 blue and 5 green balls. One is drawn at random. P(not green)?

- Total 12. Green 5 → P(green) = 5/12.
- P(not green) = 1 − 5/12 = 7/12.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a 6 is 'due' after many non-sixes. Each throw is independent.
- Treating 1 as prime (it is not).
- Writing probability greater than 1.

steps.title: Real world
steps.body: Weather forecasts ('70% chance of rain'), insurance and quality checks in factories all use probability.

activity.label: Probability scale — where does the event sit?

bands.text: Even chance, like heads on a fair coin.

quiz.why: A fair coin has 2 equally likely outcomes, and 1 is a head. So P(head) = 1/2.
Numbers greater than 4 are 5 and 6, which is 2 of 6 outcomes. P = 2/6 = 1/3.
A normal die has only 1 to 6, so getting 7 is impossible. The probability is 0.

quiz.q: Spinner with 5 equal sectors (2 red). P(red):
quiz.why: There are 5 equal sectors, and 2 are red. So P(red) = 2/5.

questions.q: The number of times an observation occurs is called:
questions.why: The frequency of an observation is the number of times it occurs.

questions.q: Class size of 40–50:
questions.why: The class size of 40–50 is 50 − 40 = 10.

questions.q: Bars of a histogram:
questions.why: The bars of a histogram have no gaps, as the class intervals are continuous.

questions.q: Central angle for 40% of the data:
questions.why: The angle for 40% is 0.4 × 360° = 144°.

questions.q: A die is thrown. P(multiple of 3):
questions.why: Multiples of 3 on a die are 3 and 6. That is 2 of 6 outcomes, so P = 1/3.

questions.q: In a class of 36, a 120° sector shows how many students?
questions.why: A 120° sector is 120/360 = 1/3 of the class. So 36 × 1/3 = 12 students.

questions.q: Which graph suits 'time spent on activities in a day (parts of 24 h)'?
questions.why: A pie chart shows parts of a whole. The time spent in a day, as parts of 24 hours, suits it.

questions.q: Assertion: The observation 30 is counted in class 30–40. Reason: Upper limits are excluded from a class.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: the observation 30 is counted in the class 30–40. R is true: the upper limit is excluded from a class and goes to the next. So R explains A.

questions.q: A bag has 3 white and 5 black balls. P(white):
questions.why: There are 3 + 5 = 8 balls, and 3 are white. P(white) = 3/8.

questions.q: Case: In a survey of 200 people, the pie sector for 'tea' is 162°. How many prefer tea?
questions.why: The fraction is 162/360 of 200, so 200 × 162/360 = 90 people prefer tea.

questions.q: Two coins tossed together: P(at least one head):
questions.why: The outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT. Three of the four have at least one head, so P = 3/4.

questions.q: Frequencies of classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30 are 5, x, 8; total 25. x =
questions.why: The frequencies add to 25. 5 + 8 = 13, so x = 25 − 13 = 12.

questions.q: A pie chart has sectors 90°, 120° and x°. x =
questions.why: The angles of a pie chart add to 360°. x = 360 − (90 + 120) = 150.

questions.q: A letter is chosen from the word 'PROBABILITY'. P(B):
questions.why: 'PROBABILITY' has 11 letters. B appears twice, so P(B) = 2/11.

questions.q: Numbers 1–20 on cards. P(card is a prime):
questions.why: The primes up to 20 are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19, which is 8 numbers. P = 8/20 = 2/5.

questions.q: Expenditure: food 35%, rent 25%, other x%, savings 15%. Central angle of 'other':
questions.why: The percentages add to 100: 35 + 25 + x + 15 = 100, so x = 25. The angle = 25% of 360° = 90°.

questions.q: A die is thrown 300 times. About how many 4s would you expect?
questions.why: Each face has probability 1/6. In 300 throws we expect about 300 × 1/6 = 50 fours.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Squares and Square Roots
courses.summary: Square numbers and their properties, interesting patterns, Pythagorean triplets, and finding square roots by repeated subtraction, prime factorisation and long division, including decimals and estimation.
outcomes: Learners can recognise perfect squares from their last digits and properties
Learners can generate Pythagorean triplets
Learners can find square roots by prime factorisation and by the division method
Learners can find square roots of decimals and estimate square roots

scenes.text: Kabir arranges 49 tiles into a perfect 7 × 7 square.
With 50 tiles he can't make a square.
49 is a *perfect square*; 50 is not.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
If m = n² for a natural number n, then m is a **square number (perfect square)**: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, …

Area of a square of side n = n², hence the name.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- A perfect square never ends in **2, 3, 7 or 8**.
- Squares end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9 — but ending in these does not guarantee a square (e.g. 19).
- If a number ends in 1 or 9, its square ends in 1; ends in 4 or 6 → square ends in 6; ends in 5 → square ends in 25.
- A square has an **even number of zeros** at the end (100, 6400 ✔, 1000 ✘).
- Square of an even number is even; of an odd number is odd.
- Between n² and (n + 1)² there are **2n** non-square numbers.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Which cannot be perfect squares: 1057, 23453, 7928, 222222, 1069?

- 1057 (ends 7), 23453 (ends 3), 7928 (ends 8), 222222 (ends 2) → cannot.
- 1069 ends in 9 → *may* be a square; checking, 32² = 1024 and 33² = 1089, so it is not.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
How many non-square numbers lie between 12² and 13²?

- n = 12 → 2n = 24 numbers (145 to 168).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming any number ending in 6 is a square (26 is not).
- Writing 3² = 6 (that's 3 × 2).

activity.prompt: Could it be a perfect square? (use last digits / zeros)

quiz.q: Which can never be a perfect square?
quiz.why: A perfect square cannot end in 2, 3, 7 or 8. 2343 ends in 3, so it cannot be a perfect square.
The units digit of a square depends on the units digit of the number. 9 × 9 = 81 ends in 1, so 79² ends in 1.
Between n² and (n + 1)² there are 2n non-square numbers. For n = 25, that is 50.

quiz.q: Square of an odd number is:
quiz.why: An odd number times an odd number is odd, so the square of an odd number is odd.

quiz.q: Number of zeros at the end of 7000²:
quiz.why: 7000² = 49,000,000, which has 6 zeros. The zeros of the number are doubled when squared.

scenes.text: Neha adds 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = 4².
The sum of the first n odd numbers is n².

steps.title: Useful patterns
steps.body:
- **1 + 3 + 5 + … (first n odd numbers) = n².** So a number is not a square if repeatedly subtracting 1, 3, 5, … never reaches exactly 0.
- **(n + 1)² − n² = (n + 1) + n = 2n + 1.** E.g. 36² − 35² = 71.
- Squares of numbers ending in 5: (a5)² = a(a + 1) followed by 25 → 35² = 12|25 = 1225; 65² = 42|25 = 4225.
- 1² = 1, 11² = 121, 111² = 12321, 1111² = 1234321.

steps.title: Pythagorean triplets
steps.body:
Three natural numbers a, b, c with a² + b² = c². For any natural number **m > 1**, the numbers **2m, m² − 1, m² + 1** form a triplet.

m = 2: 4, 3, 5 · m = 3: 6, 8, 10 · m = 4: 8, 15, 17 · m = 6: 12, 35, 37.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Find a triplet whose smallest member is 8.

- Try 2m = 8 → m = 4: m² − 1 = 15, m² + 1 = 17 → (8, 15, 17). Check: 64 + 225 = 289 = 17² ✔.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Find a triplet with one member 12.

- 2m = 12 → m = 6 → (12, 35, 37). Check 144 + 1225 = 1369 = 37² ✔.
- (Trying m² − 1 = 12 gives m² = 13, not a natural number.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 2m = 7 (odd) — m must be a natural number.
- Forgetting to check a² + b² = c².

activity.prompt: Match each m with its triplet (2m, m²−1, m²+1)

quiz.why: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n². 1 + 3 + … + 19 has 10 odd numbers, so the sum is 10² = 100.
For a number ending in 5, multiply the tens part by the next number and then put 25 after it. 8 × 9 = 72, so 85² = 7225.
A Pythagorean triplet satisfies a² + b² = c². 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13².
For a triplet 2m, m² − 1, m² + 1: 2m = 16 gives m = 8. So 8² − 1 = 63 and 8² + 1 = 65.

scenes.text: A square garden has area 1764 m².
How long is each side?
Prime factors in pairs reveal the side: 42 m.

steps.title: Square root
steps.body: Square root is the inverse of squaring: if a² = b then √b = a (we take the positive root). √49 = 7 because 7² = 49.

steps.title: Prime factorisation method
steps.body:
- Write the number as a product of primes.
- Pair equal factors.
- Take one factor from each pair and multiply.
- If a factor is left unpaired, the number is not a perfect square.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Find the smallest number by which 2352 must be multiplied to get a perfect square, and its root.

- 2352 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 × 7 → 3 is unpaired.
- Multiply by 3: 7056 = (2×2)(2×2)(3×3)(7×7) → √7056 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 = 84.

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Smallest number to divide 9408 by to get a perfect square.

- 9408 = 2⁶ × 3 × 7² → divide by 3 → 3136 = 56².

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying both members of each pair (giving the number back).
- Missing a prime factor; always multiply back to check.

activity.prompt: Find √3136 using prime factors (3136 = 2⁶ × 7²).

quiz.why: 2025 = 3⁴ × 5². Taking one of each pair gives 3² × 5 = 9 × 5 = 45.

quiz.q: Smallest multiplier to make 180 a square:
quiz.why: 180 = 2² × 3² × 5. The factor 5 has no pair, so multiply by 5.

quiz.q: Smallest divisor to make 1008 a square:
quiz.why: 1008 = 2⁴ × 3² × 7. The factor 7 is unpaired, so divide by 7.

quiz.q: Number with an unpaired prime factor is:
quiz.why: A perfect square has all its prime factors in pairs. An unpaired prime factor means it is not a perfect square.

scenes.text: Factorising 529 is slow if you don't know 23 is prime.
The division method works for any size number.
√529 = 23 in three neat steps.

steps.title: Steps of the division method
steps.body:
- Pair digits from the right (for decimals, pair the decimal part from the left of the point outward): 5|29.
- Find the largest square ≤ the first group (4 ≤ 5 → divisor and quotient 2). Subtract: 1.
- Bring down the next pair: 129. Double the quotient (4) and find the digit d so that (40 + d) × d ≤ 129 → d = 3 (43 × 3 = 129).
- Remainder 0 → √529 = 23.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
√12.25.

- Pairs: 12 . 25. 3² = 9, remainder 3; quotient 3.
- Bring down 25 → 325; put the decimal point in the quotient. Double 3 = 6; 65 × 5 = 325 ✔.
- √12.25 = 3.5.

steps.title: Number of digits
steps.body: If a perfect square has n digits, its root has n/2 digits (n even) or (n + 1)/2 digits (n odd). 7744 (4 digits) → 2-digit root; 15625 (5 digits) → 3-digit root (125).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Pairing decimals from the right end of the whole number (wrong): 2.56 pairs as 2 . 56.
- Forgetting to double the whole quotient so far.

activity.prompt: Find √1.44

quiz.why: √14400 = 120, which has 3 digits. A 5-digit perfect square has a 3-digit square root.

quiz.q: Least number to subtract from 1989 to make a square:
quiz.why: 44² = 1936 is the nearest perfect square below 1989. So subtract 1989 − 1936 = 53.

quiz.q: Least number to add to 1300 to make a square:

scenes.text: A family has a square plot of 250 m² and wants a rough side length to buy fencing.
The side is about 16 m (just under).

steps.title: Estimation
steps.body: Find the perfect squares on either side. √250: 225 < 250 < 256 → 15 < √250 < 16, and 250 is much closer to 256, so √250 ≈ 16 (more exactly 15.8).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
2025 plants are to be planted so that each row has as many plants as there are rows. How many rows?

- Rows = √2025 = 45.

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Side of a square of area 441 m² and its perimeter.

- Side = √441 = 21 m; perimeter = 4 × 21 = 84 m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Halving the number to 'estimate' a square root (√80 is not 40!).
- Forgetting units: side in m, area in m².

steps.title: Real world
steps.body: Square roots appear in diagonal lengths (TV sizes), Pythagoras in ladders and maps, and area-to-side problems in land and tiling.

activity.label: Pick a number and see between which whole numbers its square root lies

quiz.why: 17² = 289 and 18² = 324. Since 289 < 300 < 324, √300 lies between 17 and 18.

quiz.q: A square has area 576 cm². Perimeter:
quiz.why: The side of the square is √576 = 24 cm. The perimeter = 4 × 24 = 96 cm.
√99 is just under √100 = 10, so the closest whole number is 10.

quiz.q: A ladder 10 m long reaches a window 8 m high. Distance of its foot from the wall:
quiz.why: By Pythagoras, the distance from the wall = √(10² − 8²) = √(100 − 64) = √36 = 6 m.

quiz.q: 1764 soldiers in a square formation. Soldiers per row:
quiz.why: A square formation has as many soldiers per row as rows. √1764 = 42, so 42 soldiers per row.

questions.q: Which is a perfect square?
questions.why: 36 × 36 = 1296, so 1296 is a perfect square. The others end in 2, 7 or 0 (a single zero) and are not.

questions.q: A square number can end in:
questions.why: A perfect square can end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9, never in 2, 3, 7 or 8. So 6 is possible.

questions.q: Sum of first 12 odd numbers:
questions.why: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n². For n = 12, it is 12² = 144.

questions.q: Pythagorean triplet with m = 9:
questions.why: For m = 9, the triplet is 2m = 18, m² − 1 = 80 and m² + 1 = 82. Check: 18² + 80² = 324 + 6400 = 6724 = 82².

questions.q: Smallest number to multiply 1620 for a perfect square:
questions.why: 1620 = 2² × 3⁴ × 5. The factor 5 is unpaired, so multiply by 5.

questions.q: Assertion: 1000 is not a perfect square. Reason: A perfect square has an even number of zeros at its end.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: 1000 is not a perfect square. R is true: a perfect square ends in an even number of zeros, and 1000 has three. So R explains A.

questions.q: Number of non-square numbers between 50² and 51²:
questions.why: Between n² and (n + 1)² there are 2n non-square numbers. For n = 50, that is 100.

questions.q: The least 4-digit perfect square:
questions.why: 31² = 961 has 3 digits and 32² = 1024 has 4 digits. So 1024 is the least 4-digit perfect square.

questions.q: The greatest 4-digit perfect square:
questions.why: 99² = 9801 and 100² = 10000, which has 5 digits. So 9801 is the greatest 4-digit perfect square.

questions.q: Least number to be subtracted from 5607 to get a perfect square:
questions.why: 74² = 5476 and 75² = 5625. So 5607 − 5476 = 131 must be subtracted.

questions.q: Case: A school wants 1000 students in rows with equal number per row and as many rows as columns. Least students to be left out:
questions.why: 31² = 961 and 32² = 1024. For a square arrangement, the most students is 961, so 1000 − 961 = 39 are left out.

questions.q: A rectangular field is 32 m × 18 m. Side of a square field of the same area:
questions.why: The area is 32 × 18 = 576 m². The side of the square = √576 = 24 m.

questions.q: Diagonal of a square of side 12 cm, given √2 ≈ 1.414 (to one decimal):
questions.why: The diagonal of a square = side × √2 = 12 × 1.414 = 16.968, which is 17.0 cm to one decimal place.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Cubes and Cube Roots
courses.summary: Cube numbers, patterns (including the Hardy–Ramanujan number 1729), testing for perfect cubes by prime factorisation, smallest multipliers/divisors, and finding cube roots by factorisation and by estimation.
outcomes: Learners can list cubes of 1–20 and spot their unit-digit patterns
Learners can test perfect cubes by grouping prime factors in threes
Learners can find cube roots by prime factorisation
Learners can estimate cube roots of perfect cubes up to 6 digits

scenes.text: Tanvi has 27 small cubes and builds one big 3 × 3 × 3 cube.
With 30 cubes, 3 are left over.
27 is a perfect cube; 30 is not.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: n³ = n × n × n is the **cube** of n. Numbers like 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216, 343, 512, 729, 1000 are **perfect cubes**. Volume of a cube of side n = n³.

steps.title: Patterns
steps.body:
- Cubes of even numbers are even; of odd numbers are odd.
- **Unit digits:** 1→1, 2→8, 3→7, 4→4, 5→5, 6→6, 7→3, 8→2, 9→9, 0→0. Every digit can be the last digit of a cube.
- Adding consecutive odd numbers: 1 = 1³; 3 + 5 = 8 = 2³; 7 + 9 + 11 = 27 = 3³; 13 + 15 + 17 + 19 = 64 = 4³.
- **1729** (Hardy–Ramanujan number) = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³: the smallest number expressible as a sum of two cubes in two different ways.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Find the unit digit of 53³ and of 128³.

- 53 ends in 3 → cube ends in 7.
- 128 ends in 8 → cube ends in 2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing 2³ = 6 (that's 2 × 3).
- Thinking cubes, like squares, cannot end in 2, 3, 7, 8 — cubes can end in any digit.

activity.prompt: Match the number with its cube

quiz.why: 47³ ends in the unit digit of 7³ = 343, which is 3.
125 = 5 × 5 × 5, so it is a perfect cube. 200, 250 and 100 are not.

quiz.q: Cube of an odd number is:
quiz.why: The cube of an odd number is odd, as odd × odd × odd = odd.
1729 is the Hardy–Ramanujan number, the smallest number that is the sum of two cubes in two ways. 1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³.

scenes.text: A factory needs to know if 392 small cubes can make one large cube.
The 7s are not in a group of three — they need one more 7.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Write the prime factorisation. A number is a perfect cube if **every prime factor appears in groups of three** (exponent is a multiple of 3).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Smallest number to multiply 392 to make a perfect cube.

- 392 = 2³ × 7² → need one more 7.
- 392 × 7 = 2744 = 14³.

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Smallest number to divide 81 to make a perfect cube.

- 81 = 3⁴ = 3³ × 3 → divide by 3 → 27 = 3³.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Looking for pairs (that's for squares) instead of triples.
- Multiplying by the leftover factor once when two are missing: for 2² × 3³ you must multiply by 2 (to get 2³), but for 2 × 3³ you need 2² = 4.

activity.prompt: Perfect cube or not?

quiz.q: Smallest multiplier to make 675 a cube:
quiz.why: 675 = 3³ × 5². The factor 5 appears twice, so we need one more 5. Multiply by 5.

quiz.q: Smallest divisor to make 128 a cube:
quiz.why: 128 = 2⁷. Dividing by 2 gives 2⁶ = 64, a perfect cube.
1188 = 2² × 3³ × 11. The factors 2 and 11 are not in triples, so it is not a perfect cube.

quiz.q: Smallest multiplier for 100 to be a cube:
quiz.why: 100 = 2² × 5². We need one more 2 and one more 5, so multiply by 2 × 5 = 10.

scenes.text: A cube-shaped tank is built from 17,576 identical unit blocks.
Find the side: group prime factors in threes.
2³ × 13³ → side 26 units.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: ∛n: factorise, form triplets, take one factor from each triplet and multiply. ∛(−n) = −∛n because (−a)³ = −a³.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking negative numbers have no cube root (they do; only square roots of negatives are not real).
- Dividing exponents by 2 instead of 3.

quiz.why: 46656 = 2⁶ × 3⁶, so its cube root is 2² × 3² = 4 × 9 = 36.

lessons.title: Estimating cube roots of large perfect cubes

scenes.text: Olympiad question: ∛857375 in 30 seconds.
Last digit 5 → root ends in 5. First group 857 lies between 9³ and 10³ → first digit 9.
Answer: 95.

steps.title: Method (perfect cubes up to 6 digits)
steps.body:
- Make groups of three digits from the right: 857 | 375.
- The last group's **unit digit** gives the root's unit digit (use the unit-digit table).
- For the first group, find the largest cube ≤ it: that gives the tens digit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the method on numbers that are not perfect cubes (it only works if you know it is a cube).
- Mixing up 2 ↔ 8 and 3 ↔ 7 in unit digits.

steps.title: Unit-digit swap
steps.body: Only 2/8 and 3/7 swap; every other digit stays the same.

activity.prompt: Estimate ∛110592 (it is a perfect cube).

quiz.why: 13824 ends in 4, and 4³ = 64 ends in 4. So the unit digit of the cube root is 4.
32768 ends in 8, so the cube root ends in 2. Dropping the last three digits gives 32, which lies between 3³ = 27 and 4³ = 64, so the first digit is 3. The answer is 32.
68921 ends in 1, so the cube root ends in 1. The part 68 lies between 4³ = 64 and 5³ = 125, so the first digit is 4. The answer is 41.
10648 ends in 8, so the cube root ends in 2. The part 10 lies between 2³ = 8 and 3³ = 27, so the first digit is 2. The answer is 22.

quiz.q: Unit digit of the cube root of a cube ending in 3:
quiz.why: 7³ = 343 ends in 3, so a cube ending in 3 has a cube root ending in 7.

questions.q: Which is NOT a perfect cube?
questions.why: 500 = 2² × 5³. The factor 2 is not in a triple, so it is not a perfect cube.

questions.q: Unit digit of 32³:
questions.why: 32³ ends in the unit digit of 2³ = 8.

questions.q: Smallest multiplier to make 243 a cube:
questions.why: 243 = 3⁵. We need 3⁶, so multiply by 3.

questions.q: Assertion: A number ending in 2 can be a perfect cube. Reason: 8³ = 512 ends in 2.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: a cube can end in 2. R is true: 8³ = 512 ends in 2, so it is a valid example. R explains A.

questions.q: 1³ + 12³ equals:
Smallest divisor of 3600 to make a perfect cube:
questions.why: 3600 = 2⁴ × 3² × 5². To make a cube, keep the triple 2³ and remove 2 × 3² × 5² = 450. Dividing gives 8 = 2³.

questions.q: Volume of a cube is 2197 cm³. Edge:
questions.why: The edge = ∛2197 = 13 cm, since 13³ = 2197.

questions.q: Case: Parikshit makes a cuboid 5 cm × 2 cm × 5 cm from plasticine. How many such cuboids make a cube?
questions.why: The volume is 5 × 2 × 5 = 50 = 2 × 5². For a cube we need 2³ × 5³ = 1000, which is 20 cuboids (1000 ÷ 50).
592704 ends in 4, so the cube root ends in 4. The part 592 lies between 8³ = 512 and 9³ = 729, so the first digit is 8. The answer is 84.

questions.q: Sum of the consecutive odd numbers 21 + 23 + 25 + 27 + 29 =
questions.why: The cube 5³ is the sum of 5 consecutive odd numbers starting at 21: 21 + 23 + 25 + 27 + 29 = 125.

questions.q: Which is true?
options: Cube of a negative number is positive
Cube of a negative number is negative
questions.why: The cube of a negative number is negative: (−a)³ = −a³. Cubes can end in 7 (3³ = 27), and ∛(−8) = −2 is defined.

school-c8-maths-b.title: Class 8 Mathematics (part 2 of 2)
school-c8-maths-b.description: Every chapter of Class 8 Maths as its own course — concepts, solved examples in steps, common mistakes, quizzes and 15–20 question chapter tests — plus Revision & Practice. Chapters follow the rationalised NCERT Class 8 textbooks (2023–24 editions onward). courses.title: Ch 7 · Comparing Quantities
courses.summary: Ratios and percentages, percentage increase and decrease, discounts, profit and loss with overhead expenses, sales tax and GST, and compound interest with yearly and half-yearly compounding, growth and depreciation.
outcomes: Learners can compute percentage change, discounts and discount percent
Learners can solve profit/loss problems including overheads
Learners can add GST/sales tax and reverse-calculate the base price
Learners can compute compound interest using A = P(1 + R/100)ⁿ, including half-yearly, growth and depreciation

scenes.text: Tomatoes went from ₹40/kg to ₹50/kg.
A headline says 'prices up 25%'.
Increase ₹10 on ₹40 = 25% ✔ — always divide by the ORIGINAL.

steps.title: Converting
steps.body:
- Ratio to percent: 3 : 5 → part 3 of 8 total → 3/8 × 100 = 37.5% (if the ratio is part : part). A fraction a/b → (a/b) × 100%.
- x% of N = (x/100) × N.

steps.title: Percentage increase/decrease
steps.body:
**% change = (change ÷ original value) × 100.**

- New value after x% increase = original × (1 + x/100).
- After x% decrease = original × (1 − x/100).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
A school had 800 students; now it has 920. Percentage increase?

- Change = 120. % = 120/800 × 100 = 15%.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A scooter costing ₹72,000 drops in value by 15%. New value?

- 72000 × 0.85 = ₹61,200.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing by the new value instead of the original.
- Thinking +10% then −10% returns to the start (100 → 110 → 99).

activity.prompt: A price rises from ₹250 to ₹300. Percentage increase?

quiz.q: Ratio 2 : 3 of a mixture; % of first part:
quiz.why: In the ratio 2 : 3, the whole is 5 parts. The first part is 2/5 = 40%.
The decrease is 5000 − 4500 = 500. The percentage decrease = 500/5000 × 100 = 10%.
An increase of 5% means multiplying by 1.05. 1200 × 1.05 = ₹1260.

scenes.text: A jacket tagged ₹2,400 is on 'Flat 25% off'.
Pooja pays ₹1,800.
Discount is always calculated on the marked price.

steps.title: Terms
steps.body:
- **Marked price (MP):** price printed on the tag.
- **Discount:** reduction on the MP. Discount = MP − SP.
- **Discount %** = (Discount ÷ MP) × 100.
- **Selling price** SP = MP × (1 − d/100).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A sofa is sold for ₹9,600 after a 20% discount. Find MP.

- SP = 0.8 × MP → MP = 9600 ÷ 0.8 = ₹12,000.

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Two successive discounts of 10% and 10% on ₹1,000.

- After first: 900. After second: 810. Total discount 19% (not 20%).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calculating discount % on the selling price.
- Adding successive discounts directly.

activity.prompt: MP ₹1,500, discount 12%. Selling price?

quiz.why: The discount is 500 − 450 = ₹50. Discount % = 50/500 × 100 = 10%, as it is taken on the marked price.
A 20% discount means paying 80%. 350 × 0.8 = ₹280.
Discount is calculated on the marked price, not on the cost price.
After a 10% discount, SP is 90% of MP. So MP = 720 ÷ 0.9 = ₹800.

quiz.q: Successive discounts of 20% and 10% equal a single discount of:
quiz.why: Successive discounts multiply: 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72. So you pay 72%, which is a single discount of 28%.

scenes.text: Raju buys a used cycle for ₹2,500, spends ₹300 on repairs and sells it for ₹3,080.
His real cost is ₹2,800.
Profit ₹280 = 10%.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Cost price (CP)** includes **overhead expenses** (repairs, transport, labour).
- Profit = SP − CP (if SP > CP); Loss = CP − SP.
- **Profit % = Profit ÷ CP × 100; Loss % = Loss ÷ CP × 100.**
- SP = CP × (1 + P%/100) or CP × (1 − L%/100).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Two TVs bought at ₹10,000 each. One sold at 4% profit, the other at 4% loss. Overall?

- SPs: 10,400 and 9,600 → total 20,000 = total CP → no profit, no loss.

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
By selling a table for ₹1,800 a man loses 10%. At what price should he sell to gain 10%?

- CP = 1800/0.9 = 2000 → SP for 10% gain = 2200.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calculating profit % on SP instead of CP.
- Leaving out overhead expenses from the CP.

a.text: You buy 12 notebooks for ₹240 and pay ₹24 for transport. You sell each at ₹25. What is your total cost price?

choices.feedback: Yes — overheads are part of CP.
Transport is an overhead; include it.

b2.text: Profit % is always on cost price: 36 ÷ 264 × 100 ≈ 13.6%.

e.text: Done! Remember: CP includes overheads, and % is on CP.

quiz.why: A 5% loss means SP is 95% of CP. 800 × 0.95 = ₹760.
Overhead expenses such as repairs and transport are added to the cost price.

quiz.q: Bought for ₹1,200, repairs ₹300, sold for ₹1,350. Result:
quiz.why: CP includes repairs: 1200 + 300 = ₹1500. SP is ₹1350, so the loss is ₹150. Loss % = 150/1500 × 100 = 10%.

scenes.text: The menu total is ₹1,500; the bill shows ₹1,575.
'5% GST' is printed at the bottom.
Tax is charged on the selling price of the item.

steps.title: Tax on sales
steps.body:
Governments collect tax on goods and services. In India, **GST (Goods and Services Tax)** has applied since 1 July 2017, replacing many earlier taxes like VAT and sales tax in most cases.

**Bill amount = price × (1 + tax rate/100).** Tax amount = price × rate/100. (GST rates vary by item and are revised by the GST Council; problems give you the rate.)

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
An item costs ₹2,500 + 18% GST. Bill?

- Tax = 2500 × 0.18 = ₹450. Bill = ₹2,950.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Price including 12% GST is ₹1,120. Original price?

- 1.12 × P = 1120 → P = ₹1,000.

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
A shirt is ₹800 with 10% discount, then 5% GST on the discounted price. Pay?

courses.title: Ch 8 · Algebraic Expressions and Identities
courses.summary: Terms, factors and coefficients; monomials, binomials and polynomials; adding and subtracting expressions; multiplying monomials and polynomials; the standard identities and using them for fast calculation.
outcomes: Learners can identify terms, coefficients and like terms
Learners can add, subtract and multiply algebraic expressions
Learners can state and verify the four standard identities
Learners can use identities for mental arithmetic and simplification

scenes.text: A pen costs ₹x and a notebook ₹y.
Ali buys 3 pens and 2 notebooks: 3x + 2y. Sara buys 5 pens and 1 notebook: 5x + y.
Together: 8x + 3y — we just added like terms.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **Expression:** combination of variables and constants with +, −, ×, ÷ (e.g. 3x² − 5xy + 7).
- **Terms:** parts separated by + or −: 3x², −5xy, 7.
- **Coefficient:** numerical factor of a term (−5 in −5xy).
- **Like terms:** same variables with same powers (3x²y and −7x²y). Unlike: 3x²y and 3xy².
- **Monomial** (1 term), **binomial** (2), **trinomial** (3), **polynomial** (one or more terms with whole-number powers).

steps.title: Adding and subtracting
steps.body: Only like terms can be combined: add/subtract their coefficients. When subtracting an expression, change the sign of **every** term being subtracted.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Add 5x² − 3x + 2 and 2x² + 4x − 7.

- x² terms: 5 + 2 = 7x²
- x terms: −3 + 4 = x
- constants: 2 − 7 = −5
- Sum: 7x² + x − 5.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Subtract 4a − 7ab + 3b + 12 from 12a − 9ab + 5b − 3.

- 12a − 9ab + 5b − 3 − 4a + 7ab − 3b − 12
- = 8a − 2ab + 2b − 15.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Combining unlike terms: 3x + 2y ≠ 5xy.
- Changing the sign of only the first term when subtracting.
- Treating x² and x as like terms.

7x − 3 − 4x + 5. The terms in x give 3x, and −3 + 5 = 2. So 3x + 2.
Like terms have the same variables with the same powers. 3m²n and −m²n are like terms.

steps.body:
- Multiplying powers instead of adding: x² × x³ = x⁵, not x⁶.
- Forgetting to multiply the last term: 3x(2x + 5) = 6x² + **15x**.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Multiply every term of the first by every term of the second, then combine like terms. For two binomials this gives 4 products (FOIL: first, outer, inner, last).

steps.body:

- Sign errors with negative terms.

scenes.text: A square of side (a + b) splits into an a² square, a b² square and two a × b rectangles.
So (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² — true for every a and b.
An *identity* is true for all values, unlike an equation.

steps.title: The four identities
steps.body:
- **I** (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²
- **II** (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²
- **III** (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b²
- **IV** (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab

steps.title: Identity vs equation
steps.body: An **equation** is true only for some values (2x + 1 = 7 only for x = 3). An **identity** is true for all values of the variables.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- (a + b)² = a² + b² — **wrong**; the 2ab is missing.
- (a − b)² = a² − b² — wrong; that is (a + b)(a − b).
- Squaring the coefficient but not the variable: (3x)² = 9x², not 3x².

An identity is true for every value of the variable. (a + 1)² = a² + 2a + 1 holds for all a. The others hold for only some a.

scenes.text: In a quiz, Rohan computes 103² in 3 seconds.

steps.title: Strategy
steps.body: Rewrite numbers near a round number (100, 200, 1000) and apply an identity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

- Forgetting that 2ab doubles the product.

questions.why: The plot's area is (2a + 3)² = 4a² + 12a + 9. The pond's area is (a + 1)² = a² + 2a + 1. The difference is 3a² + 10a + 8 m².

questions.why: Each product is a difference of squares: (a² − b²) + (b² − c²) + (c² − a²). All terms cancel, so the result is 0.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Mensuration
courses.summary: Areas of trapeziums, general quadrilaterals, rhombuses and polygons; surface areas of cubes, cuboids and cylinders; volumes and capacity, with units and conversions.
outcomes: Learners can find areas of trapeziums, rhombuses and general quadrilaterals
Learners can split polygons into simpler shapes to find areas

scenes.text: Farmer Gopal's field has two parallel sides along roads: 60 m and 40 m, 30 m apart.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
**Area of a trapezium = ½ × h × (a + b)**, where a and b are the parallel sides and h the perpendicular distance between them.

Why: a diagonal splits it into two triangles of heights h with bases a and b: ½ah + ½bh.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Parallel sides 10 cm and 6 cm, height 4 cm.

- Area = ½ × 4 × 16 = 32 cm².

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A trapezium has area 34 cm², one parallel side 10 cm and height 4 cm. Find the other parallel side.

- 34 = ½ × 4 × (10 + b) → 17 = 10 + b → b = 7 cm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a slanting side as the height.
- Forgetting the ½.
- Mixing units (cm and m) — convert first.

steps.title: Real world
steps.body: Many land plots, dam cross-sections and bag side-panels are trapeziums.

steps.title: General quadrilateral
steps.body: With diagonal d and perpendiculars h₁, h₂ from the other two vertices: **Area = ½ × d × (h₁ + h₂)**.

steps.title: Rhombus
steps.body: Diagonals are perpendicular: **Area = ½ × d₁ × d₂**. (Also base × height, since a rhombus is a parallelogram.)

steps.body:

steps.title: Formulas (right circular cylinder)
steps.body:
- **Curved surface area (CSA) = 2πrh** (unrolled rectangle: length 2πr, width h)
- **TSA = 2πrh + 2πr² = 2πr(r + h)**
- Use π = 22/7 or 3.14 as stated.

steps.body:

- × 500 = 15840000 cm² = 1584 m².

steps.body:
- Using diameter in place of radius.
- Adding both circles when the cylinder is open (e.g. a pipe or an open tank uses fewer circles).
- Unit mix: 10000 cm² = 1 m².

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Cuboid:** V = l × b × h
- **Cube:** V = a³
- **Cylinder:** V = πr²h (base area × height)

Units: 1 cm³ = 1 mL, **1000 cm³ = 1 L**, **1 m³ = 1000 L**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing volume in cm² (it is cubic units).
- Converting m³ to L by × 100 (it is × 1000).
- Using CSA instead of volume for 'how much does it hold'.

If the radius of a cylinder is doubled (h same), its volume becomes:

Volume of a cuboid 4 × 3 × 2 cm:

questions.why: TSA of a cube = 6a² = 6 × 10² = 600 cm².

questions.q: Rhombus with diagonals 20 cm and 15 cm. Area:
questions.why: Area of a rhombus = ½ × 20 × 15 = 150 cm².

questions.q: CSA of cylinder r = 3.5 cm, h = 10 cm (π = 22/7):
Capacity in litres of a cube of side 50 cm:
questions.why: Volume = 50³ = 125000 cm³. Since 1000 cm³ = 1 L, the capacity is 125 L.

questions.q: Assertion: Doubling every edge of a cube makes its volume 8 times. Reason: Volume = a³.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: doubling every edge of a cube makes its volume 8 times. R is true: volume = a³, and (2a)³ = 8a³. So R explains A.

questions.q: Area of a quadrilateral with diagonal 24 cm and offsets 7 cm and 9 cm:
questions.why: The offsets add to 7 + 9 = 16 cm. Area = ½ × 24 × 16 = 192 cm².

questions.q: A trapezium of area 1080 cm² has parallel sides 55 cm and 35 cm. Height:
Cost of painting four walls of a room 10 m × 8 m × 5 m at ₹15/m²:
questions.why: The four walls have area 2h(l + b) = 2 × 5 × 18 = 180 m². The cost is 180 × 15 = ₹2,700.

questions.q: Case: A cylindrical pillar of diameter 50 cm and height 3.5 m is painted on its curved surface at ₹12.50/m². Cost (π = 22/7):
questions.why: The radius is 0.25 m and the height is 3.5 m. CSA = 2 × 22/7 × 0.25 × 3.5 = 5.5 m². Cost = 5.5 × 12.50 = ₹68.75.

questions.q: How many 2 cm cubes fit exactly in a box 10 cm × 8 cm × 6 cm?
questions.why: Along the edges, 10 ÷ 2 = 5, 8 ÷ 2 = 4 and 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cubes fit. So 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 cubes.

questions.q: A closed cylindrical tank of r = 7 m and h = 3 m is made of metal sheet. Sheet needed (π = 22/7):
questions.why: A closed tank has TSA = 2πr(r + h) = 2 × 22/7 × 7 × (7 + 3) = 44 × 10 = 440 m².

questions.q: Water flows into a 2 m × 1 m × 0.5 m tank at 10 L per minute. Time to fill:
questions.why: Volume = 2 × 1 × 0.5 = 1 m³ = 1000 L. At 10 L per minute, it takes 1000 ÷ 10 = 100 minutes.

questions.q: A rectangular sheet 44 cm × 20 cm is rolled along its length (44 cm becomes the circumference) to form a cylinder. Its volume (π = 22/7):
questions.why: The 44 cm side becomes the circumference, so 2πr = 44 and r = 7 cm. The height is 20 cm. Volume = 22/7 × 49 × 20 = 3080 cm³.

courses.title: Ch 10 · Exponents and Powers
courses.summary: Negative exponents, the laws of exponents for integer powers, expressing very small numbers in standard form, and comparing very large and very small quantities.
outcomes: Learners can evaluate negative and zero exponents
Learners can apply all laws of exponents with integer powers
Learners can write very small and very large numbers in standard form
Learners can compare quantities written in standard form

scenes.text: 1 pizza → ½ → ¼ → ⅛ as you keep halving.
Each step down divides by 2 — that's what a negative exponent means.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body:
For a ≠ 0 and natural n: **a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ** and **aⁿ = 1/a⁻ⁿ**. So a⁻ⁿ is the multiplicative inverse of aⁿ.

- 10⁻² = 1/100 = 0.01
- (2/3)⁻² = (3/2)² = 9/4
- (−3)⁻² = 1/9, (−2)⁻³ = −1/8
- **a⁰ = 1** (a ≠ 0).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 2⁻³ = −8 ✘ (a negative exponent does NOT make the number negative): 2⁻³ = 1/8.
- 5⁰ = 0 ✘; it is 1.
- (−2)⁻² = −1/4 ✘; even power → +1/4.

activity.prompt: Match each expression with its value

quiz.why: A negative power means the reciprocal. 4⁻² = 1/4² = 1/16.
(−4)⁻² = 1/(−4)² = 1/16. An even power makes the result positive.
A negative power flips the fraction: (3/4)⁻² = (4/3)² = 16/9.
Any non-zero number raised to the power 0 is 1, so (−7)⁰ = 1.

scenes.text: Kiran must simplify 2⁵ × 2⁻³ ÷ 2⁻⁴.
Same base → add/subtract exponents.

steps.title: Laws (a, b ≠ 0; m, n integers)
steps.body:
- aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ
- aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ
- (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
- aᵐ × bᵐ = (ab)ᵐ
- aᵐ ÷ bᵐ = (a/b)ᵐ
- a⁰ = 1

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Find m if 5ᵐ ÷ 5⁻³ = 5⁵.

- 5ᵐ⁺³ = 5⁵ → m + 3 = 5 → m = 2.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Simplify (2⁻¹ × 4⁻¹) ÷ 2⁻².

- 4⁻¹ = 2⁻². Numerator: 2⁻¹ × 2⁻² = 2⁻³.
- 2⁻³ ÷ 2⁻² = 2⁻¹ = 1/2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding exponents for different bases: 2³ × 3² ≠ 6⁵.
- (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ ✘ — it is aᵐⁿ.
- Thinking aᵐ + aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ (laws work only for × and ÷).

activity.prompt: Fill in the exponent.

quiz.why: Add the exponents: (−2)³ × (−2)⁻⁵ = (−2)⁻². This is 1/(−2)² = 1/4.
5⁻¹ × 2⁻¹ = 1/10. Its inverse is (1/10)⁻¹ = 10.
Add the exponents: m + 3 = −2, so m = −5.
Adding the exponents: (2/5)⁻³ × (2/5)³ = (2/5)⁰ = 1.

lessons.title: Standard form of very small numbers

scenes.text: A red blood cell is about 0.000007 m across.
Too many zeros to read quickly!
Standard form: 7 × 10⁻⁶ m.

steps.title: Standard (scientific) form
steps.body:
A number is written as **k × 10ⁿ**, where **1 ≤ k < 10** and n is an integer.

- Large: 150,000,000,000 m = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m (approx. Earth–Sun distance).
- Small: 0.000035 = 3.5 × 10⁻⁵ (move the decimal 5 places right → power −5).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 35 × 10⁻⁶ is not standard form (k must be < 10): write 3.5 × 10⁻⁵.
- Moving the decimal the wrong way: small numbers get negative powers.

quiz.why: 0.007 = 7/1000 = 7 × 10⁻³. We move the decimal 3 places to get 7.
0.016 = 1.6 × 10⁻² cm. In standard form the number before the power of 10 is between 1 and 10.
5.8 × 10⁻⁵ means moving the decimal 5 places left: 0.000058.
Standard form needs a number from 1 up to (not including) 10. Only 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ fits.

quiz.q: Speed of light ≈ 300,000,000 m/s in standard form:
quiz.why: 300,000,000 = 3 followed by 8 zeros = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

lessons.title: Comparing very large and very small numbers

scenes.text: Diameter of the Sun ≈ 1.4 × 10⁹ m; Earth ≈ 1.2756 × 10⁷ m.
Divide: about 1.1 × 10² — the Sun is roughly 100 times wider.
Standard form makes giant comparisons easy.

steps.title: Comparing
steps.body: Compare the powers of 10 first; if they are equal, compare k. To add, convert to the same power of 10 first.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Sun diameter ÷ Earth diameter = (1.4 × 10⁹)/(1.2756 × 10⁷) ≈ 1.1 × 10² ≈ 110 (about a hundred times).

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Which is smaller: 2.7 × 10⁻⁶ or 9.1 × 10⁻⁷?

- 10⁻⁷ is smaller than 10⁻⁶, so 9.1 × 10⁻⁷ is smaller.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding numbers with different powers by adding k's directly.
- Thinking 10⁻⁷ > 10⁻⁶ because 7 > 6.

statements.s: 3 × 10⁻⁵ is smaller than 3 × 10⁻⁴.
1 micrometre = 10⁻⁶ m.

quiz.why: Divide the numbers and subtract the powers: 6/3 = 2 and 10⁵⁻² = 10³. So 2 × 10³.
4.1 × 10⁸ = 410,000,000 and 9.9 × 10⁷ = 99,000,000. A higher power of ten wins here, so 4.1 × 10⁸ is larger.
1.5 × 4 = 6, and −3 + 5 = 2. So the product is 6 × 10².

quiz.q: A virus is 3 × 10⁻⁷ m; a bacterium 2 × 10⁻⁶ m. The bacterium is about how many times larger?
quiz.why: The ratio is (2 × 10⁻⁶)/(3 × 10⁻⁷) = (2/3) × 10 ≈ 6.7. So the bacterium is about 7 times larger.
0.00001 has 5 places after the decimal point, so it is 10⁻⁵.

questions.q: Any non-zero number to the power 0 is:
questions.why: Any non-zero number to the power 0 equals 1.

questions.q: 0.00008 in standard form:
questions.why: 0.00008 = 8 × 10⁻⁵, since the decimal moves 5 places.
(−3)⁻³ = 1/(−3)³ = 1/(−27) = −1/27. An odd power keeps the negative sign.

questions.q: Find m: 7ᵐ × 7⁻⁴ = 7⁻¹
Assertion: 5⁻³ = −125. Reason: A negative exponent makes a number negative.
questions.why: Both are false. 5⁻³ = 1/125, not −125, and a negative exponent means a reciprocal, not a negative number.
The bracket is a non-zero number, and any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1.

questions.q: Usual form of 4.5 × 10⁻⁴:
questions.why: 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ means moving the decimal 4 places left: 0.00045.

questions.q: Case: A stack has 20 books each 20 mm thick and 10 sheets each 0.016 mm thick. Total thickness in standard form:
questions.why: 20 books × 20 mm = 400 mm. 10 sheets × 0.016 mm = 0.16 mm. The total is 400.16 mm = 4.0016 × 10² mm.
Add the exponents: (m + 1) + 5 = 7, so m + 6 = 7 and m = 1.

questions.q: Distance Earth–Sun ≈ 1.496 × 10¹¹ m; Earth–Moon ≈ 3.84 × 10⁸ m. The Sun is roughly how many times farther than the Moon?
questions.why: The ratio is (1.496 × 10¹¹)/(3.84 × 10⁸) ≈ 0.39 × 10³ = 390. So the Sun is about 390 times farther than the Moon.

questions.q: Which is the smallest?
questions.why: The numbers have the same 3.4 but different powers. The most negative power, 10⁻⁸, gives the smallest value.

courses.title: Ch 11 · Direct and Inverse Proportions
courses.summary: Recognising when two quantities vary directly or inversely, using x/y = k and xy = k, and solving real problems on cost, maps, shadows, speed, work and food supplies.
outcomes: Learners can test whether two quantities are in direct or inverse proportion
Learners can solve direct-proportion problems by unitary method and by x₁/y₁ = x₂/y₂
Learners can solve inverse-proportion problems using x₁y₁ = x₂y₂
Learners can choose the right type of proportion in word problems

scenes.text: 5 m of cloth costs ₹210.
Double the length → double the cost; 15 m → 3 times → ₹630.
Cost is directly proportional to length.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: x and y are in **direct proportion** if x/y = k (constant), i.e. when one increases (or decreases), the other increases (decreases) in the same ratio. **x₁/y₁ = x₂/y₂**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A 14 m pole casts a 10 m shadow. At the same time, a tree casts a 15 m shadow. Height of tree?

- 14/10 = h/15 → h = 21 m.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — map scale
steps.body:
On a map 1 cm = 5 km. Two towns are 8.5 cm apart. Actual distance?

- 8.5 × 5 = 42.5 km.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking any two quantities that both increase are directly proportional — the ratio must stay **constant** (age and height both grow but not proportionally).
- Mixing units (cm and m).

activity.prompt: If 6 kg of rice costs ₹300, how much do 10 kg cost?

quiz.q: x and y are directly proportional; x = 4 when y = 12. y when x = 7:
quiz.why: In direct proportion y = kx. With x = 4 and y = 12, k = 3. So when x = 7, y = 21.

quiz.q: Which pair is in direct proportion?
options: Workers and days for a job
Number of pens and their total cost
Speed and time for fixed distance
quiz.why: The cost of pens goes up in the same ratio as the number of pens, so they are in direct proportion. More workers means fewer days, which is inverse.

quiz.q: A car uses 4 L petrol for 50 km. Petrol for 250 km:
quiz.why: 250 km is 5 times 50 km, so the petrol needed is 5 × 4 = 20 L.

quiz.q: Scale 1 : 50000 on a map. 3 cm on the map is (actual):
If x/y is constant, x and y are in:
quiz.why: If x/y is constant, x and y are in direct proportion.

scenes.text: 20 workers can build a wall in 15 days.
With 25 workers, will it take longer or shorter?
Shorter: 20 × 15 = 25 × d → d = 12 days.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: x and y are in **inverse proportion** if xy = k (constant): when one increases, the other decreases in the same ratio. **x₁y₁ = x₂y₂**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
20 workers → 15 days. 25 workers?

- 20 × 15 = 25 × d → d = 12 days.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A car at 60 km/h takes 2 h for a journey. At 80 km/h?

- 60 × 2 = 80 × t → t = 1.5 h.

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Food for 100 students lasts 20 days. With 125 students?

- 100 × 20 = 125 × d → d = 16 days.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using direct proportion just because a problem has two numbers — ask 'if one doubles, does the other double or halve?'.
- Forgetting to convert hours/minutes consistently.

activity.prompt: Direct or inverse proportion?

items.text: Speed and time for a fixed distance
Number of pipes and time to fill a tank
Weight of sugar and its cost
Number of people sharing a pizza and slices each
Hours worked and wages earned (hourly pay)

quiz.why: In inverse proportion xy is constant. With xy = 48 and x = 6, y = 48 ÷ 6 = 8.

quiz.q: 6 pipes fill a tank in 80 min. 5 pipes take:
quiz.why: More pipes means less time. 6 × 80 = 480, so with 5 pipes the time is 480 ÷ 5 = 96 min.

quiz.q: In inverse proportion, if x is halved, y is:
quiz.why: In inverse proportion xy stays constant. If x is halved, y must double.

quiz.q: A journey takes 6 h at 40 km/h. At 60 km/h:
quiz.why: The distance is 6 × 40 = 240 km. At 60 km/h the time is 240 ÷ 60 = 4 h.

quiz.q: 10 people finish a job in 6 days. Days for 15 people:
quiz.why: The total work is 10 × 6 = 60 person-days. With 15 people, days = 60 ÷ 15 = 4.

scenes.text: A class plans a picnic: bus fare, sandwiches, travel time.
Some quantities rise together; some trade off.
Decide the type FIRST, then calculate.

steps.title: Decision test
steps.body:
Ask: *If one quantity doubles, what must happen to the other?*

- Doubles → direct (use ratio equal).
- Halves → inverse (use product equal).
- Neither → not proportional.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
A machine fills 840 bottles in 6 hours. How many in 5 hours?

- Direct: 840/6 = x/5 → x = 700 bottles.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A batch of bricks is unloaded by 12 workers in 7 hours. How many workers to do it in 4 hours?

- Inverse: 12 × 7 = w × 4 → w = 21 workers.

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
A school has 8 periods of 45 min. If it has 9 periods in the same total time, each period lasts?

- Inverse: 8 × 45 = 9 × t → t = 40 min.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Not checking whether the answer is sensible (more workers should mean fewer hours).

a.text: A rail track: 15 men lay it in 12 days. How long would 20 men take?

choices.label: Direct: 15/12 = 20/d
choices.feedback: That would make 20 men take MORE days.

w.text: Check sense: more men should finish faster, so it is inverse proportion.

e.text: 9 days. Always test the type before calculating!

quiz.q: A typist types 540 words in 15 min. Words in 25 min:
quiz.why: Words typed are directly proportional to time. 540 ÷ 15 = 36 words a minute, so in 25 min: 36 × 25 = 900.

quiz.q: 12 taps fill a tank in 3 h. Time for 9 taps:
quiz.why: Fewer taps take more time. 12 × 3 = 36 tap-hours, so 9 taps take 36 ÷ 9 = 4 h.

quiz.q: Cost of 12 sweets ₹180. Cost of 20 sweets:
quiz.why: One sweet costs 180 ÷ 12 = ₹15, so 20 sweets cost 20 × 15 = ₹300.

quiz.q: Number of sides of a regular polygon and each exterior angle are:
quiz.why: For a regular polygon, n × exterior angle = 360, a constant. So they are inversely proportional.

quiz.q: A car covers 14 km in 25 min. Distance in 5 hours at the same speed:
quiz.why: 5 hours = 300 minutes, which is 12 times 25 minutes. So the distance is 14 × 12 = 168 km.

questions.q: x and y in direct proportion: x = 3, y = 9. When x = 5, y =
questions.why: From x = 3 and y = 9, y = 3x. When x = 5, y = 15.

questions.q: Speed and time for a fixed distance are in:
questions.why: For a fixed distance, speed × time is constant. So speed and time are in inverse proportion.

questions.q: If xy = 36 and y = 4, x =
9 notebooks cost ₹270. Cost of 13:
questions.why: One notebook costs 270 ÷ 9 = ₹30, so 13 cost 13 × 30 = ₹390.

questions.q: 24 workers build a wall in 10 days. 30 workers take:
questions.why: The work is 24 × 10 = 240 worker-days. With 30 workers: 240 ÷ 30 = 8 days.

questions.q: A train at 75 km/h takes 4 h. At 100 km/h:
questions.why: The distance is 75 × 4 = 300 km. At 100 km/h, time = 300 ÷ 100 = 3 h.

questions.q: Assertion: Number of workers and days to finish a job are inversely proportional. Reason: More workers share the same total work.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: workers and days are inversely proportional. R is true: more workers share the same total work, so each needs fewer days. R explains A.

questions.q: A map scale is 1 cm : 25 km. Actual distance 175 km on the map is:
questions.why: On the map 1 cm stands for 25 km, so 175 km is 175 ÷ 25 = 7 cm.

questions.q: Food for 400 soldiers lasts 31 days. If 120 more join, it lasts:
questions.why: The food is 400 × 31 soldier-days. With 520 soldiers: 400 × 31 ÷ 520 ≈ 23.8 days.

questions.q: Case: A hostel has food for 60 students for 30 days. After 10 days, 20 students leave. How many more days will the food last?
questions.why: After 10 days, food for 60 students for 20 days remains: 60 × 20 = 1200 student-days. With 40 students it lasts 1200 ÷ 40 = 30 more days.

questions.q: If 15 boxes weigh 600 kg, weight of 22 boxes:
questions.why: One box weighs 600 ÷ 15 = 40 kg, so 22 boxes weigh 22 × 40 = 880 kg.

questions.q: A 5 m 60 cm pole casts a 3 m 20 cm shadow. At the same time, a 10 m 50 cm tree casts a shadow of:
questions.why: Heights and shadows are in proportion: 5.6/3.2 = 10.5/s. So s = 10.5 × 3.2 ÷ 5.6 = 6 m.

questions.q: x and y are inversely proportional; x = 15 when y = 8. Find y when x = 24.
questions.why: In inverse proportion xy is constant: 15 × 8 = 120. So when x = 24, y = 120 ÷ 24 = 5.

questions.q: A contractor estimates 3 workers rewire a house in 4 days. How many workers to do it in 1 day?
questions.why: The job takes 3 × 4 = 12 worker-days. To finish in 1 day, 12 workers are needed.

questions.q: A car covers 20 km on 1 L of petrol. Petrol for 250 km:
questions.why: Petrol used is distance ÷ 20 km per litre = 250 ÷ 20 = 12.5 L.

questions.q: If 35 kg of rice feeds 30 people for 7 days, how many days will 45 kg feed 30 people?
questions.why: 35 kg lasts 7 days for 30 people, so they eat 5 kg a day. 45 kg lasts 45 ÷ 5 = 9 days.

courses.title: Ch 12 · Factorisation
courses.summary: Factorising by common factors, by regrouping, using identities and the (x + a)(x + b) pattern; dividing algebraic expressions; and finding and correcting common algebra errors.
outcomes: Learners can factorise by taking out common factors and by regrouping
Learners can factorise using a² ± 2ab + b², a² − b² and x² + (a + b)x + ab
Learners can divide polynomials by monomials and by factors
Learners can spot and correct common algebraic errors

scenes.text: A shop packs 12a²b pencils and 15ab² erasers into identical kits.
The biggest common chunk is 3ab.
12a²b + 15ab² = 3ab(4a + 5b).

steps.title: What is factorisation?
steps.body: Writing an expression as a **product of factors**. It is the reverse of expanding. Irreducible factors (like 2, a, b, (a + 1)) cannot be split further.

steps.title: Method of common factors
steps.body: Find the HCF of the numerical coefficients and the lowest power of each common variable; take it outside a bracket.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Factorise 12a²b + 15ab².

- HCF of 12 and 15 = 3; common variables a and b.
- = 3ab(4a + 5b).

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Factorise 6xy − 4y + 6 − 9x.

- Rearrange: 6xy − 9x − 4y + 6 = 3x(2y − 3) − 2(2y − 3) = (2y − 3)(3x − 2).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not taking the HIGHEST common factor: 12a²b + 15ab² = 3(4a²b + 5ab²) is incomplete.
- Losing a 1: 3x + 3 = 3(x + 1), not 3x.

activity.prompt: Factorise by taking common factors.

quiz.why: 7x − 42 = 7 × x − 7 × 6 = 7(x − 6). The common factor is 7.
The numbers 6, 24 and 12 have HCF 6. The letters a and b are common to all terms, so the common factor is 6ab.
Group the terms: x(a + b) + y(a + b) = (a + b)(x + y).

scenes.text: Meena sees x² + 8x + 16 and remembers (a + b)².
Pattern spotting saves lots of work.

steps.title: Identity forms
steps.body:
- a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)²
- a² − 2ab + b² = (a − b)²
- a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stopping too early: x⁴ − 256 must be factorised completely.
- Trying a² + b² = (a + b)(a − b) — sums of squares do not factorise this way.
- Checking only the first and last terms: x² + 6x + 16 is not a perfect square (middle should be 8x).

activity.prompt: Match each expression with its factorised form

quiz.why: x² − 81 = x² − 9², a difference of squares. It factorises as (x − 9)(x + 9).
(l + m)² − 4lm = l² + 2lm + m² − 4lm = l² − 2lm + m² = (l − m)².

lessons.title: Factors of the form (x + a)(x + b)

scenes.text: To factorise x² + 5x + 6, find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5.
2 and 3!

steps.title: Method (splitting the middle term)
steps.body:
For x² + px + q, find a and b with **a + b = p** and **ab = q**. Then x² + px + q = (x + a)(x + b).

Sign guide: q > 0 → a, b same sign as p; q < 0 → opposite signs.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: y² − 7y + 12: need sum −7, product 12 → −3, −4 → (y − 3)(y − 4).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Picking numbers that multiply correctly but don't add correctly.
- Sign mix-ups when q is negative.
- Always expand your answer to check.

activity.prompt: x² + 9x + 20 = (x + 4)(x + b). What is b?

quiz.why: We need two numbers that add to 7 and multiply to 10. They are 2 and 5, so x² + 7x + 10 = (x + 2)(x + 5).
We need two numbers with sum −10 and product 21. They are −3 and −7, so (m − 3)(m − 7).
We need two numbers with sum −1 and product −20. They are −5 and 4, so (x − 5)(x + 4).
We need two numbers with sum 2 and product −15. They are 5 and −3, so (y + 5)(y − 3).
We need two numbers with sum −10 and product 24. They are −4 and −6, so (q − 4)(q − 6).

scenes.text: An expression 24xy²z³ must be shared in 6yz² equal parts.
Divide coefficients and subtract powers.
Each gets 4xyz.

steps.title: Monomial ÷ monomial
steps.body: Divide coefficients; subtract exponents of the same variable. 24xy²z³ ÷ 6yz² = 4xyz.

steps.title: Polynomial ÷ monomial
steps.body: Divide **each term**: (5x² − 6x) ÷ 3x = (5/3)x − 2.

steps.title: Polynomial ÷ polynomial
steps.body: Factorise the numerator, then cancel the common factor: (y² + 7y + 10) ÷ (y + 5) = (y + 2)(y + 5)/(y + 5) = y + 2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

steps.title: Common mistakes summary
steps.body: Most errors come from: missing the middle term, wrong sign distribution, cancelling terms instead of factors, and squaring a negative incorrectly.

courses.title: Ch 13 · Introduction to Graphs
courses.summary: Bar graphs, pie charts, histograms and line graphs; linear graphs; locating points with coordinates; and reading and drawing graphs of real relationships such as distance–time, quantity–cost and principal–interest.
outcomes: Learners can choose the right graph for a data set

lessons.title: Types of graphs and line graphs

scenes.text: A nurse records a patient's temperature every hour.
She joins the dots with lines.
The rise and fall over time is easy to see — that's a line graph.

steps.title: Which graph when?
steps.body:
- **Bar graph:** compare categories.
- **Pie chart:** parts of a whole.
- **Histogram:** grouped continuous data (intervals).
- **Line graph:** how a quantity changes over **time** (or another continuous variable). Points are joined by segments.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
A line graph shows a patient's temperature: 9 am 37.5 °C, 10 am 38 °C, 11 am 38.5 °C, 12 noon 38.5 °C, 1 pm 37.5 °C.

- Highest: 38.5 °C (11 am to noon).
- It stayed constant between 11 am and noon (flat segment).
- It fell fastest between noon and 1 pm (steepest downward segment).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Sales of a shop: Jan ₹20k, Feb ₹30k, Mar ₹25k. Which month had the largest increase over the previous month? Feb (+₹10k).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading the vertical value wrongly because the scale is not 1 unit per grid.
- Using a line graph for unrelated categories (e.g. favourite fruits).

steps.title: Slope sense
steps.body: Steeper segment = faster change. Flat segment = no change.

pairs: Height of a plant every week

quiz.why: A line graph shows how a quantity changes over time, so it suits time series data.

A pie chart shows how a whole is divided into parts, with sectors that add up to 360°.

quiz.q: In a line graph, a steeper rise shows:
quiz.why: A steeper rise means a greater change per unit of time, so a faster increase.
Histograms show grouped, continuous data in class intervals.

steps.title: The coordinate plane
steps.body:
- Horizontal line: **x-axis**; vertical line: **y-axis**. They meet at the **origin O (0, 0)**.
- A point is written **(x, y)**: x-coordinate (abscissa) first, then y-coordinate (ordinate).
- Points on the x-axis have y = 0, e.g. (4, 0). Points on the y-axis have x = 0, e.g. (0, 3).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Plot A(2, 3): from O move 2 units right, then 3 units up. B(3, 2) is a different point — order matters!

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Do (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3) lie on a line? Plot them: yes, they lie on a straight line through the origin (y = x).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing (y, x) instead of (x, y).
- Thinking (0, 5) lies on the x-axis — it lies on the y-axis.

steps.title: Real world
steps.body: Maps (latitude–longitude), chess boards (e4), spreadsheets (cell B7) and game screens all use coordinate ideas.

activity.prompt: Where does each point lie?

The order of the coordinates matters. (2, 5) is 2 right and 5 up, while (5, 2) is 5 right and 2 up. They are different points.

steps.title: Linear graph
steps.body: If the points of a relationship lie on a straight line, the graph is **linear**. Direct proportion (y = kx) gives a straight line through the origin.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — simple interest
steps.body:
SI at 8% for 1 year: deposit ₹100 → ₹8, ₹200 → ₹16, ₹300 → ₹24.

- From the graph, SI on ₹250 is ₹20; deposit for ₹40 interest is ₹500.

steps.body: Side 1, 2, 3, 4 cm → perimeter 4, 8, 12, 16 cm. Graph is linear: P = 4s. For s = 2.5 cm, P = 10 cm.

steps.body: Side 1, 2, 3 → area 1, 4, 9. The points (1,1), (2,4), (3,9) do NOT lie on a straight line, so area vs side is not linear.

steps.title: Reading a distance–time graph
steps.body:
- Time on x-axis, distance on y-axis.
- Straight sloping line = constant speed; **speed = distance ÷ time** for that segment.
- Flat (horizontal) part = stopped.
- Steeper = faster.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Ajit: 0–1 h: 0 → 20 km; 1–1.5 h: stays at 20 km; 1.5–2.5 h: 20 → 50 km.

- Speed in first hour: 20 km/h.
- Rest: 30 minutes.
- Speed in last part: 30 km/h (faster, steeper).

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Reading total distance from one segment only.

courses.title: Class 8 Maths · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: A one-stop formula sheet for every Class 8 chapter, two full mock papers with step-by-step answers, and an exam-day strategy.
outcomes: Learners can recall all key Class 8 formulas
Learners can solve mixed questions across all chapters under time pressure
Learners can plan an exam strategy and check answers efficiently

scenes.text: Kavya has her final exam tomorrow.
She wants one page with every formula.
Here it is — read it, then cover and recall.

steps.title: Numbers
steps.body:
- Rational: p/q, q ≠ 0. Closed under +, −, ×. Additive inverse −a, reciprocal 1/a.
- Squares end in 0,1,4,5,6,9; between n² and (n+1)² → 2n non-squares; 1 + 3 + … (n odd numbers) = n²; triplet 2m, m² − 1, m² + 1.
- Cubes: groups of three prime factors; 1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³.
- a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ; aᵐaⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ; a⁰ = 1; standard form k × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ k < 10.

steps.title: Algebra
steps.body:
- (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²; (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²; (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b²; (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab.
- Linear equation: transpose (change sign), clear fractions with LCM, check by substitution.
- Factorise: common factor → regroup → identity → split middle term.

steps.title: Geometry & mensuration
steps.body:
- Polygon angle sum (n − 2) × 180°; exterior sum 360°; regular exterior 360°/n; diagonals n(n − 3)/2.
- Parallelogram: opp. sides & angles equal, adjacent supplementary, diagonals bisect.
- Trapezium ½h(a + b); quadrilateral ½d(h₁ + h₂); rhombus ½d₁d₂.
- Cuboid TSA 2(lb + bh + hl), LSA 2h(l + b), V = lbh; cube 6a², 4a², a³; cylinder CSA 2πrh, TSA 2πr(r + h), V = πr²h; 1 m³ = 1000 L.

steps.title: Data, proportion, money
steps.body:
- Pie angle = (value/total) × 360°; P(E) = favourable/total.
- Direct x/y = k; inverse xy = k.
- % change on original; discount on MP; profit % on CP (incl. overheads); tax on SP.
- CI: A = P(1 + R/100)ⁿ; half-yearly R/2, 2n; depreciation (1 − R/100)ⁿ.

steps.title: How to revise
steps.body: Cover each block, write it from memory, then check. Repeat the ones you missed tomorrow morning.

steps.title: Top 5 exam errors
steps.body:
- (a + b)² written as a² + b².
- Percent on the wrong base.
- 2⁻³ taken as negative.
- Diameter used as radius.
- Forgetting units (cm², cm³, L).

The lateral surface area of a cube covers only the four side faces, so it is 4a². The total surface area is 6a².

steps.title: Time plan
steps.body:
- First 5 minutes: read the paper; tick easy questions.
- Do easy questions first, then medium, then hard.
- Leave 10 minutes to check.

steps.title: Checking tricks
steps.body:
- Equations: substitute back.
- Factorisation: expand back.
- Percentages: estimate (is the answer sensible?).
- Mensuration: units and radius/diameter.

steps.title: Example of a sense-check
steps.body: If you get 'a car's speed is 600 km/h' in a city problem, something is wrong — recheck the division.

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body:
- Spending 10 minutes on a 1-mark question.
- Rubbing out working: cross it out neatly; examiners may give method marks.

steps.title: Feeling anxious?
steps.body: Slow breathing (in 4, hold 4, out 4) for one minute helps. If exam fear is overwhelming, talk to a teacher, parent or counsellor.

quiz.why: Keeping about 10 minutes at the end is enough to check the key answers.
If you are stuck, skip the question and return to it later, so that you do not waste time.

quiz.q: Crossing out wrong working neatly instead of erasing:
quiz.why: Neatly crossing out wrong work still lets examiners see the correct method. This can still earn method marks.

NCERT has been introducing new Class 8 books from 2025–26; if your school uses those, chapter names and order differ, but most topics here still apply. Independent material, not affiliated with NCERT or any board.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Crop Production and Management
courses.summary: Why we grow crops, kharif and rabi seasons, and every agricultural practice: preparing soil, sowing, manures and fertilisers, irrigation, weed control, harvesting, storage, and food from animals.
outcomes: Learners can classify crops as kharif or rabi with examples
Learners can explain each agricultural practice in order and its tools
Learners can compare manure and fertiliser and explain crop rotation
Learners can describe traditional and modern irrigation, harvesting and storage methods

lessons.title: Crops, seasons and preparing the soil

scenes.text: Dadi says, 'We sow paddy when the monsoon arrives and wheat when winter begins.'
Before sowing, her son ploughs the field and levels it.
Why plough at all? Why different seasons?

steps.title: Crops and seasons
steps.body:
A **crop** is a plant of the same kind grown on a large scale in one place. India has two main cropping seasons:

- **Kharif** (sown with the monsoon, about June–September): paddy (rice), maize, soybean, groundnut, cotton.
- **Rabi** (sown in winter, about October–March): wheat, gram, pea, mustard, linseed.

Pulses and vegetables are also grown in summer in many places.

steps.title: Agricultural practices (in order)
steps.body:
- Preparation of soil
- Sowing
- Adding manure and fertilisers
- Irrigation
- Protection from weeds
- Harvesting
- Storage

steps.title: Preparing the soil
steps.body:
**Ploughing (tilling)** loosens and turns the soil so that:

- roots can go deep and breathe,
- earthworms and microbes thrive and add humus,
- nutrients from deeper layers come up.

Very dry soil may be watered before ploughing. **Levelling** with a wooden or iron leveller prevents erosion and helps even irrigation.

**Tools:** plough (wooden/iron ploughshare pulled by bullocks), **hoe** (removes weeds, loosens soil), **cultivator** (tractor-driven; saves labour and time).

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
A farmer sows wheat in July. What goes wrong?

- Wheat is a rabi crop that needs cool weather to grow and dry, mild weather to ripen. Sown in the monsoon it would face heavy rain and heat → poor yield. Correct time: Oct–Nov.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body:
Why is a field levelled after ploughing?

- So water spreads evenly during irrigation and topsoil is not washed away by wind or rain.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling cotton a rabi crop (it is kharif).
- Thinking ploughing is only for removing weeds — its main job is loosening and turning soil.

activity.prompt: Sort the crops by season

quiz.why: Wheat is a rabi crop, sown in winter and harvested in spring. Paddy, maize and cotton are kharif crops.

quiz.q: Loosening and turning soil is called:
