quiz.why: Loosening and turning the soil is called tilling or ploughing.

quiz.q: The tool used for removing weeds and loosening soil:
quiz.why: A hoe is a simple tool used to remove weeds and loosen the soil.
Loose soil lets air and water reach the roots, so roots can breathe and grow deep.

quiz.q: Kharif crops are sown in the:
quiz.why: Kharif crops are sown in the rainy season, when the monsoon arrives, from about June to July.

scenes.text: Before sowing, Meena drops seeds into a bucket of water.
Some float — they're damaged or hollow.
She sows only the seeds that sink.

steps.title: Sowing
steps.body:
- **Seed selection:** good seeds are clean, healthy and of a good variety. In water, damaged (lighter, hollow) seeds float; good seeds sink.
- **Traditional tool:** a funnel-shaped tool with pointed tubes that drops seeds into furrows.
- **Seed drill:** tractor-driven; sows at uniform distance and depth, covers seeds with soil (protects from birds), saves time.
- Correct spacing avoids overcrowding (competition for light, water, nutrients). Some crops (paddy) are first grown in a nursery and then **transplanted**.

steps.title: Manure vs fertiliser
steps.body:
Repeated cropping removes nutrients. Replacing them:

- **Manure:** organic, from decomposed plant and animal waste; adds **humus**, improves soil texture and water holding; rich in fewer nutrients; made on farms.
- **Fertiliser:** inorganic salt made in factories (urea, ammonium sulphate, superphosphate, potash, NPK); rich in specific nutrients (N, P, K); no humus; overuse harms soil fertility and pollutes water.

steps.title: Other ways to restore fertility
steps.body:
- **Fallow:** leaving land uncultivated for a season.
- **Crop rotation:** alternating cereals with **leguminous** crops (pulses, beans). Legumes carry **Rhizobium** bacteria in their root nodules, which fix atmospheric nitrogen into the soil.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
A farmer grows wheat every year and yields drop. Suggest two remedies.

- Rotate with a legume (e.g. gram/moong) to restore nitrogen.
- Add farmyard manure or compost to replace humus.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body:
Why does a seed drill give a better crop than broadcasting seeds by hand?

- Uniform depth and spacing → each plant gets enough light, water and nutrients; seeds are covered, so birds can't eat them.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying fertilisers add humus (only manure does).
- Thinking more fertiliser always means more crop — overuse damages soil and water bodies.

statements.s: Manure adds humus to soil.
Urea is a manure.
statements.why: Urea is a fertiliser made in factories.

statements.s: Rhizobium fixes nitrogen in legume roots.
Seeds that float in water are the best seeds.
Overuse of fertilisers can reduce soil fertility.

quiz.q: Bacteria in root nodules of legumes:
quiz.why: Rhizobium is a bacterium that lives in root nodules of legumes. It changes nitrogen from air into a form the plant can use.
Manure is made from decayed plant and animal matter. It adds humus, which improves the soil. Urea, NPK and superphosphate are fertilisers.
Growing different crops one after another in the same field is crop rotation. It helps keep the soil fertile.
A seed drill sows seeds at an even depth and spacing, and covers them with soil. This saves seeds and effort.

quiz.q: Paddy seedlings are first raised in a nursery and then:
quiz.why: Paddy seedlings are raised in a nursery first. Then they are transplanted to the field.

scenes.text: In dry Rajasthan, Ramesh's orchard gets water drop by drop near each root.
His cousin in Kerala relies on rain and a canal.
Different places, different irrigation.

steps.title: Why irrigate?
steps.body: Water is needed for germination, for carrying nutrients, and protects crops from frost and hot winds. Supplying water to crops at intervals is **irrigation**. Sources: wells, tube wells, ponds, lakes, rivers, dams and canals.

steps.title: Traditional and modern methods
steps.body:
- **Traditional:** moat (pulley system), **chain pump**, **dhekli**, **rahat** (Persian wheel) — often animal or human powered; pumps run on diesel, electricity, biogas or solar.
- **Sprinkler system:** perpendicular pipes with rotating nozzles spray water like rain; good for uneven land and sandy soil.
- **Drip system:** water falls drop by drop at the roots; best for fruit plants, gardens and trees; wastes almost no water.

steps.title: Weeds and their control
steps.body:
**Weeds** are unwanted plants growing with the crop (e.g. *Amaranthus*, *Chenopodium*/bathua, grass). They compete for water, nutrients, space and light; some are poisonous.

Control: tilling before sowing, manual removal with a **khurpi** or harrow, and **weedicides** (e.g. 2,4-D) sprayed during the vegetative growth of weeds before flowering. Sprayers should cover nose and mouth — weedicides can harm health.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Suggest an irrigation method for a mango orchard in a region with scarce water. → Drip irrigation: water reaches each root with minimal loss.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why spray weedicides before weeds flower? → Before flowering and seeding, so the weeds cannot spread seeds for the next season.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying sprinklers are best for paddy (paddy needs standing water; sprinklers suit uneven/sandy land).
- Forgetting the safety step when spraying chemicals.

activity.prompt: Match the method to its best use
pairs: Fruit plants and trees where water is scarce

quiz.q: Which irrigation wastes the least water?
quiz.why: Drip irrigation gives water drop by drop right at the roots, so it wastes the least water.

quiz.q: Unwanted plants in a field are:
quiz.why: Unwanted plants growing in a crop field are called weeds.
2,4-D is a weedicide, a chemical that kills weeds. Neem and urea are not weedicides.

options: Land is uneven and water is less
quiz.why: Sprinklers suit uneven or sandy land where water is scarce. They spray water like rain.

options: Compete for water, light and nutrients
quiz.why: Weeds take water, light and nutrients that the crop needs. So they reduce the crop's growth.

lessons.title: Harvesting, storage and food from animals

scenes.text: In April, families in Punjab celebrate Baisakhi when the wheat is harvested.
Machines called combines cut and thresh in one go.
Grain then goes to silos so it doesn't rot.

steps.title: Harvesting
steps.body: Cutting a mature crop is **harvesting**: by hand with a **sickle**, or by a **harvester**. **Threshing** separates grain from chaff; a **combine** harvests and threshes together. Small farmers use **winnowing** (wind blows away light chaff). Harvest festivals: Pongal, Baisakhi, Holi, Diwali, Nabanya, Bihu.

steps.title: Storage
steps.body: Grain must be **dried** first (moisture lets fungi and pests grow). Farmers store in jute bags or metal bins; large-scale storage is in **silos** and **granaries** with chemical protection against pests and rats. At home, dried **neem leaves** are used.

steps.title: Food from animals
steps.body: **Animal husbandry** is rearing animals at home or farms for food (milk, eggs, meat, fish) and other products, providing them proper food, shelter and care. Fishing and poultry are also important.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Why must freshly harvested grain be dried before storage? → Moisture allows microorganisms (fungi) and insects to grow and spoil the grain; drying prevents this.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Arrange: harvesting → threshing → winnowing → drying → storage. (Combines merge the first two.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing threshing (separating grain) with winnowing (separating chaff by wind).
- Saying storage needs moisture to keep grain fresh — it's the opposite.

activity.prompt: Put the agricultural practices in order
items: Preparation of soil
Sowing
Adding manure and fertilisers
Irrigation
Protection from weeds
Harvesting
Storage

quiz.q: Machine that harvests and threshes together:
quiz.why: A combine harvests the crop and also threshes the grain in one go.

quiz.q: Separating grain from chaff using wind:
quiz.why: In winnowing, wind blows away the light husk (chaff), and the heavier grain falls down.
Large amounts of grain are stored in silos and granaries, which protect them from pests and moisture.

quiz.q: Neem leaves are used in storage because:
quiz.why: Dried neem leaves keep pests away from stored grain. They are a natural pest repellent.

quiz.q: Rearing animals for food is called:
quiz.why: Animal husbandry means rearing animals, such as cattle, poultry and fish, for food and other products. Agriculture is about growing crops.

questions.q: Which is a kharif crop?
questions.why: Paddy is a kharif crop, sown in the rainy season. Wheat, gram and mustard are rabi crops.

questions.q: A tool used for sowing seeds uniformly:
questions.why: A seed drill sows seeds uniformly at the right depth and spacing. A sickle and a combine are used for harvesting.

questions.q: Manure differs from fertiliser because manure:
questions.why: Manure is made from decayed plant and animal waste, so it adds humus to the soil. Fertilisers are made in factories and do not add humus.

questions.q: Drip irrigation is best for:
questions.why: Drip irrigation puts water right at the roots, drop by drop. It wastes very little, so it suits fruit trees in dry areas.

questions.q: Bacteria fixing nitrogen in root nodules:
questions.why: Rhizobium bacteria live in root nodules of legumes. They fix nitrogen from air into a form the plant can use.

questions.q: Assertion: Seeds that float in water are rejected. Reason: Damaged seeds are hollow and lighter.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: floating seeds are rejected. R is true: damaged seeds are hollow and lighter, so they float. R explains A.

questions.q: Weedicides are best sprayed:
questions.why: Weedicides work best when sprayed before the weeds flower and make seeds. This stops them spreading.

questions.q: Which is NOT a method of replenishing soil nutrients?
questions.why: Fallow land, crop rotation and manure restore soil nutrients. Winnowing separates grain from chaff and has nothing to do with the soil.

questions.q: Case: A farmer in a dry district with sandy, uneven land wants to save water while growing vegetables. Best choice:
questions.why: Sprinklers suit sandy, uneven land, where water would flow away or sink in fast. They also save water.

questions.q: Crop rotation with legumes increases soil:
questions.why: Legumes have Rhizobium in their roots, which fixes nitrogen. So growing legumes in rotation adds nitrogen to the soil.

questions.q: Grain stored with high moisture is likely to be attacked by:
questions.why: Grain with a lot of moisture lets fungi and insects grow. Dry grain stores better.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.why: Wheat is a rabi crop, sown in winter. Paddy is a kharif crop, and gram and pea are rabi crops.

questions.q: Why is excessive use of fertilisers harmful?
options: Reduces soil fertility and pollutes water
questions.why: Too much fertiliser can harm the soil over time and wash into water bodies, polluting them. It does not add humus.

questions.q: A farmer plants paddy seedlings raised in a nursery. This practice is:
questions.why: Raising seedlings in a nursery and then moving them to the field is called transplantation.

questions.q: Assertion: Ploughing increases the number of earthworms and microbes. Reason: Loose soil allows air and moisture to reach them.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: ploughing helps earthworms and microbes. R is true: loose soil lets air and moisture reach them. So R explains A.

questions.q: Case: Wheat yields fall after five years of growing only wheat. The likely cause and best fix:
options: Seeds too heavy; use floating seeds
Nutrient depletion; rotate with pulses and add manure
questions.why: Growing only wheat for years uses up the same nutrients. Rotating with pulses, which add nitrogen, and adding manure restores fertility.

questions.q: Which correctly describes the sequence after harvesting wheat by sickle on a small farm?
questions.why: After cutting wheat, the grain is separated from the stalk by threshing. Winnowing removes the chaff, then the grain is dried and stored.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Microorganisms: Friend and Foe
courses.summary: The main groups of microorganisms and viruses, where they live, how they help us (curd, bread, fermentation, medicines, vaccines, soil fertility, cleaning) and harm us (diseases in humans, animals and plants, food poisoning), food preservation and the nitrogen cycle.
outcomes: Learners can name the major groups of microorganisms with examples
Learners can explain useful roles of microbes in food, medicine and agriculture
Learners can link common diseases to their microbes and modes of spread
Learners can describe methods of food preservation and the nitrogen cycle

scenes.text: Ayaan looks at a drop of pond water under a microscope.
Tiny wriggling shapes, green threads and blobs appear.
A whole living world too small for the naked eye!

steps.title: Microorganisms
steps.body:
Organisms too small to see with the naked eye are **microorganisms (microbes)**; we use a magnifying glass or microscope. Main groups:

- **Bacteria** (rod, spiral, round shapes) — e.g. *Lactobacillus*, *Rhizobium*.
- **Fungi** — bread mould (*Rhizopus*), *Penicillium*, *Aspergillus*, yeast.
- **Protozoa** — *Amoeba*, *Paramecium*, *Plasmodium*.
- **Algae** — *Chlamydomonas*, *Spirogyra*.

**Viruses** are also microscopic but different: they reproduce **only inside the cells of a host** (bacterium, plant or animal). Examples of viral diseases: common cold, influenza, measles, polio, chickenpox.

steps.title: Where they live
steps.body: Everywhere: soil, water, air, ice-cold regions, hot springs, deserts, marshes, and inside animals including humans. Some are single-celled (bacteria, some algae, protozoa); others are multicellular (many algae and fungi). Some live alone, others in colonies.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
Classify: Amoeba, Penicillium, Spirogyra, Lactobacillus.

- Amoeba → protozoa; Penicillium → fungus; Spirogyra → alga; Lactobacillus → bacterium.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why are viruses not grouped with bacteria? → They are much smaller, and cannot reproduce on their own — only inside a host cell.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking all microbes are harmful (most are harmless or helpful).
- Calling yeast a bacterium (it is a fungus).

activity.prompt: Sort into groups

quiz.why: Yeast is a single-celled fungus. It is used to make bread and to ferment sugar.

quiz.q: Which reproduces only inside a host cell?
quiz.why: A virus cannot multiply outside a living cell. It reproduces only inside a host cell.
Plasmodium is a protozoan. It causes malaria.
Spirogyra is a green alga that grows as thin green threads in ponds.
Microbes live almost everywhere, from hot springs to ice, as well as in soil, water, air and bodies.

scenes.text: Mum adds a spoon of curd to warm milk and leaves it overnight.
By morning it's thick curd.
*Lactobacillus* bacteria multiplied and turned milk into curd.

steps.title: In food
steps.body:
- **Curd:** *Lactobacillus* converts milk into curd. Bacteria also help make cheese, pickles.
- **Bread, cakes, idli:** **yeast** respires and releases carbon dioxide; gas bubbles make dough rise.
- **Fermentation:** yeast converts sugar into **alcohol** (used commercially). Louis Pasteur discovered fermentation in 1857.

steps.title: In medicine
steps.body:
- **Antibiotics** are medicines made from microbes (bacteria and fungi) that kill or stop the growth of disease-causing microbes, e.g. streptomycin, tetracycline, erythromycin. **Alexander Fleming** discovered **penicillin** from a mould in 1929 (his famous observation was made in 1928).
- Antibiotics do **not** work against colds and flu (caused by viruses). Take them only as prescribed by a doctor and complete the course.
- **Vaccines:** dead or weakened microbes are introduced so the body makes antibodies and remembers. **Edward Jenner** developed the smallpox vaccine in 1798. Smallpox has been eradicated worldwide.

steps.title: In soil and environment
steps.body:
- **Nitrogen fixation:** *Rhizobium* and some blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) fix atmospheric nitrogen, increasing soil fertility.
- **Cleaning:** microbes decompose dead plants, animals and waste into simple substances (manure). That's why composting works.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Why does dough with yeast rise? → Yeast respires, producing CO₂ gas that forms bubbles and increases the volume.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why shouldn't you take antibiotics for a common cold? → Cold is viral; antibiotics don't act on viruses. Misuse helps bacteria become resistant, so antibiotics may fail when truly needed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Antibiotics cure all infections' — not viral ones.
- Fleming discovered penicillin, Jenner the smallpox vaccine — don't swap them.

activity.prompt: Match the microbe to its friendly use

quiz.why: Yeast releases carbon dioxide gas as it feeds on sugar in dough. The gas bubbles make the bread rise.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin from the mould Penicillium.

quiz.q: Vaccine for smallpox was developed by:
quiz.why: Edward Jenner developed the first vaccine, for smallpox, in 1798.
Antibiotics work against bacteria. Colds and flu are caused by viruses, so antibiotics are not effective.

quiz.q: Fermentation of sugar to alcohol is done by:
quiz.why: Yeast ferments sugar to alcohol and carbon dioxide. It is used to make wine and beer.

scenes.text: After the rains, several people in Riya's colony get fever.
Doctors test for malaria and dengue.
Volunteers clear stagnant water — mosquitoes breed there.

steps.title: Pathogens and spread
steps.body:
Disease-causing microbes are **pathogens**. **Communicable diseases** spread from an infected person to a healthy one through air, water, food or physical contact, or via **carriers** (vectors) like the housefly and mosquitoes.

- The housefly carries germs from garbage to uncovered food.
- Female *Anopheles* mosquito carries the malaria parasite (*Plasmodium*).
- Female *Aedes* mosquito carries the dengue virus.

steps.title: Human diseases
steps.body:
- **Tuberculosis** — bacteria — air
- **Measles** — virus — air
- **Chickenpox** — virus — air/contact
- **Polio** — virus — air/water
- **Cholera** — bacteria — water/food
- **Typhoid** — bacteria — water
- **Hepatitis B** — virus — blood/body fluids (and from mother to baby)
- **Malaria** — protozoan — mosquito

steps.title: Animal and plant diseases; food poisoning
steps.body:
- Animals: **anthrax** (bacterium; affects humans and cattle), **foot-and-mouth disease** in cattle (virus).
- Plants: **citrus canker** (bacteria, air), **rust of wheat** (fungi, air/seeds), **yellow vein mosaic of bhindi/okra** (virus, insects).
- **Food poisoning:** some microbes growing on food produce toxins; eating such food can make us very ill.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Suggest three ways to prevent malaria. → No stagnant water near homes (mosquitoes breed there), use mosquito nets/repellents, spray where needed and keep surroundings clean.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why cover food? → Houseflies carry germs from garbage; they sit on food and contaminate it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying malaria is caused by a mosquito — the mosquito is the carrier; *Plasmodium* is the cause.
- Thinking cholera spreads through air (it spreads via contaminated water/food).

activity.prompt: Who causes it?

quiz.why: The female Anopheles mosquito carries the malaria parasite from person to person.
Typhoid is caused by bacteria. It spreads through contaminated food and water.
Anthrax is a bacterial disease that affects humans and cattle.

quiz.q: Rust of wheat is caused by:
quiz.why: Rust of wheat is a fungal disease. It spreads through air and seeds.

options: Air, water, food, contact or carriers
quiz.why: Communicable diseases spread from an infected person to another through air, water, food, contact or carriers like insects.

lessons.title: Food preservation and the nitrogen cycle

scenes.text: Dadi preserves raw mango with salt, oil and spices; it lasts months.
Jam uses lots of sugar; milk packets say 'pasteurised'.
All of these stop microbes from spoiling food.

steps.title: Preservation methods
steps.body:
- **Chemicals:** salts and edible oils; **sodium benzoate** and **sodium metabisulphite** are common preservatives (jams, squashes).
- **Common salt:** meat, fish, amla, raw mangoes, tamarind — salt removes moisture.
- **Sugar:** jams, jellies, squashes — reduces moisture that microbes need.
- **Oil and vinegar:** pickles — bacteria cannot live in such an environment.
- **Heat and cold:** boiling kills many microbes; refrigeration slows their growth.
- **Pasteurisation:** milk heated to about 70 °C for 15–30 seconds, then suddenly chilled and stored (named after Louis Pasteur).
- **Storage and packing:** airtight packets for dry fruits and vegetables.

steps.title: Nitrogen cycle
steps.body:
Air is about 78% nitrogen, but plants can't use it directly.

- *Rhizobium* and blue-green algae **fix** nitrogen into compounds; lightning also fixes some.
- Plants absorb nitrogen compounds from soil to make proteins; animals get them by eating plants.
- When plants and animals die, **decomposers** convert their nitrogen back into compounds in soil; some bacteria convert compounds back to **nitrogen gas** in the air.
- So the % of nitrogen in the air stays roughly constant.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Why does pasteurised milk last longer than raw milk? → Heating kills most microbes; rapid chilling prevents survivors from multiplying.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why does a farmer growing pulses need less nitrogen fertiliser? → Pulse roots have Rhizobium that fixes nitrogen.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying pasteurisation means boiling (it's controlled heating then chilling).
- Thinking plants take nitrogen gas directly from air.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of the nitrogen cycle
items: Nitrogen gas in the air
Fixed into soil compounds by Rhizobium, blue-green algae or lightning
Absorbed by plants to make proteins
Eaten by animals
Dead remains broken down by decomposers
Some bacteria release nitrogen gas back to the air

quiz.q: Milk heated to about 70 °C and suddenly chilled is:
quiz.why: Milk heated to about 70 °C and then quickly chilled is pasteurised. This kills harmful microbes without changing the milk much.
Jams are preserved by sugar. Sugar reduces the moisture available, so microbes cannot grow.
Sodium benzoate is a chemical preservative used in squashes and jams. It stops the growth of microbes.
Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air. Oxygen is about 21%.
Pickles are preserved with oil and vinegar, which stop bacteria from growing.

questions.q: Lactobacillus helps make:
questions.why: Lactobacillus bacteria turn milk into curd.

questions.q: Which disease is caused by a virus?
questions.why: Measles is a viral disease. Cholera, typhoid and tuberculosis are caused by bacteria.

questions.q: Antibiotic discovered by Fleming:
questions.why: Fleming discovered penicillin, an antibiotic made by the mould Penicillium.

questions.q: Malaria is caused by:
questions.why: Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium. The mosquito only carries it.

questions.q: Which microbe is used to make bread?
questions.why: Yeast is used to make bread. Its carbon dioxide makes the dough rise.

questions.q: Assertion: Antibiotics should not be taken for flu. Reason: Flu is caused by a virus.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: antibiotics should not be taken for flu. R is true: flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not work on viruses. R explains A.

questions.q: Pasteurisation involves heating milk to about:
questions.why: In pasteurisation, milk is heated to about 70 °C for 15–30 seconds, then chilled quickly. This kills harmful microbes.

questions.q: Citrus canker is caused by:
questions.why: Citrus canker is a plant disease caused by bacteria.

questions.q: Which is a carrier of disease?
questions.why: A housefly carries disease germs on its body from dirty places to food. Rhizobium, yeast and Lactobacillus are useful microbes.

questions.q: Blue-green algae help soil by:
questions.why: Blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) fix nitrogen from the air and enrich the soil, as in paddy fields.

questions.q: Case: After a flood, many people in a village get diarrhoea and vomiting. The most likely route and disease:
questions.why: After floods, drinking water may get contaminated. Diarrhoea and vomiting suggest a water-borne disease like cholera.

questions.q: Why is salt used to preserve fish?
options: It removes water and checks microbial growth
questions.why: Salt removes water from the fish by osmosis. Without moisture, microbes cannot grow, so the fish keeps longer.

questions.q: Which is true of viruses?
options: They multiply only inside host cells
questions.why: Viruses can multiply only inside host cells. They are much smaller than bacteria.

questions.q: Assertion: Nitrogen percentage in air stays nearly constant. Reason: Nitrogen is cycled between air, soil and organisms.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: nitrogen in the air stays almost constant. R is true: it is cycled between the air, soil and living things, so it is returned to the air. R explains A.

questions.q: Vaccines work by:
options: Training the body to make antibodies
questions.why: A vaccine trains the body to make antibodies. If the real germ comes later, the body can respond quickly.

questions.q: Case: A family's bread develops black cottony growth after a week in a humid kitchen. It is:
questions.why: Black, cottony growth on bread in a damp kitchen is bread mould, a fungus like Rhizopus.

questions.q: Which pairing is WRONG?
questions.why: Polio is caused by a virus, not bacteria. The other pairs are correct.

questions.q: Overuse of antibiotics is dangerous mainly because:
questions.why: Overusing antibiotics lets some bacteria survive and become resistant. Then the medicines stop working against them.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Coal and Petroleum
courses.summary: Exhaustible and inexhaustible natural resources; how coal, petroleum and natural gas formed; products of coal and of petroleum refining; and how to conserve fossil fuels.
outcomes: Learners can classify natural resources as exhaustible or inexhaustible
Learners can explain the formation of coal and petroleum
Learners can list products of coal processing and petroleum refining with uses
Learners can suggest ways to save fuels and reduce pollution

scenes.text: Sunlight falls on Earth every day.
But the petrol pump owner says prices rise as oil gets harder to find.
Some resources are endless; some can be used up.

steps.title: Two kinds
steps.body:
- **Inexhaustible:** present in unlimited quantity in nature and not likely to be exhausted by human use — sunlight, air.
- **Exhaustible:** limited amount; can be used up — forests, wildlife, minerals, **coal, petroleum, natural gas**.

Forests and wildlife can regrow if conserved, but fossil fuels take millions of years to form.

steps.title: Fossil fuels
steps.body: Coal, petroleum and natural gas are **fossil fuels** — formed from the dead remains of living organisms (fossils) over millions of years. They are exhaustible and their burning causes air pollution.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
Classify: sunlight, coal, air, forest, natural gas.

- Inexhaustible: sunlight, air.
- Exhaustible: coal, forest, natural gas.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why is coal called a fossil fuel? → It formed from buried remains of ancient plants over millions of years.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling forests inexhaustible: they can be destroyed if over-used.
- Thinking fossil fuels can be made again quickly in nature.

activity.prompt: Exhaustible or inexhaustible?

quiz.why: Sunlight is inexhaustible, as it will not run out. Coal, petroleum and natural gas are limited.
Fossil fuels are formed from the dead remains of plants and animals, buried and changed over millions of years.
Minerals are exhaustible, as there is only a limited amount in the Earth. Sunlight, air and wind are not used up.

quiz.q: Fossil fuels take how long to form?
quiz.why: Fossil fuels take millions of years to form. That is why they are exhaustible.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a fossil fuel?
quiz.why: Wood comes from trees, which can regrow, so it is not a fossil fuel. Coal, petroleum and natural gas are.

scenes.text: In Jamshedpur, a steel plant heats coal without air in huge ovens.
What comes out is coke — almost pure carbon.
Black, sticky coal tar from the process once surfaced roads.

steps.title: Formation of coal
steps.body: About 300 million years ago, dense forests in low-lying wetlands were buried under soil by floods. Under high pressure and high temperature, deep underground and without air, the dead vegetation slowly turned into coal. This slow conversion is **carbonisation**. Coal is mainly carbon.

steps.title: Uses and products
steps.body:
Coal is burnt to cook, to make electricity in thermal power plants, and earlier to run railway engines. Burning coal gives mainly CO₂.

Industrial processing (heating in absence of air) gives:

- **Coke:** tough, porous, black, almost pure carbon; used in making steel and extracting many metals.
- **Coal tar:** black, thick liquid with an unpleasant smell; a mixture of about 200 substances; used to make synthetic dyes, drugs, explosives, perfumes, plastics, paints, photographic material, roofing materials. **Naphthalene balls** (moth repellent) come from coal tar. Bitumen (a petroleum product) has largely replaced coal tar for metalling roads.
- **Coal gas:** obtained during coke making; used as fuel in many industries near coal plants. It was first used for street lighting in London (1810) and New York (around 1820).

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Name the product used to make steel and why. → Coke: almost pure carbon, porous and tough; acts as fuel and reducing agent.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why are naphthalene balls kept in woollen clothes? → They are obtained from coal tar and repel moths and insects.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying coal is formed from marine animals (that's petroleum).
- Thinking coke is made by burning coal in air (it is heating in the absence of air).

activity.prompt: Match the coal product with its use
pairs: Slow conversion of dead plants into coal

quiz.q: Slow process of conversion of dead vegetation into coal:
quiz.why: Carbonisation is the slow change of dead vegetation into coal under heat and pressure over millions of years.
Coke is a tough, porous black substance that is almost pure carbon. It is made by heating coal in the absence of air.
Naphthalene balls come from coal tar, a black thick liquid obtained from coal.
Coal is mainly carbon. This is why burning it gives carbon dioxide.

quiz.q: Gas mainly produced when coal burns:
quiz.why: Burning coal, which is mostly carbon, mainly gives carbon dioxide.

scenes.text: Millions of years ago, tiny sea organisms died and settled on the sea bed.
Covered by sand and clay, under heat and pressure, they turned into oil and gas.
Today refineries split this 'black gold' into many useful fuels.

steps.title: Formation and location
steps.body: **Petroleum** formed from organisms living in the sea. Their remains settled at the bottom, were covered by sand and clay, and over millions of years — in the absence of air, under high temperature and pressure — became petroleum and natural gas. Petroleum (lighter than water) lies above water and below gas in rock layers. In India, oil was first struck at **Makum in Assam in 1867** (the world's first oil well was drilled in Pennsylvania, USA, in 1859); other fields include Digboi, Mumbai High, Gujarat and the Krishna–Godavari basin.

steps.title: Refining
steps.body:
Petroleum is a dark, oily mixture. Separating its parts in a **refinery** is **refining** (by fractional distillation). Main fractions and uses:

- **LPG** — fuel for homes and industry
- **Petrol** — motor fuel, aviation fuel, solvent for dry cleaning
- **Kerosene** — stoves, lamps, jet aircraft
- **Diesel** — heavy vehicles, generators
- **Lubricating oil** — reduces friction in machines
- **Paraffin wax** — candles, ointments, Vaseline
- **Bitumen** — paints, road surfacing

Petroleum is also the source of **petrochemicals** used for detergents, fibres (polyester, nylon, acrylic), polythene and plastics. Hydrogen gas from natural gas is used to make fertilisers (urea). Because it is so valuable, petroleum is called **'black gold'**.

steps.title: Natural gas
steps.body: A very important fossil fuel: easy to transport by pipes, and stored as **CNG (Compressed Natural Gas)** under high pressure. Used in power generation, homes and vehicles; it is a **cleaner fuel** (less pollution). Found in Tripura, Rajasthan, Maharashtra and the Krishna–Godavari delta.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Why is CNG preferred in city buses? → It burns more cleanly than diesel, producing less smoke and fewer harmful pollutants.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Which petroleum product is used for candles? → Paraffin wax.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing petrol (one product) with petroleum (crude oil mixture).
- Saying petroleum formed from land plants (that's coal).

activity.prompt: Match the refinery product with its use

quiz.q: Process of separating petroleum into fractions:
quiz.why: Refining is the process of separating petroleum into useful fractions, such as petrol, diesel and kerosene. It is done in a refinery.

quiz.q: In 1867 oil was first struck in India at:
quiz.why: Oil was first struck in India in 1867 at Makum in Assam. The first oil well in the world was drilled in Pennsylvania, USA, in 1859.
CNG stands for Compressed Natural Gas, natural gas stored under high pressure.

quiz.q: Petroleum is called black gold because:
options: It is rare in all countries
It is very valuable with many uses
quiz.why: Petroleum is called black gold because it is dark and very valuable, giving many products used everywhere.
Paraffin wax, a petroleum product, is used to make candles.

scenes.text: Raju's dad switches off his car engine at long red lights.
He saves petrol and the air is cleaner.
Small habits add up for a whole country.

steps.title: Why conserve?
steps.body: Fossil fuels are limited; burning them causes air pollution and contributes to global warming. Use them only when necessary.

steps.title: Tips for saving petrol/diesel (PCRA)
steps.body:
The Petroleum Conservation Research Association (PCRA) advises:

- Drive at a constant and moderate speed.
- Switch off the engine at traffic lights or while waiting.
- Keep correct tyre pressure.
- Ensure regular maintenance of the vehicle.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Suggest three things your family can do to save fuel. → Walk or cycle short distances, share rides/use public transport, switch off engine at long stops, keep tyres properly inflated.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why do alternative sources like solar and wind matter? → They are renewable and cause little pollution, reducing dependence on fossil fuels.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking only big industries can save fuel; household and travel habits matter too.
- Driving fast thinking it saves fuel — moderate constant speed is more efficient.

activity.prompt: Fuel-saver pledge — tick the habits you will try
items: Walk or cycle for short trips
Use public transport or share rides
Remind elders to switch off the engine at long red lights
Check tyre pressure every month
Switch off lights and fans when leaving a room (saves power-plant coal)

quiz.why: PCRA advises driving at a steady, moderate speed. This uses less fuel than speeding up and slowing down.

quiz.q: Switching off the engine at traffic lights:
quiz.why: Switching off the engine at traffic lights saves fuel that would be burnt while idling.

quiz.q: Which is a renewable alternative to fossil fuels?
quiz.why: Solar energy is renewable and will not run out. Coal, diesel and kerosene are fossil fuels.
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, which traps heat and contributes to global warming.
Correct tyre pressure reduces the resistance of the road, so the engine uses less fuel.

questions.q: Which is an inexhaustible resource?
questions.why: Air is inexhaustible. Forests, coal and petroleum can be used up.

questions.q: Coke is used in making:
questions.why: Coke is used to make steel and to extract metals from their ores.

questions.q: Petroleum formed from organisms living in:
questions.why: Petroleum was formed from tiny sea organisms that died and sank, and were buried and changed over millions of years.

questions.q: Product used for road surfacing today:
questions.why: Bitumen, a petroleum product, is used to surface roads. It has replaced coal tar for this.

questions.q: Coal gas was first used for street lighting in:
questions.why: Coal gas was first used for street lighting in London, in 1810.

questions.q: Assertion: CNG is a cleaner fuel. Reason: It produces less pollution on burning.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: CNG is a cleaner fuel. R is true: it gives less pollution on burning, and that is why it is called clean. R explains A.

questions.q: Refining of petroleum is done by:
questions.why: Petroleum is refined by fractional distillation, which separates its parts by their boiling points.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.why: Paraffin wax from petroleum is used for candles. Diesel, LPG and bitumen have other uses.

questions.q: Coal tar is used to make:
questions.why: Coal tar is used to make about 200 substances, including synthetic dyes, drugs and explosives.

questions.q: Hydrogen from natural gas is used to make:
questions.why: Hydrogen from natural gas is used to make fertilisers like urea.

questions.q: In rock layers, petroleum is found:
questions.why: Underground, petroleum is lighter than water but heavier than gas. So it lies above water and below the gas layer.

questions.q: Case: A city switches its buses from diesel to CNG. The expected result:
questions.why: CNG burns more cleanly than diesel. So switching the buses to CNG reduces air pollution.

questions.q: Which is NOT a coal product?
questions.why: Paraffin wax comes from petroleum, not coal. Coke, coal tar and coal gas are coal products.

questions.q: Assertion: Forests are exhaustible natural resources. Reason: Forests can be destroyed faster than they regrow by overuse.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: forests are exhaustible resources. R is true: if forests are cut faster than they regrow, they can be used up. R explains A.

questions.q: Why is petroleum lighter than water important for drilling?
options: Oil sinks to the deepest layer
Oil rises and collects above water in rock layers
questions.why: Petroleum is lighter than water, so it rises and collects above the water in rock layers. This helps in locating and drilling for oil.

questions.q: Which habit saves the MOST fuel over a year for a car driver in city traffic?
options: Idling the engine to stay cool
Switching off at long waits and steady driving
questions.why: Switching off the engine at long waits and driving steadily avoids wasting fuel. Idling, hard braking and low tyre pressure waste fuel.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Combustion and Flame
courses.summary: Combustion and the conditions it needs (fuel, air, ignition temperature), types of combustion, controlling fire, the zones of a candle flame, fuels and calorific value, and the harmful effects of burning fuels.
outcomes: Learners can state the three conditions needed for combustion
Learners can distinguish rapid, spontaneous combustion and explosion
Learners can explain how fire extinguishers work and which to use
Learners can describe the zones of a flame and compare fuels by calorific value

lessons.title: What is combustion? Conditions for burning

scenes.text: A teacher heats water in a paper cup over a candle.
The water boils, but the cup does not burn!
Water keeps the paper below its ignition temperature.

steps.title: Combustion
steps.body: **Combustion** is a chemical process in which a substance reacts with **oxygen** to give off **heat** (and often light). Substances that burn are **combustible** (wood, paper, kerosene, LPG); those that don't are **non-combustible** (stone, glass, iron nails).

steps.title: Three conditions (fire triangle)
steps.body:
- **Fuel** (combustible substance)
- **Supply of air (oxygen)**
- **Heating to ignition temperature** — the lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire.

Remove any one, and fire stops. **Inflammable** substances have very low ignition temperatures and catch fire easily (petrol, alcohol, LPG).

steps.title: Worked example 1 — paper cup
steps.body: Why doesn't the paper cup burn? → Heat given to the paper is passed to the water by conduction, so the paper never reaches its ignition temperature.

steps.title: Worked example 2 — candle in a jar
steps.body: A lit candle covered with a glass jar goes out after some time. → Oxygen inside is used up; without air supply, combustion stops.

steps.title: Worked example 3 — matchstick
steps.body: Striking a safety match: the head (antimony trisulphide + potassium chlorate) rubs against the side strip (powdered glass + a little red phosphorus); friction heat turns some red phosphorus into white phosphorus, which ignites and starts the head burning.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking fire needs only fuel and heat — air is essential.
- Confusing combustible (can burn) with inflammable (catches fire very easily).

activity.prompt: Combustible or non-combustible?

quiz.q: Lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire:
quiz.why: The lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire is its ignition temperature.
Petrol catches fire very easily, as its ignition temperature is low. So it is inflammable. Stone, glass and water do not burn.

quiz.q: A candle under a jar goes out because:
quiz.why: Burning needs oxygen. Under a jar, the candle uses up the oxygen and goes out.

quiz.q: Which is NOT needed for combustion?
quiz.why: Combustion needs fuel, oxygen and heat to reach the ignition temperature. Carbon dioxide is not needed. It actually helps put fires out.

quiz.q: The paper cup with water does not burn because:
quiz.why: The water takes away the heat, so the paper stays below its ignition temperature and does not catch fire.

lessons.title: Types of combustion and controlling fire

scenes.text: At a school fire drill, the fire officer shows a red cylinder.
'Never pour water on an oil or electrical fire,' she warns.
'Use CO₂ — it blankets the fire and cuts off oxygen.'

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Rapid combustion:** burns fast, producing heat and light (LPG at a gas stove).
- **Spontaneous combustion:** bursts into flames without any apparent cause (white phosphorus at room temperature; some forest fires and coal-dust fires).
- **Explosion:** sudden reaction with heat, light and sound, releasing a lot of gas (firecrackers). Also possible by pressure.

steps.title: Fighting fire
steps.body:
Remove one side of the fire triangle:

- **Water:** cools the fuel below ignition temperature and its vapour cuts off air. Best for wood and paper fires.
- Water must NOT be used on **electrical fires** (water conducts electricity — risk of shock) or **oil/petrol fires** (oil floats on water and keeps burning, spreading the fire).
- **CO₂ extinguisher:** CO₂ is heavier than oxygen, covers the fire like a blanket and cuts off oxygen; it also cools the fuel; it doesn't harm electrical equipment. Powder extinguishers (sodium/potassium bicarbonate) release CO₂ on heating.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: A pan of oil catches fire in the kitchen. What should you do? → Turn off the gas if safe, cover the pan with a lid or damp cloth (cuts air), never pour water. Call **112** if it spreads.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why is a person whose clothes catch fire wrapped in a blanket? → It cuts off the air supply.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Throwing water on electrical fires.
- Opening windows widely during a fire (more oxygen can feed it) — follow the fire service's advice and get out safely first.

a.text: An electrical socket in your room sparks and catches fire. What first?

choices.label: Switch off the main power supply if you can do it safely

w.text: Water + electricity can give a deadly shock. Step back and switch off the mains if safe.

b.text: Power is off, but flames remain on the plastic board. What now?

choices.label: Use a CO₂ extinguisher and alert adults; call 112 if it grows
Fan it to blow it out

f.text: Fanning feeds the fire with air. Use CO₂ and call for help.

e.text: Fire out safely. Remember: get people out first; your safety matters more than property.

quiz.q: Burning of LPG at a stove is:
quiz.why: An LPG stove burns the gas fast, giving heat and light. That is rapid combustion.

quiz.q: White phosphorus burning at room temperature:
quiz.why: White phosphorus catches fire at room temperature without any outside heat. That is spontaneous combustion.
CO₂ extinguishers are best for electrical fires, since CO₂ does not conduct electricity and does not damage equipment. Water conducts electricity.

quiz.q: Water should not be used on oil fires because:
options: Oil floats on water and keeps burning
quiz.why: Oil is lighter than water, so it floats on it. Water would just spread the burning oil.

quiz.q: Firecrackers bursting with sound is an:
quiz.why: A firecracker releases a lot of gas and heat suddenly, with a loud sound. That is an explosion.

scenes.text: A goldsmith blows air through a metal pipe into a flame.
He uses the outermost blue part to melt gold.
Different parts of a flame have different temperatures!

steps.title: Flame or no flame?
steps.body: Substances that **vaporise** while burning give flames (kerosene, molten wax). Charcoal and coke glow without a flame.

steps.title: Zones of a candle flame
steps.body:
- **Innermost zone (dark):** unburnt wax vapours; least hot.
- **Middle zone (luminous, yellow):** partial combustion; moderately hot; unburnt carbon particles glow and give light (a glass plate held here gets a black soot ring).
- **Outermost zone (non-luminous, blue):** complete combustion; **hottest** part. Goldsmiths use it to melt gold and silver.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Where to hold a test tube for fastest heating? → In the outermost (blue) zone — hottest.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: A glass slide held in the yellow zone turns black. Why? → Unburnt carbon particles (soot) from incomplete combustion deposit on it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the bright yellow part is the hottest (it's the blue outer zone).
- Thinking all fuels burn with a flame.

activity.prompt: Match the zone with its feature
pairs: Unburnt carbon from the middle zone

quiz.q: Hottest part of a candle flame:
quiz.why: The outermost zone of a flame is the hottest. Combustion there is complete, as plenty of oxygen is available.
Goldsmiths use the outermost zone of the flame because it is the hottest.
Charcoal burns without a flame because it does not vaporise. Wax, LPG and kerosene give off vapours that form a flame.

quiz.q: Yellow colour in a flame is due to:
quiz.why: The yellow colour is from tiny glowing particles of unburnt carbon. Complete combustion would give a blue flame.

quiz.q: Innermost zone of a flame contains:
quiz.why: The innermost zone of a flame has unburnt wax vapour. It is the least hot zone.

lessons.title: Fuels, calorific value and the environment

scenes.text: Nani cooked with cow-dung cakes and wood — smoky eyes, black pots.
Mum cooks with LPG — clean and quick.
LPG gives far more heat per kg and much less smoke.

steps.title: A good fuel
steps.body:
- Readily available and cheap
- Burns easily in air at a moderate rate
- Produces a large amount of heat
- Leaves no undesirable substances (little smoke/ash, few pollutants)

No fuel is ideal; choose based on use.

steps.title: Calorific value
steps.body:
Heat produced by complete combustion of **1 kg** of fuel, measured in **kJ/kg**. Approximate values:

- Cow-dung cake 6,000–8,000 · Wood 17,000–22,000 · Coal 25,000–33,000
- Petrol, kerosene, diesel ~45,000 · Methane, CNG ~50,000 · LPG ~55,000
- Biogas 35,000–40,000 · **Hydrogen ~1,50,000** (highest)

steps.title: Harmful effects of burning fuels
steps.body:
- Unburnt carbon particles cause respiratory problems (e.g. asthma).
- Incomplete combustion gives **carbon monoxide (CO)**, a very poisonous gas — never sleep in a closed room with a coal fire.
- Excess **CO₂** contributes to **global warming** (rise in Earth's temperature), melting glaciers, sea-level rise.
- **Sulphur dioxide** and **nitrogen oxides** dissolve in rain to form **acid rain**, harming crops, buildings and soil.
- Cleaner fuels like CNG produce harmful products in much smaller amounts.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
4.5 kg of a fuel completely burnt gives 1,80,000 kJ of heat. Calorific value?

- 180000 ÷ 4.5 = 40,000 kJ/kg (in the biogas range).

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why is it dangerous to burn coal in a closed room? → Limited oxygen gives incomplete combustion, producing carbon monoxide which can kill a sleeping person.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying CO₂ is the poisonous gas from incomplete burning — it is CO.
- Calorific value is per kg, not per litre or per item.

activity.prompt: A fuel releases 1,25,000 kJ when 2.5 kg burns completely. Calorific value?

quiz.q: Fuel with the highest calorific value:
quiz.why: Hydrogen has the highest calorific value, about 150,000 kJ/kg. It gives the most heat per kilogram.
Calorific value is the heat produced by burning 1 kg of fuel, so the unit is kJ/kg.
Incomplete combustion gives carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas.

quiz.q: Acid rain is caused by oxides of:
quiz.why: Oxides of sulphur and nitrogen dissolve in rain water and make acid rain.

quiz.q: Excess CO₂ in air leads to:
quiz.why: Too much CO₂ traps heat in the atmosphere, which leads to global warming.

questions.q: Combustion needs:
questions.why: Burning needs fuel, air (oxygen) and heat to reach the ignition temperature. These three are the fire triangle.

questions.q: Hottest zone of a flame:
questions.why: The outer blue zone of a flame is the hottest, because combustion is complete there.

questions.q: Which is NOT combustible?
questions.why: Glass does not burn. Kerosene, paper and wood are combustible.

questions.q: Best fire extinguisher for electrical equipment:
questions.why: CO₂ is best for electrical fires, since it does not conduct electricity. Water could cause shocks.

questions.q: Calorific value is measured in:
questions.why: Calorific value is heat energy per kilogram of fuel, so it is measured in kJ/kg.

questions.q: Assertion: Water should not be used to extinguish burning oil. Reason: Oil is lighter than water and floats on it.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: water should not be used on burning oil. R is true: oil is lighter than water and floats on it, so burning oil would spread. R explains A.

questions.q: Spontaneous combustion example:
questions.why: White phosphorus burning at room temperature, with no external ignition, is spontaneous combustion.

questions.q: Gas causing acid rain:
questions.why: Sulphur dioxide dissolves in rain water to form acids. It is a main cause of acid rain.

questions.q: A fuel gives 3,60,000 kJ from 8 kg. Calorific value:
questions.why: Calorific value = heat produced ÷ mass = 3,60,000 kJ ÷ 8 kg = 45,000 kJ/kg.

questions.q: Why does a paper cup with water not burn on a flame?
options: Water takes away heat; paper stays below ignition temperature
questions.why: The water takes heat from the paper, so it stays below its ignition temperature. The paper does not burn.

questions.q: Case: A family sleeps in a closed room with a coal angithi burning for warmth. The main danger:
questions.why: A coal fire in a closed room burns with limited air, giving carbon monoxide. This poisonous gas is the main danger.

questions.q: Why do CO₂ extinguishers work well?
options: CO₂ is heavier than air and blankets the fire
questions.why: CO₂ is heavier than air and covers the fire like a blanket, cutting off oxygen. It also cools the fire.

questions.q: Which zone gives light in a candle flame?
questions.why: The middle zone is the luminous zone, which gives light. The glowing particles of carbon are in it.

questions.q: Assertion: A matchstick doesn't catch fire on its own at room temperature. Reason: Its ignition temperature is higher than room temperature.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: a matchstick does not catch fire at room temperature. R is true: its ignition temperature is higher than room temperature, so heat from friction is needed. R explains A.

questions.q: Which fuel choice is best for both heat output and low pollution for a city kitchen?
questions.why: LPG has a high calorific value and burns cleanly with little smoke. Wood, coal and dung cakes give more smoke.

questions.q: Why is hydrogen not commonly used as household fuel despite its high calorific value?
options: It is difficult and risky to store and transport
questions.why: Hydrogen burns explosively and is hard to store and carry safely. That is why it is not used in homes.

questions.q: Global warming may cause:
options: Melting of polar ice and rising sea levels
questions.why: Global warming melts polar ice and raises sea levels. It also thins glaciers.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Conservation of Plants and Animals
courses.summary: Deforestation and its effects, protected areas (biosphere reserves, wildlife sanctuaries, national parks), flora, fauna and endemic species with the Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve as a case study, endangered species and the Red Data Book, migration, paper recycling and reforestation.
outcomes: Learners can explain causes and consequences of deforestation
Learners can distinguish biosphere reserve, wildlife sanctuary and national park
Learners can define flora, fauna, endemic and endangered species with examples
Learners can suggest conservation actions like recycling paper and reforestation

scenes.text: Ten years ago Kabir's village had a dense grove; now there are fields and a highway.
Summers feel hotter, the stream dries up early, and rain washes topsoil away.
Is it connected? Yes — deforestation.

steps.title: Causes
steps.body: Clearing forests for other uses is **deforestation**. Causes: procuring land for cultivation, building houses and factories, making furniture or using wood as fuel; natural causes include forest fires and severe droughts.

steps.title: Consequences
steps.body:
- Higher temperature and more pollution; more CO₂ in the atmosphere (fewer trees to absorb it) → global warming.
- Lower groundwater level; disturbed water cycle → less rainfall → **droughts**.
- **Soil erosion**: without roots, topsoil is removed; fertile land can turn into desert — **desertification**.
- Decreased water-holding capacity of soil; more **floods**.
- Loss of habitat for wildlife.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: How does deforestation reduce rainfall? → Trees release water vapour by transpiration and help form clouds; fewer trees → less transpiration → less rain.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: How can deforestation lead to floods? → Roots hold soil and help water soak in; without them, rainwater runs off quickly into rivers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking deforestation affects only animals — it affects climate, water and soil for people too.
- Confusing desertification (land becoming desert) with deforestation (cutting forests).

activity.prompt: Order the chain of effects of large-scale deforestation
items: Trees are cut down
Less transpiration and fewer roots holding soil
Rainfall decreases and topsoil erodes
Soil loses fertility and water-holding capacity
Land may turn into desert (desertification)

quiz.why: Clearing forests is deforestation. Afforestation and reforestation mean planting trees.
A forest fire is a natural cause of deforestation. Furniture, roads and farming are human causes.

quiz.q: Conversion of fertile land into desert:
quiz.why: The change of fertile land into desert is desertification.
With fewer trees to absorb carbon dioxide, more CO₂ stays in the air.

options: Less water soaks into the soil
quiz.why: Without trees, less rain soaks into the soil and more runs off. So the groundwater level falls.

lessons.title: Protected areas: biosphere reserves, sanctuaries, national parks

scenes.text: Class 8 visits Pachmarhi in the Satpura hills.
The guide says this whole region is a biosphere reserve with a national park and two sanctuaries inside.
'Here, plants, animals and local people's ways of life are all protected.'

steps.title: Three kinds of protected areas
steps.body:
- **Wildlife sanctuary:** area where animals are protected from disturbance; killing (poaching) or capturing animals is prohibited. People may live nearby; some activities like grazing may be allowed under rules.
- **National park:** large area reserved for wildlife where they freely use habitats and natural resources; protects whole ecosystems (flora, fauna, landscape, historic objects).
- **Biosphere reserve:** large protected area for conserving biodiversity — plants, animals, microorganisms — and also the traditional life of tribals living there. It may contain national parks and sanctuaries.

steps.title: Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve (Madhya Pradesh)
steps.body: Contains **Satpura National Park** and the **Bori** and **Pachmarhi Wildlife Sanctuaries**. Satpura has some of India's finest teak. Rock shelters with ancient paintings show the presence of early humans; they also show animals and people as they lived then.

steps.title: Other well-known examples
steps.body: Project Tiger (1973) aims to protect tigers; tiger reserves include several national parks. Other famous national parks include Jim Corbett (Uttarakhand), Kaziranga (Assam — one-horned rhinoceros) and Gir (Gujarat — Asiatic lion).

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Where can local tribal people continue traditional life along with conservation? → In a biosphere reserve, which protects both biodiversity and culture.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why are national parks better for whole ecosystems than zoos? → Animals live in natural habitats with natural food chains; zoos protect individuals but not ecosystems.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a biosphere reserve is smaller than a national park (it is usually larger and may contain parks and sanctuaries).
- Mixing up Kaziranga (rhino) and Gir (lion).

activity.prompt: Match the protected area or project with its feature
pairs: Animals protected from hunting and capture

quiz.why: Satpura National Park is part of the Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve in Madhya Pradesh.

quiz.q: Area that protects biodiversity and tribal culture:
quiz.why: A biosphere reserve protects biodiversity and also the traditional life of the people living there.
Project Tiger was launched in 1973 to protect tigers.

options: Illegal killing or capturing of animals
quiz.why: Poaching is illegal killing or capturing of animals, which is banned in protected areas.

quiz.q: Gir National Park is famous for:
quiz.why: Gir National Park in Gujarat is famous for the Asiatic lion.

lessons.title: Flora, fauna, endemic and endangered species

scenes.text: The guide lists sal and wild mango, then bison and the Indian giant squirrel.
'These are endemic to this area — found naturally only here.'
'Some species elsewhere are endangered — numbers so low they could vanish.'

steps.title: Flora and fauna
steps.body: Plants of an area are its **flora**; animals are its **fauna**. In Pachmarhi: flora — sal, teak, mango, jamun, silver ferns, arjun; fauna — chinkara, blue bull, barking deer, cheetal, leopard, wild dog, wolf.

steps.title: Endemic species
steps.body: Species found **exclusively** in a particular area (state, region, country) are **endemic**. In Pachmarhi, sal and wild mango are examples of endemic flora; bison, Indian giant squirrel and flying squirrel are endemic fauna. Destroying their habitat endangers them.

steps.title: Endangered and extinct; Red Data Book
steps.body:
- **Endangered:** numbers diminishing to a level that they might face extinction (e.g. tiger, which was once very threatened).
- **Extinct:** no longer exist (e.g. dinosaurs).
- **Red Data Book:** a source book keeping a record of all endangered animals and plants. It is maintained internationally (by the IUCN); India also maintains records for its own species.
- **Ecosystem:** all plants, animals and microorganisms of an area together with non-living components like climate, soil, river, deltas.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Why does protecting one endangered species help many others? → Saving its habitat protects the whole food chain and ecosystem it lives in.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Is a species endemic to India found naturally in Australia? → No — endemic means found naturally only in that area.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Endangered ≠ extinct.
- Endemic ≠ 'rare' — endemic is about location, though endemic species are often vulnerable.

cards.back: Found naturally only in a particular area
Numbers so low they may face extinction
Record of endangered plants and animals

quiz.q: Plants of a particular area are its:
quiz.why: The plants of a particular area are called its flora. Its animals are the fauna.
Endemic species are found only in a particular area, and nowhere else.
The Red Data Book lists endangered species. It is kept by the IUCN.
Dinosaurs no longer exist, so they are extinct animals.

quiz.q: Which is endemic fauna of Pachmarhi?
quiz.why: The Indian giant squirrel is among the endemic fauna recorded in the Pachmarhi reserve. Kangaroos, penguins and pandas are not found in India.

scenes.text: Every winter, birds fly thousands of km to Indian wetlands.
Meanwhile, Meera's school collects old notebooks for recycling.
And the eco-club plants saplings on the school boundary.

steps.title: Migration
steps.body: **Migratory birds** fly to far-away areas every year at a particular time because of climatic changes — e.g. to lay eggs, as the weather in their natural habitat becomes very cold and inhospitable. Example: Siberian cranes historically visited Indian wetlands in winter.

steps.title: Recycling paper
steps.body: It takes about **17 full-grown trees** to make **one tonne** of paper. Paper can be recycled **five to seven times** for use. Saving and recycling paper saves trees, energy and water, and reduces harmful chemicals used in paper-making.

steps.title: Reforestation
steps.body: Restocking destroyed forests by planting new trees (of the same species found there, ideally). Natural reforestation also happens if a deforested area is left undisturbed. India's **Forest (Conservation) Act** aims to preserve and conserve natural forests and to meet the basic needs of people living in or near forests.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: A school uses 2 tonnes of paper a year. Trees saved if it is all recycled once? → About 2 × 17 = 34 trees.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why plant native species in reforestation? → They suit local soil and climate and support local wildlife.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking birds migrate only for food; climate and breeding are key reasons.
- Thinking paper can be recycled endlessly (fibres shorten; about 5–7 times).

activity.prompt: Eco-club actions — tick what you'll do this month
items: Use both sides of paper
Collect old newspapers and notebooks for recycling
Plant and care for one native sapling
Carry a cloth bag instead of plastic
Tell your family three facts about endangered animals

quiz.q: Trees needed for one tonne of paper (approx.):
quiz.why: About 17 full-grown trees are needed to make one tonne of paper, as in the textbook.
Paper can be recycled about 5 to 7 times, since its fibres get weaker each time.

quiz.q: Restocking destroyed forests by planting trees:
quiz.why: Replanting trees in areas where forests were destroyed is reforestation.

quiz.q: Birds fly long distances every year mainly because of:
quiz.why: Birds migrate long distances mainly because of changes in climate and to breed.

options: Preserve natural forests and meet forest-dwellers' needs
quiz.why: The Forest (Conservation) Act aims to protect natural forests while meeting the needs of the forest dwellers.

questions.q: Animals of an area are its:
questions.why: The animals of an area are called its fauna. Its plants are the flora.

questions.q: Satpura National Park is in:
questions.why: Satpura National Park is in Madhya Pradesh, as part of the Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve.

questions.q: Species found only in one area:
questions.why: A species found only in one particular area is endemic.

questions.q: Desertification is a result of:
questions.why: Cutting trees loosens the topsoil, which is then washed or blown away. This can turn the land into desert.

questions.q: Red Data Book records:
questions.why: The Red Data Book records endangered species.

questions.q: Assertion: Deforestation can cause floods. Reason: Fewer roots means less water soaks into the soil.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: deforestation can cause floods. R is true: fewer roots means less water soaks in, so more runs off. R explains A.

questions.q: A biosphere reserve may contain:
questions.why: A biosphere reserve is a large area that can include national parks and sanctuaries.

questions.q: Project Tiger began in:
questions.why: Project Tiger began in 1973.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.why: Kaziranga in Assam is famous for the one-horned rhinoceros. The other pairs are wrong.

questions.q: Endemic flora of Pachmarhi includes:
questions.why: Sal and wild mango are among the flora of the Pachmarhi reserve. Coconut and rubber are from other regions.

questions.q: Case: A school recycles 5 tonnes of paper. Roughly how many full-grown trees are saved?
questions.why: About 17 trees are saved per tonne of paper. So 5 × 17 = 85 trees.

questions.q: Migratory birds come to India in winter mainly because:
options: Their natural habitats become very cold
questions.why: Migratory birds come to India in winter because their own habitats become too cold. They return when it warms up.

questions.q: Assertion: All endangered species are extinct. Reason: Endangered species are still alive but at risk.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is false: endangered species are still living but at risk of dying out. Extinct species are gone. R is true.

questions.q: Why do biosphere reserves include the traditional life of tribals?
options: To conserve culture along with biodiversity
questions.why: Biosphere reserves protect both nature and the traditional life of tribal people, so culture and biodiversity are conserved together.

questions.q: Which is the best long-term fix for a hillside losing topsoil after logging?
questions.why: Planting native trees brings back roots that hold the soil. This is reforestation.

questions.q: Case: A rare frog lives only in one valley. A dam will flood the valley. Which is most accurate?
options: The frog will migrate to Australia
The frog is endemic and may become extinct
It doesn't matter as it's not a tiger
questions.why: The frog is endemic, as it lives only in that valley. If the valley is flooded, it may become extinct.

questions.q: An ecosystem consists of:
options: All living things of an area and non-living components like soil and climate
questions.why: An ecosystem includes all the living things of an area together with non-living parts like soil, water and climate.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Reproduction in Animals
courses.summary: Why reproduction matters; sexual reproduction (reproductive organs, fertilisation, internal and external fertilisation, embryo and foetus development); viviparous and oviparous animals; metamorphosis; and asexual reproduction by budding and binary fission, with a note on cloning.
outcomes: Learners can name the parts of male and female reproductive systems and their roles, in factual scientific language
Learners can explain fertilisation, zygote, embryo and foetus
Learners can distinguish internal/external fertilisation and viviparous/oviparous animals
Learners can describe metamorphosis, budding and binary fission
courses.guardianNote: Covers reproduction in animals as in the Class 8 science syllabus: names of reproductive organs in scientific language, fertilisation, embryo development, IVF in one line, metamorphosis and asexual reproduction. Factual, non-explicit, no images beyond emoji; suitable for ages 12–14 and useful to discuss together at home.

scenes.text: A hen sits on her eggs; three weeks later, chicks hatch.
Under a microscope, a tiny Hydra grows a bump that becomes a new Hydra.
Two very different ways to make the next generation.

steps.title: Why reproduction?
steps.body:
Reproduction ensures the **continuation of a species** generation after generation. Two modes:

- **Sexual reproduction:** two parents; male and female **gametes** fuse.
- **Asexual reproduction:** only one parent; offspring are almost identical copies.

steps.title: Gametes
steps.body:
- Male gamete: **sperm** — a single cell with a head, middle piece and tail; it can swim.
- Female gamete: **ovum (egg)** — a single cell, much larger than a sperm.

Each sperm and egg is a single cell, yet a new individual develops from their fusion.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Classify: a calf born to a cow; a new Amoeba splitting from one Amoeba. → Calf: sexual. Amoeba: asexual.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why does a sperm have a tail? → To swim (move) towards the egg.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking eggs are always large like hens' eggs; a human ovum is microscopic.
- Thinking asexual reproduction needs two parents.

activity.prompt: Sexual or asexual?

quiz.why: Reproduction produces new individuals of the same kind, so the species continues from generation to generation.
The male gamete is the sperm. The female gamete is the ovum (egg).

quiz.q: Number of parents in asexual reproduction:
quiz.why: Asexual reproduction needs only one parent.
The ovum is a single cell.

quiz.q: The tail of a sperm helps it to:
quiz.why: The tail of a sperm helps it swim and move towards the egg.

scenes.text: Ms Rao draws simple labelled diagrams on the board, in scientific words.
'Every body part has a proper name — we use them respectfully,' she says.
'Today: how life begins with one cell.'

steps.title: Male reproductive organs
steps.body:
- A pair of **testes** — produce **sperms** (millions of them).
- Two **sperm ducts** — carry sperms.
- **Penis** — the organ through which sperms are transferred.

steps.title: Female reproductive organs
steps.body:
- A pair of **ovaries** — produce **ova (eggs)**; in humans usually one mature egg is released by one of the ovaries every month.
- Two **oviducts (fallopian tubes)** — carry the egg; fertilisation happens here.
- **Uterus** — where the baby develops.

steps.title: Fertilisation
steps.body:
The fusion of a sperm and an egg is **fertilisation**; it produces a **zygote** (one cell) — the beginning of a new individual. The zygote receives one set of characteristics from the mother and one from the father, which is why children resemble both parents.

- **Internal fertilisation:** fusion inside the female's body (humans, cows, dogs, hens).
- **External fertilisation:** fusion outside the body, usually in water (frogs, fish, starfish). These animals lay hundreds of eggs because many are washed away, eaten or not fertilised.
- **IVF (in vitro fertilisation):** for some couples, eggs and sperms are fused outside the body in a laboratory and the early embryo is placed in the mother's uterus. Babies born this way are popularly called 'test-tube babies' — a misleading name, as the baby grows in the mother's uterus.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Why do frogs lay hundreds of eggs? → Fertilisation is external; many eggs and sperms are lost to water movement, wind, rain or predators.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Where does fertilisation take place in humans? → In the oviduct (fallopian tube).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the baby grows in the ovary (it grows in the uterus).
- Thinking 'test-tube babies' grow in a test tube.

activity.prompt: Match the organ to its function

quiz.why: The fusion of a sperm and an egg is fertilisation.
The cell formed by fertilisation is the zygote.
Frogs and fish release eggs and sperm into water, where they fuse. That is external fertilisation.
The ovaries are the female organs that produce eggs.

quiz.q: In IVF, the baby develops in:
quiz.why: In IVF, fertilisation happens in a laboratory, but the embryo is then placed in the mother's uterus, where the baby grows.

lessons.title: Development: embryo, foetus; viviparous and oviparous

scenes.text: A hen's fertilised egg is kept warm by her body.
After about three weeks a chick hatches.
In humans, a baby develops inside the mother for about nine months.

steps.title: Development of the embryo
steps.body: The zygote divides repeatedly to form a ball of cells that develops into an **embryo**, which gets embedded in the wall of the uterus. It continues to develop: body parts like hands, legs, head, eyes and ears form. The stage of the embryo in which all body parts can be identified is the **foetus**. When development is complete, the mother gives birth.

steps.title: Hens
steps.body: In hens, after fertilisation the zygote divides as it travels down the oviduct; protective layers and the **hard shell** form around it. The hen then lays the egg; the embryo takes about **3 weeks** to develop into a chick, which hatches from the shell. (Unfertilised eggs sold in shops do not develop into chicks.)

steps.title: Viviparous and oviparous
steps.body:
- **Viviparous:** give birth to young ones — humans, cows, dogs, cats.
- **Oviparous:** lay eggs — hen, frog, lizard, butterfly, fish, most birds and reptiles.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Classify: dog, crow, lizard, cat, frog. → Viviparous: dog, cat. Oviparous: crow, lizard, frog.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why can't hatching chicks be seen from eggs bought in shops? → Those are usually unfertilised eggs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the very early embryo a foetus — 'foetus' is the stage when body parts are identifiable.
- Thinking all animals that live in water lay eggs (whales and dolphins are viviparous mammals).

activity.prompt: Viviparous or oviparous?

quiz.q: The stage when all body parts can be identified:
quiz.why: When all the body parts can be identified, the developing baby is called a foetus.
Animals that lay eggs are oviparous. 'Ovi' means egg.

quiz.q: A hen's egg takes about how long to hatch?
quiz.why: A hen's egg takes about 3 weeks to hatch when kept warm.
A cat gives birth to its young, so it is viviparous. Snakes, frogs and crows lay eggs.

quiz.q: The hard shell of a hen's egg forms:
options: After fertilisation, as the zygote moves down the oviduct
quiz.why: The zygote starts to divide as it moves down the oviduct, and protective layers form around it. The hard shell is added after fertilisation.

scenes.text: Class 8 keeps tadpoles in a tank (and later releases the frogs).
Week by week, legs appear and the tail shrinks.
Under a microscope, an Amoeba simply splits into two.

steps.title: Metamorphosis
steps.body:
Transformation of a larva into an adult through **drastic changes** is **metamorphosis**.

- Frog: egg → **tadpole** (larva) → adult frog.
- Silkworm: egg → larva (caterpillar) → **pupa** → adult moth.

Humans do not undergo metamorphosis: a baby has the same body parts as an adult.

steps.title: Asexual reproduction
steps.body:
- **Budding (Hydra):** a bulge (bud) grows from the parent body, develops into a new individual and detaches.
- **Binary fission (Amoeba):** the nucleus divides into two, then the body divides, producing two Amoebae.

steps.title: Cloning (extension)
steps.body: **Cloning** produces an exact copy of a cell, part or whole organism. **Dolly the sheep**, born in 1996 in Scotland, was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell (by Ian Wilmut and colleagues). Dolly was genetically identical to the sheep whose cell nucleus was used. Cloning of animals is difficult and raises important ethical questions.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Is the tadpole a fish? → No; it is the larval stage of a frog, living in water with a tail and gills before metamorphosis.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why are Amoeba offspring identical to the parent? → Only one parent; the nucleus simply divides, so no mixing of characteristics.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling binary fission 'budding'.
- Saying human babies undergo metamorphosis.

activity.prompt: Order the life cycle of a frog
items: Eggs laid in water
Eggs fertilised outside the body
Tadpoles hatch
Tadpoles grow legs; tail shrinks
Adult frog

quiz.why: Hydra reproduces asexually by budding. A bud grows on its body and then separates.
Amoeba reproduces by binary fission. It splits into two daughter cells.
The tadpole is the larva of a frog.

quiz.q: Dolly was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell. She was a:
quiz.why: Dolly was a sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, in 1996.

quiz.q: Drastic change from larva to adult:
quiz.why: The change from a larva to an adult, as from a tadpole to a frog, is metamorphosis.

questions.q: Female gamete:
questions.why: The female gamete is the ovum, or egg.

questions.q: Sperms are produced in:
questions.why: Sperms are made in the testes, the male reproductive organs.

questions.q: Which animal is oviparous?
questions.why: A lizard lays eggs, so it is oviparous. Cows, dogs and humans give birth to young.

questions.q: Fertilisation produces a:
questions.why: Fertilisation produces a zygote.

questions.q: Hydra reproduces by:
questions.why: Hydra reproduces by budding.

questions.q: External fertilisation is seen in:
questions.why: Fish have external fertilisation, in water. Humans, cows and hens have internal fertilisation.

questions.q: Assertion: Frogs lay hundreds of eggs. Reason: In external fertilisation many eggs are lost or not fertilised.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: frogs lay hundreds of eggs. R is true: in external fertilisation many eggs are lost or not fertilised, so many are needed. R explains A.

questions.q: In humans, fertilisation takes place in the:
