questions.why: In humans fertilisation takes place in the oviduct (Fallopian tube).

questions.q: The embryo gets embedded in the wall of the:
questions.why: The embryo gets attached to the wall of the uterus, where it grows.

questions.q: Which pair is WRONG?
questions.why: Amoeba reproduces by binary fission, not budding. The other pairs are correct.

questions.q: Case: A couple cannot have a baby because the woman's oviducts are blocked. Doctors suggest IVF. Where does fertilisation occur in IVF?
options: Outside the body in a laboratory
questions.why: In IVF the egg and sperm are joined outside the body in a laboratory. The word 'in vitro' means in glass.

questions.q: Silkworm life cycle order:
questions.why: A silkworm goes through egg, larva, pupa and adult stages.

questions.q: Why do children resemble both parents?
options: The zygote gets characteristics from both
questions.why: The zygote gets characteristics from both parents, as it is formed from the egg and the sperm. So children resemble both.

questions.q: Assertion: Human babies undergo metamorphosis. Reason: Body parts of a baby are similar to those of adults.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is false: human babies do not go through metamorphosis. R is true: a baby's body parts are similar to an adult's, just smaller.

questions.q: Dolly the sheep was genetically identical to:
options: The sheep whose cell nucleus was used
questions.why: Dolly was made using the nucleus of a cell from one sheep. So she was genetically identical to that sheep.

questions.q: Why are hens' eggs from shops usually unable to hatch?
questions.why: Eggs sold in shops are usually unfertilised, with no zygote. So they cannot hatch.

questions.q: Which is the correct sequence?
questions.why: The order is zygote, embryo, foetus, then baby.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Reaching the Age of Adolescence
courses.summary: Adolescence and puberty: physical, emotional and mental changes in boys and girls, secondary sexual characters, hormones and endocrine glands, the menstrual cycle, how the sex of a baby is determined, and reproductive health — nutrition, hygiene, exercise, and saying no to drugs.
outcomes: Learners can describe the changes at puberty in both boys and girls calmly and accurately
Learners can explain the role of hormones and the main endocrine glands
Learners can explain the menstrual cycle and sex determination in humans
Learners can plan for nutrition, hygiene and wellbeing, and know where to get help
courses.guardianNote: Covers puberty in boys and girls, hormones, menstruation (including period care and myths), sex determination, nutrition, hygiene, drug refusal and basic HIV facts, as in the Class 8 science syllabus. Language is factual, calm and non-explicit, aligned with UNESCO ITGSE 2018 and WHO guidance for ages 12–14. Helplines 1098, 14416 and 112 are included. Parents are encouraged to read along and invite questions.

scenes.text: Arjun's voice suddenly squeaks in class. Some kids laugh.
His friend Sana has grown 8 cm in a year and feels awkward.
Their teacher explains: 'These are normal changes of puberty. Everyone goes through them — at their own pace.'

steps.title: Adolescence and puberty
steps.body: The period of life when the body undergoes changes leading to reproductive maturity is **adolescence** — roughly **11 to 19 years** (the 'teens'). In girls it may begin a year or two earlier than in boys, and it varies from person to person. The changes that make a person capable of reproduction are called **puberty**.

steps.title: Physical changes
steps.body:
- **Increase in height:** a sudden growth spurt as long bones grow. Height and body proportions settle by the end of adolescence; initially hands and legs may look out of proportion — this evens out.
- **Change in body shape:** in boys, shoulders broaden and muscles grow more prominent; in girls, the region below the waist becomes wider.
- **Voice:** the larynx (voice box) grows. In boys it becomes a visible bump at the throat called the **Adam's apple**, and the voice becomes deeper (it may crack for a while). Girls' voices become higher-pitched.
- **Sweat and oil glands** become more active, so many teens get **acne (pimples)**.
- **Reproductive organs develop:** testes begin to produce sperms; ovaries enlarge and eggs begin to mature and be released.

steps.title: Emotional and mental changes
steps.body: Adolescents become more independent and self-conscious; the intellect develops and they think more deeply. Feelings may change quickly; feeling unsure or moody is common. Talking to trusted adults — parents, teachers, a school counsellor — helps.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Arjun's friends tease him about his voice. What is the science? → His larynx is growing; the voice deepens over time. It is normal and temporary — teasing is unkind.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Sana is taller than most boys in her class. Why? → Girls often start their growth spurt earlier; boys usually catch up later.

steps.title: Common mistakes and myths
steps.body:
- 'Everyone should change at the same age' — no, timing varies widely and is normal.
- 'Pimples mean you are dirty' — they're mostly due to hormones making oil glands active; gentle washing helps.

statements.s: Adolescence is roughly 11 to 19 years.
Puberty begins at exactly the same age for everyone.
statements.why: It varies from person to person.

statements.s: The Adam's apple is the growing larynx in boys.
Acne is caused by increased activity of sweat and oil glands.
Emotional ups and downs during adolescence mean something is wrong.

quiz.why: Adolescence is the period of growth and change that leads to reproductive maturity.

options: A fruit stuck in the throat
quiz.why: The Adam's apple is the enlarged voice box (larynx). It shows more in boys as it grows during puberty.

quiz.q: Pimples during adolescence are mainly due to:
quiz.why: During adolescence hormones make the oil and sweat glands more active. This can cause pimples, which are common and normal.

options: A year or two earlier than in boys
quiz.why: Puberty often starts a year or two earlier in girls than in boys. It varies from person to person.

quiz.q: Best response to a friend's worries about body changes:
options: Reassure them it's normal and suggest talking to a trusted adult
quiz.why: A kind response is to reassure a friend that these changes are normal and suggest talking to a trusted adult. Teasing hurts.

scenes.text: Nanhi asks, 'What starts all these changes?'
Her mother explains: 'A tiny gland below the brain sends signals; the body answers with hormones.'
Hormones are chemical messengers carried in the blood.

steps.title: Secondary sexual characters
steps.body:
Features that help tell mature males and females apart (other than reproductive organs):

- Both: hair grows in the armpits and in the pubic region (the area between the thighs).
- Boys: facial hair (moustache, beard) and hair on the chest.
- Girls: breasts develop.

steps.title: Hormones
steps.body:
These changes are controlled by **hormones** — chemical substances secreted by **endocrine glands** (ductless glands) directly into the blood, reaching target body parts.

- At puberty, the **testes** produce **testosterone** in boys, and the **ovaries** produce **estrogen** in girls.
- The production of these hormones is controlled by a hormone from the **pituitary gland**.

steps.title: Other endocrine glands
steps.body:
- **Thyroid** → thyroxine (lack of iodine in diet can cause **goitre**, a swollen neck).
- **Pancreas** → insulin (deficiency causes **diabetes**).
- **Adrenal** → adrenalin (helps the body deal with stress, anger, fear; also controls salt and water balance).
- **Pituitary** → growth hormone and hormones that control other glands.

In frogs, **thyroxine** (which needs iodine) is required for a tadpole to become an adult frog; insects too need hormones for metamorphosis.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: A person's neck is swollen and the doctor suspects thyroid problems. Which dietary element may be lacking? → Iodine (use iodised salt).

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why does your heart race before a big exam? → The adrenal glands release adrenalin, preparing the body to deal with stress.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying hormones travel through ducts — endocrine glands are ductless; hormones travel in blood.
- Mixing insulin (pancreas) with thyroxine (thyroid).

activity.prompt: Match the gland to its hormone

quiz.why: Hormones are released into the blood by ductless (endocrine) glands. The blood carries them to other parts of the body.

scenes.text: Meera, 12, notices a red stain and feels scared.
Her aunt hugs her: 'This is your first period — a healthy sign your body is growing up.'
Together they pack a small pouch with pads and a spare pair of underwear for school.

steps.title: The reproductive phase
steps.body: People become capable of reproduction after puberty. In women, the reproductive phase starts at puberty (about **10–12 years**) and generally lasts till about **45–50 years**.

steps.title: The menstrual cycle
steps.body:
- About once a month, an egg matures and is released by one of the ovaries.
- At the same time, the wall of the uterus thickens to be ready to receive a fertilised egg.
- If fertilisation does not occur, the egg and the thickened lining break down and flow out of the body along with blood. This is **menstruation (a period)**.
- The cycle repeats about every **28 to 30 days** (it can vary, and is often irregular in the first year or two).
- The first menstrual flow is **menarche**; stopping of menstruation at around 45–50 years is **menopause**.

steps.title: Period care
steps.body:
- Use a sanitary pad, cloth pad, tampon or menstrual cup — whatever is safe and comfortable; change pads regularly (often every 4–6 hours, or sooner if needed).
- Wash hands; bathe normally; wrap used pads and put them in the bin.
- Mild cramps are common; a warm water bottle, gentle movement and rest help.
- Sport, school, cooking, temples or touching things — periods don't make anyone 'impure' or weak; these are myths.
- See a doctor if bleeding is very heavy, lasts more than about 7 days, pain stops daily life, or periods haven't started by about 15.

steps.title: For boys too
steps.body: Boys also go through changes; many experience a 'wet dream' (night-time release of semen during sleep). It is completely normal and nothing to feel guilty or worried about. Boys should learn about periods too, so they can be respectful and supportive classmates and family members.

steps.title: Myths vs facts
steps.body:
- Myth: periods are dirty. Fact: menstrual blood is a normal body fluid.
- Myth: you can't exercise during periods. Fact: activity often eases cramps.
- Myth: talking about periods is shameful. Fact: accurate knowledge keeps everyone healthy.

activity.prompt: Questions young people often don't ask aloud

items.q: Is my cycle broken if it's not exactly 28 days?
items.a: No. 21–35 days is common, and the first couple of years are often irregular.

items.q: Can others tell I'm on my period?
items.a: Usually not. Carrying a small kit helps you feel prepared.

items.q: Is it OK for boys to learn about periods?
items.a: Yes — understanding prevents teasing and makes you a better friend and family member.

items.q: What if I have questions I feel shy to ask?
items.a: Ask a parent, school nurse, teacher or doctor. You can also call 1098 (Childline) or 14416 (Tele-MANAS) to talk confidentially.

quiz.why: The menstrual cycle repeats about every 28 to 30 days, though it can vary.

quiz.why: The first menstrual flow is called menarche.
Menstruation stops at about 45 to 50 years. This is called menopause.

options: The egg is not fertilised and the uterus lining breaks down
quiz.why: If the egg is not fertilised, the lining of the uterus breaks down and leaves the body. This is menstruation.

options: Periods are a normal body process
Girls must not play sports during periods

quiz.why: It is a myth that girls must not play sports during periods. Periods are a normal body process, and exercise is fine.

lessons.title: How is a baby's sex determined?

scenes.text: An aunt is blamed by relatives for 'only having daughters'.
Her son, studying science, explains chromosomes at dinner.
Everyone learns: the mother has no role in deciding the baby's sex.

steps.title: Chromosomes
steps.body:
Inside the nucleus of every human cell are thread-like **chromosomes** — **23 pairs**. Two of these are **sex chromosomes**: **X** and **Y**.

- Females: **XX**
- Males: **XY**

steps.title: How sex is determined
steps.body:
- Every egg (ovum) carries one **X** chromosome.
- Sperms are of two kinds: half carry **X**, half carry **Y**.
- Egg (X) + sperm with X → **XX** → girl.
- Egg (X) + sperm with Y → **XY** → boy.

So **the father's sperm determines the sex of the baby** — and it is a matter of chance. Blaming a mother for a child's sex is scientifically wrong and unfair. In India, finding out the sex of a foetus for sex selection is illegal.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: What are the chances of a baby being a girl? → About 1 in 2 each time (half the sperms carry X).

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: A zygote has XY. What will the baby be? → A boy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'The mother decides the sex' — false.
- Thinking eggs can carry Y — eggs always carry X.

activity.prompt: Complete the chromosome facts.
activity.text: Humans have ___ pairs of chromosomes. A female has ___ and a male has ___. The sex of the baby is determined by the chromosome in the ___ (egg/sperm).

quiz.why: A female has two X chromosomes, so her sex chromosomes are XX.
Every human egg carries an X chromosome.

quiz.q: A zygote with XY develops into:
quiz.why: A zygote with XY develops into a boy.

quiz.q: Who determines the sex of a baby?
options: The chromosome in the father's sperm
quiz.why: The sperm carries either X or Y, but the egg always carries X. So the father's sperm decides the sex of the baby.

quiz.q: Number of chromosome pairs in human cells:
quiz.why: Human cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes, which is 46 in total.

lessons.title: Reproductive health: food, hygiene, exercise, no drugs

scenes.text: At a school health fair, stalls show iron-rich foods, yoga and a 'say no to drugs' poster.
A doctor answers anonymous questions dropped in a box.
'Your health in these years builds the adult you'll become.'

steps.title: Nutritional needs
steps.body:
Adolescence is a period of rapid growth, so a **balanced diet** is essential: proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins and minerals (milk, pulses, cereals, green leafy vegetables, fruits, nuts, eggs/meat/fish if eaten).

- **Iron** builds blood — iron-rich foods (leafy vegetables, jaggery, amla, meat, citrus to help absorption) are especially important for adolescent girls to prevent anaemia.
- Avoid relying on chips, packaged snacks and sugary drinks.

steps.title: Hygiene and exercise
steps.body:
- Bathe daily, wash the face (acne), keep underarms and genitals clean, wear clean underwear; girls should maintain cleanliness during periods.
- Walking, sports, yoga and play keep the body fit and the mind happy.
- Sleep 8–10 hours.

steps.title: Say NO to drugs
steps.body:
Curiosity and peer pressure may push some teens towards drugs, tobacco or alcohol. Drugs are **addictive** and harm the body and mind. **Using injected drugs with shared needles** can spread **HIV**, which causes **AIDS**.

HIV spreads through: unprotected sexual contact with an infected person; infected blood/shared needles; from an infected mother to her baby (during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding). It does **not** spread by touching, hugging, sharing food, or mosquito bites.

steps.title: Where to get help
steps.body: If you feel pressured, unsafe, sad for a long time or confused, talk to a trusted adult. In India: **1098** (Childline, children in need of help), **14416** (Tele-MANAS mental-health helpline), **112** (all emergencies).

steps.title: Myths
steps.body:
- 'A girl becomes pregnant if a boy just touches her' — false.
- 'HIV spreads by shaking hands' — false.
- 'Drugs help you study' — false; they damage memory and health.

a.text: At a party, an older teen offers you a 'special' pill: 'Everyone's trying it, don't be a baby.'

choices.label: Say 'No thanks' firmly and move to friends you trust
choices.feedback: Strong choice — you can say no without explaining.

choices.label: Take it so they don't laugh
choices.feedback: Peer pressure is real, but your health is yours.

c.text: You feel dizzy and scared. What now?

choices.label: Tell a trusted adult immediately / call 112 if very unwell
choices.feedback: Getting help fast is the right move.

choices.label: Leave the place and tell a parent or teacher later
Argue for an hour
choices.feedback: You don't owe an argument — leaving is simpler.

e.text: Remember: real friends respect 'no'. Help is available — 1098, 14416, 112.

quiz.why: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin. Iron-rich food helps prevent anaemia, which is common in adolescent girls.
HIV spreads through infected blood, such as on shared needles. It also spreads by unprotected sex with an infected person and from an infected mother to her baby.

options: Unprotected sexual contact with an infected person
quiz.why: HIV does not spread by shaking hands, hugging or sharing food. It spreads only through blood, certain body fluids and from mother to child.
Childline is 1098, a free helpline for children who need help.

quiz.q: A balanced diet for adolescents should include:
options: Proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins and minerals
quiz.why: A balanced diet includes proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins and minerals. This is vital for growth in adolescence.

questions.q: Adolescence roughly spans:
questions.why: Adolescence roughly covers the ages of 11 to 19 years.

questions.q: Hormone produced by the ovaries:
questions.why: The ovaries make estrogen, the female hormone.

questions.q: Sex chromosomes of a male:
questions.why: A male has one X and one Y chromosome, so XY.

questions.q: Endocrine glands release hormones into:
questions.why: Endocrine glands have no ducts. They release hormones directly into the blood.

questions.q: Which gland controls production of sex hormones?
questions.why: The pituitary is the master gland. It controls other glands, including those that make sex hormones.

questions.q: Assertion: The father's sperm determines the sex of the baby. Reason: Sperms carry either X or Y while all eggs carry X.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is true: the sperm decides the baby's sex. R is true: sperms carry X or Y, but eggs always carry X. So R explains A.

questions.q: Menstrual cycle duration is about:
questions.why: The menstrual cycle lasts about 28 to 30 days, though it may vary.

questions.q: Goitre is caused by deficiency of:
questions.why: Goitre is caused by a lack of iodine, which the thyroid needs to make thyroxine.

questions.q: Adam's apple is the:
questions.why: The Adam's apple is the enlarged larynx (voice box) in the neck.

questions.q: Which hormone helps adjust to stress?
questions.why: Adrenalin is released by the adrenal glands. It helps the body to deal with stress, danger or fear.

questions.q: A tadpole fails to become a frog if water lacks iodine because:
questions.why: Thyroxine needs iodine to be made. It controls metamorphosis in frogs, so without it the tadpole cannot become a frog.

questions.q: Case: Ritu, 13, has irregular periods in her first year. Her mother worries. The best scientific response:
options: Irregular cycles are common at first; see a doctor if very heavy, very painful or prolonged
Periods should always be exactly 28 days
questions.why: Irregular periods are common in the first year or two. A doctor should be seen if they are very heavy, very painful or last long.

questions.q: Which is a secondary sexual character in boys?
questions.why: Facial hair is a secondary sexual character in boys. Ovulation, menstruation and breast development are in girls.

questions.q: HIV can spread from:
options: An infected mother to her baby
questions.why: HIV can pass from an infected mother to her baby. It does not spread by sharing a classroom, mosquito bites or swimming pools.

questions.q: Assertion: Acne in adolescence means poor hygiene. Reason: Hormones make oil glands more active during adolescence.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: A is false: acne during adolescence is mainly hormonal, not a sign of poor hygiene. R is true: hormones make the oil glands more active.

questions.q: A zygote formed from a sperm carrying X will develop into:
questions.why: A sperm with X joins an egg with X, giving XX, which is a girl.

questions.q: Case: A friend says he's been feeling hopeless for weeks and won't eat. Best action:
options: Tell him to stop being dramatic
Encourage him to talk to a trusted adult or counsellor and share the 14416 helpline; tell an adult if he's at risk
questions.why: Feeling hopeless for weeks and not eating needs help. Encourage him to talk to a trusted adult or counsellor, share the helpline 14416, and tell an adult if he may be at risk. Do not keep it secret.

questions.q: The reproductive phase of women generally lasts from:
questions.why: A woman's reproductive phase runs from puberty (about 10–12 years) to menopause (about 45–50 years).
